title: Qaṭr al-nadā
author: Ibn Hishām
subject: nahw
summary: Qaṭr al-nadā wa-ball al-ṣadā, “the drop of dew and the quenching of thirst”, is the short matn of naḥw by Ibn Hishām al-Anṣārī of Cairo (d. 761/1360), who explained it himself in his Sharḥ Qaṭr al-nadā. At al-Azhar and in the North-African madrasas it is read after the Ājurrūmiyya and before the Alfiyya: it covers the whole of naḥw again, more closely, with the conditions of each rule, the views of the grammarians where they differ, and many verses of the Qurʾān as examples. It runs from the word and iʿrāb through the muḍāriʿ, the definite noun, the sentence and what annuls it, the doer and its deputy, the objects and the other words in naṣb, khafḍ, the words that work like verbs and the followers, to number, the diptote, wonder, the pause and the hamza of connection. The lessons follow an Indian lithograph of the matn of 1261/1845, a passage or a few at a time.

lessons.title: The word and its kinds; the inflected and the fixed noun
body: Ibn Hishām opens with the shortest definition he can give: “the word (kalima) is a single utterance (qawl mufrad)”. An utterance (qawl) is a sound that means something; “single” (mufrad) leaves out a phrase such as ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”, which is two words. There are three kinds of word and no more: the noun, the verb and the particle (ism, fiʿl, ḥarf).

The noun has three signs: al- (al-rajul, “the man”), tanwīn (rajulun, “a man”) and “being spoken about” (al-ḥadīth ʿanhu): only a noun can be the thing of which something is said. The third sign does work the other two cannot. The tāʾ of ḍarabtu, “I hit”, takes neither al- nor tanwīn, but it is the one of whom the hitting is said, so it is a noun: a pronoun. The Ājurrūmiyya counted khafḍ and the particles of khafḍ among the signs; Ibn Hishām's third sign reaches the pronouns as well.

The noun is either inflected (muʿrab), “that whose end changes because of the governors that come upon it”, as Zaydun, Zaydan, Zaydin, or fixed (mabnī), which keeps one ending whatever governs it. The fixed noun keeps one of four endings, and the book gives each its examples: the kasra (hāʾulāʾi, “these”; Ḥadhāmi, a woman's name, and amsi, “yesterday”, in the speech of the Ḥijāz); the fatḥa (aḥada ʿashara, “eleven”, and the numbers with it up to nineteen); the ḍamma (qablu, “before”, baʿdu, “after”, and words like them); and the sukūn (man, “who”, kam, “how many”). The sukūn is “the origin of bināʾ”: the commentators explain that the lightest state suits the word that does not change.

Two conditions hide in these examples. Ḥadhāmi and amsi are fixed only for the people of the Ḥijāz; the Banū Tamīm inflect them, as the chapter on the diptote will say (lesson 46). And qablu and baʿdu are fixed on the ḍamma only “when the muḍāf ilayhi is dropped and its meaning is intended”: li-llāhi al-amru min qablu wa-min baʿdu, “the matter is God's, before and after” (Q 30:4), that is, before and after the victory. When the noun after them is spoken, they are inflected: min qabli dhālika, “before that”.

terms.en: the word: a single utterance
inflected: its end changes with the governors
fixed: it keeps one ending
being spoken about: the sign of the noun that reaches the pronouns

examples.en: al-rajul, rajulun, the tāʾ of ḍarabtu: the three signs of the noun
hāʾulāʾi, fixed on the kasra; aḥada ʿashara, fixed on the fatḥa
man and kam, fixed on the sukūn, “the origin of bināʾ”

tasks.prompt: Why is the tāʾ of ḍarabtu a noun, though it takes neither al- nor tanwīn?
tasks.answer: It has the third sign: something is said of it. It is the one who did the hitting, so the hitting is “spoken about” it. Only a noun can be that.

tasks.prompt: On what is each word fixed: hāʾulāʾi; aḥada ʿashara; man; qablu in min qablu?
tasks.arabic: هَؤُلَاءِ — أَحَدَ عَشَرَ — مَنْ — مِنْ قَبْلُ
tasks.answer: Hāʾulāʾi on the kasra; aḥada ʿashara on the fatḥa; man on the sukūn; qablu on the ḍamma, because the word it was joined to is dropped and its meaning intended.

tasks.prompt: Why does the book say that amsi is fixed “in the speech of the people of the Ḥijāz”?
tasks.answer: Because the Banū Tamīm treat it otherwise: they inflect it (as a diptote when it is in rafʿ), as the chapter on the diptote says. Only in the Ḥijāz does it keep the kasra in every state.

quiz.prompt: The word (kalima) is…
options: an utterance that conveys a full meaning
quiz.explanation: Qawl mufrad: “single” leaves out phrases and sentences.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of word are there?
quiz.explanation: Noun, verb and particle.

quiz.prompt: By which sign is the tāʾ of ḍarabtu known to be a noun?
quiz.explanation: Something is said of it: it is the one who hit.

quiz.prompt: The inflected (muʿrab) noun is the one whose end…
quiz.explanation: As Zaydun, Zaydan, Zaydin.

quiz.prompt: Hāʾulāʾi is fixed on…
quiz.explanation: It keeps the kasra in every state.

quiz.prompt: Which ending is “the origin of bināʾ”?
quiz.explanation: As in man and kam.

quiz.prompt: When is qablu fixed on the ḍamma?
options: When its muḍāf ilayhi is dropped and its meaning intended
quiz.explanation: Min qablu (Q 30:4); but min qabli dhālika is inflected.

text.original: الْكَلِمَةُ قَوْلٌ مُفْرَدٌ، وَهِيَ اسْمٌ وَفِعْلٌ وَحَرْفٌ.
text.en: The word (kalima) is a single utterance (qawl mufrad). It is a noun (ism), a verb (fiʿl) or a particle (ḥarf).

text.original: فَأَمَّا الِاسْمُ فَيُعْرَفُ بِأَلْ كَالرَّجُلِ، وَبِالتَّنْوِينِ كَرَجُلٍ، وَبِالْحَدِيثِ عَنْهُ كَتَاءِ ضَرَبْتُ. وَهُوَ ضَرْبَانِ: مُعْرَبٌ، وَهُوَ مَا يَتَغَيَّرُ آخِرُهُ بِسَبَبِ الْعَوَامِلِ الدَّاخِلَةِ عَلَيْهِ كَزَيْدٍ، وَمَبْنِيٌّ، وَهُوَ بِخِلَافِهِ،
text.en: The noun is known by al-, as al-rajul “the man”; by tanwīn, as rajulin “a man”; and by being spoken about, as the tāʾ of ḍarabtu “I hit”. It is of two kinds: inflected (muʿrab), which is that whose end changes because of the governors (ʿawāmil) that come upon it, as Zayd; and with a fixed ending (mabnī), which is the opposite of that,

text.original: كَهَؤُلَاءِ فِي لُزُومِ الْكَسْرِ، وَكَذَلِكَ حَذَامِ وَأَمْسِ فِي لُغَةِ الْحِجَازِيِّينَ، وَكَأَحَدَ عَشَرَ وَأَخَوَاتِهِ فِي لُزُومِ الْفَتْحِ، وَكَقَبْلُ وَبَعْدُ وَأَخَوَاتِهِمَا فِي لُزُومِ الضَّمِّ إِذَا حُذِفَ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ وَنُوِيَ مَعْنَاهُ، وَكَمَنْ وَكَمْ فِي لُزُومِ السُّكُونِ، وَهُوَ أَصْلُ الْبِنَاءِ.
text.en: as hāʾulāʾi “these”, in keeping always to the kasra, and likewise Ḥadhāmi [a woman's name] and amsi “yesterday” in the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz; as aḥada ʿashara “eleven” and its sisters, in keeping always to the fatḥa; as qablu “before”, baʿdu “after” and their sisters, in keeping always to the ḍamma when the muḍāf ilayhi is dropped and its meaning is intended; and as man “who” and kam “how many”, in keeping always to the sukūn, which is the origin of bināʾ.

lessons.title: The past verb and the imperative
body: The verb has three divisions, and each has its own sign. The past (māḍī) is known by the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine: ḍarabat, “she hit”. Any word that takes it is a past verb. That is why niʿma, biʾsa, ʿasā and laysa are verbs “in the soundest view”, though they do not change like other verbs: they take the tāʾ, as in niʿmati al-marʾatu Hindun, “how good a woman Hind is!”, which the book gives in the chapter of the doer.

The past is fixed on the fatḥa, ḍaraba, with two exceptions caused by what is joined to it: with the wāw of the group it takes a ḍamma, ḍarabū, “they hit”; with a vowelled pronoun in rafʿ it takes a sukūn, ḍarabtu, “I hit”, ḍarabnā, “we hit”.

The imperative (amr) is known by two things together: it asks for something to be done, and it accepts the yāʾ of the woman addressed: iḍrib, “hit!”, iḍribī, “hit! (to a woman)”. Both are needed. Ṣah, “be silent!”, asks but does not take the yāʾ, so it is a noun of a verb (lesson 38); taḍribīna, “you (woman) hit”, takes the yāʾ but does not ask, so it is a muḍāriʿ. For the same reason hāti, “give!”, and taʿāla, “come!”, are verbs, since one says hātī and taʿālay; halumma, “come here!”, is a verb only for the Banū Tamīm, who say halummī; for the people of the Ḥijāz it does not change.

Ibn Hishām counts the imperative as fixed (mabnī), the view of the Baṣrans; the Kūfans held it to be a muḍāriʿ in jazm. It is fixed on what the muḍāriʿ would lose in jazm: on the sukūn, iḍrib; on the dropping of its last letter if that letter is weak, ughzu, “raid!”, ikhsha, “fear!”, irmi, “throw!”; and on the dropping of the nūn in qūmā, qūmū, qūmī, “stand up!” to two, to many and to a woman.

terms.en: the past verb: known by the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine
the imperative: it asks, and accepts the yāʾ of the woman addressed
the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine, as in ḍarabat
the yāʾ of the woman addressed, as in iḍribī

examples.en: ḍaraba, ḍarabū, ḍarabtu: fixed on the fatḥa, the ḍamma, the sukūn
iḍrib, iḍribī: the imperative takes the yāʾ of the woman addressed
ughzu, ikhsha, irmi: fixed on the dropping of the weak letter

examples.en: qūmā, qūmū, qūmī (the book), iḍribā, iḍribū, iḍribī (the engine): fixed on the dropping of the nūn

tasks.prompt: Give the ending on which each past verb is fixed, and the reason: ḍaraba, ḍarabū, ḍarabtu.
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba: the fatḥa, the rule. Ḍarabū: the ḍamma, because of the wāw of the group. Ḍarabtu: the sukūn, because of the vowelled pronoun in rafʿ.

tasks.prompt: Why is ṣah not an imperative verb, though it commands, and why is taʿāla one?
tasks.answer: The imperative needs two signs: it asks, and it accepts the yāʾ of the woman addressed. Ṣah asks but never takes the yāʾ, so it is a noun of a verb. Taʿāla asks and takes the yāʾ (taʿālay), so it is a verb.

tasks.prompt: On what is each imperative fixed: iḍrib; irmi; qūmū?
tasks.answer: Iḍrib: on the sukūn. Irmi: on the dropping of its weak last letter, the yāʾ. Qūmū: on the dropping of the nūn.

quiz.explanation: Ḍarabat, “she hit”: whatever takes it is a past verb.

quiz.prompt: Why are niʿma and laysa counted as verbs?
options: They begin with a letter of naʾaytu
They take the tāʾ of the feminine
quiz.explanation: Niʿmati al-marʾatu, laysat: the sign of the past.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabū is fixed on…
quiz.explanation: Because of the wāw of the group.

quiz.prompt: Ḍarabtu is fixed on…
quiz.explanation: Because of the vowelled pronoun in rafʿ, the tāʾ.

quiz.prompt: The imperative is known by…
options: asking, together with accepting the yāʾ of the woman addressed
quiz.explanation: Both are needed; ṣah asks but takes no yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Irmi, “throw!”, is fixed on…
options: the dropping of its last letter
quiz.explanation: Its last letter is weak, so it drops.

quiz.prompt: For whom is halumma a verb?
options: For the people of the Ḥijāz
quiz.explanation: Tamīm conjugate it (halummī); in the Ḥijāz it does not change.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْفِعْلُ فَثَلَاثَةُ أَقْسَامٍ: مَاضٍ، وَيُعْرَفُ بِتَاءِ التَّأْنِيثِ السَّاكِنَةِ، وَبِنَاؤُهُ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ كَضَرَبَ، إِلَّا مَعَ وَاوِ الْجَمَاعَةِ فَيُضَمُّ كَضَرَبُوا، وَالضَّمِيرِ الْمَرْفُوعِ الْمُتَحَرِّكِ فَيُسَكَّنُ كَضَرَبْتُ، وَمِنْهُ نِعْمَ وَبِئْسَ وَعَسَى وَلَيْسَ فِي الْأَصَحِّ.
text.en: As for the verb, it is of three divisions. The past (māḍī), which is known by the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine. It is fixed on the fatḥa, as ḍaraba “he hit”, except with the wāw of the group, where it takes a ḍamma, as ḍarabū “they hit”, and with a vowelled pronoun in rafʿ, where it takes a sukūn, as ḍarabtu “I hit”. Among them are niʿma “how good”, biʾsa “how bad”, ʿasā “it may be that” and laysa “is not”, in the soundest view.

text.original: وَأَمْرٌ، وَيُعْرَفُ بِدَلَالَتِهِ عَلَى الطَّلَبِ مَعَ قَبُولِهِ يَاءَ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَبِنَاؤُهُ عَلَى السُّكُونِ كَاضْرِبْ، إِلَّا الْمُعْتَلَّ الْآخِرِ فَعَلَى حَذْفِ آخِرِهِ كَاغْزُ وَاخْشَ وَارْمِ، وَنَحْوُ قُومَا وَقُومُوا وَقُومِي فَعَلَى حَذْفِ النُّونِ، وَمِنْهُ هَلُمَّ فِي لُغَةِ تَمِيمٍ، وَهَاتِ، وَتَعَالَ فِي الْأَصَحِّ.
text.en: The imperative (amr), which is known by its indicating a demand together with its accepting the yāʾ of the woman addressed. It is fixed on the sukūn, as iḍrib “hit!”, except what has a weak last letter: it is fixed on the dropping of its last letter, as ughzu “raid!”, ikhsha “fear!” and irmi “throw!”; and the like of qūmā, qūmū and qūmī “stand up!” [to two, to many, to a woman] is fixed on the dropping of the nūn. Among them are halumma “come here!” in the dialect of Tamīm, hāti “give!” and taʿāla “come!”, in the soundest view.

lessons.title: The muḍāriʿ: its signs and when it is fixed
body: The muḍāriʿ is known by lam: a word before which lam can stand is a muḍāriʿ, as lam yaqum, “he did not stand”. It also begins with one of the four letters of naʾaytu (n, ʾ, y, t): naqūmu, “we stand”, aqūmu, “I stand”, yaqūmu, “he stands”, taqūmu, “you stand” or “she stands”. The letters alone are not the sign, since akrama, a past verb, also begins with a hamza; lam is.

The vowel of the first letter depends on the past. If the past has four letters it is a ḍamma: yudaḥriju from daḥraja, yukrimu from akrama. Otherwise it is a fatḥa, whether the past has three letters, yaḍribu from ḍaraba, or more than four, yastakhriju from istakhraja. Count the letters of the past, not of the muḍāriʿ.

Of the three verbs only the muḍāriʿ is inflected, but it too is fixed in two cases. With the nūn of the women it is fixed on the sukūn: yatarabbaṣna, “they (women) wait” (Q 2:228). With the nūn of emphasis joined directly to it, it is fixed on the fatḥa: la-yunbadhanna, “he shall surely be cast” (Q 104:4). In all else it is inflected: yaqūmu Zaydun.

The words “joined directly, in wording or by implication” decide the hard cases. When the alif of the dual, the wāw of the group or the yāʾ of the woman stands between the verb and the nūn of emphasis, the verb is not fixed: it is one of the five patterns (lesson 7), inflected, with its own nūn dropped. So wa-lā tattabiʿānni, “and do not you two follow” (Q 10:89), la-tublawunna, “you shall surely be tried” (Q 3:186), and fa-immā tarayinna, “and if you see” (Q 19:26), are inflected. In wa-lā yaṣuddunnaka (Q 28:87) the wāw of the group has dropped from the wording, but it is still there in implication, so the verb is inflected too.

terms.en: the present-future verb: known by lam
the four letters that begin the muḍāriʿ: n, ʾ, y, t
the nūn of the women: the muḍāriʿ is fixed on the sukūn with it
the nūn of emphasis: the muḍāriʿ is fixed on the fatḥa when it is joined directly

examples.en: naqūmu, aqūmu, yaqūmu, taqūmu: the letters of naʾaytu
yudaḥriju, yukrimu with ḍamma (a past of four letters); yaḍribu, yastakhriju with fatḥa
yatarabbaṣna (Q 2:228), fixed on the sukūn; la-yunbadhanna (Q 104:4), fixed on the fatḥa
la-tublawunna (Q 3:186): the wāw stands between, so the verb is inflected

tasks.prompt: Why does yukrimu begin with a ḍamma and yastakhriju with a fatḥa?
tasks.answer: The vowel follows the number of letters of the past. Akrama has four letters, so its muḍāriʿ takes a ḍamma; istakhraja has six, so its muḍāriʿ takes a fatḥa, as does every past that is not of four letters.

tasks.prompt: Is yatarabbaṣna inflected or fixed? Why?
tasks.answer: Fixed on the sukūn, because the nūn of the women is joined to it.

tasks.prompt: Why is la-yunbadhanna fixed, but la-tublawunna inflected?
tasks.answer: In la-yunbadhanna the nūn of emphasis is joined directly to the verb, so it is fixed on the fatḥa. In la-tublawunna the wāw of the group stands between the verb and the nūn, so the verb is one of the five patterns and stays inflected.

quiz.prompt: The muḍāriʿ is known by…

quiz.explanation: Lam yaqum: a word that can follow lam is a muḍāriʿ.

quiz.prompt: Which letters begin the muḍāriʿ?
quiz.explanation: Nūn, hamza, yāʾ, tāʾ: naqūmu, aqūmu, yaqūmu, taqūmu.

quiz.prompt: Yudaḥriju begins with a ḍamma because…

quiz.explanation: Daḥraja has four letters.

quiz.prompt: Yastakhriju begins with…
quiz.explanation: Its past has six letters; only a past of four gives a ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: With the nūn of the women the muḍāriʿ is…
quiz.explanation: Yatarabbaṣna (Q 2:228).

quiz.explanation: The nūn of emphasis is joined directly to the verb.

options: It has no nūn of emphasis
The yāʾ of the woman stands between the verb and the nūn
quiz.explanation: Only a nūn joined directly makes the verb fixed.

text.original: وَمُضَارِعٌ، وَيُعْرَفُ بِلَمْ، وَافْتِتَاحُهُ بِحَرْفٍ مِنْ «نَأَيْتُ» نَحْوُ: نَقُومُ وَأَقُومُ وَيَقُومُ وَتَقُومُ، وَيُضَمُّ أَوَّلُهُ إِنْ كَانَ مَاضِيهِ رُبَاعِيًّا كَيُدَحْرِجُ وَيُكْرِمُ، وَيُفْتَحُ فِي غَيْرِهِ كَيَضْرِبُ وَيَسْتَخْرِجُ.
text.en: The muḍāriʿ, which is known by lam, and by its beginning with a letter of naʾaytu, as naqūmu “we stand”, aqūmu “I stand”, yaqūmu “he stands” and taqūmu “you stand, she stands”. Its first letter takes a ḍamma if its past has four letters, as yudaḥriju “he rolls” and yukrimu “he honours”, and a fatḥa in the others, as yaḍribu “he hits” and yastakhriju “he brings out”.

text.original: وَيُسَكَّنُ آخِرُهُ مَعَ نُونِ النِّسْوَةِ نَحْوُ: يَتَرَبَّصْنَ، وَيُفْتَحُ مَعَ نُونِ التَّوْكِيدِ الْمُبَاشِرَةِ لَفْظًا وَتَقْدِيرًا نَحْوُ: لَيُنْبَذَنَّ، وَيُعْرَبُ فِيمَا عَدَا ذَلِكَ نَحْوُ: يَقُومُ زَيْدٌ، وَلَا تَتَّبِعَانِّ، لَتُبْلَوُنَّ، فَإِمَّا تَرَيِنَّ، وَلَا يَصُدُّنَّكَ.
text.en: Its end takes a sukūn with the nūn of the women, as yatarabbaṣna “they (f.) wait” [2:228], and a fatḥa with the nūn of emphasis joined directly to it, in wording or by implication, as la-yunbadhanna “he shall surely be cast” [104:4]. In all else it is inflected, as yaqūmu Zaydun “Zayd stands”, wa-lā tattabiʿānni “and do not you two follow” [10:89], la-tublawunna “you shall surely be tried” [3:186], fa-immā tarayinna “and if you see” [19:26] and wa-lā yaṣuddunnaka “and let him not turn you away” [28:87].

lessons.title: The particle; and speech
body: The particle is known by a sign that is an absence: it accepts none of the signs of the noun and none of the signs of the verb, as hal, “whether?”, and bal, “rather”. No al-, no tanwīn, nothing is said of it; no tāʾ of the feminine, no lam, no yāʾ of the woman. All the particles are fixed (mabnī).

Then Ibn Hishām settles four disputed words. Mahmā, “whatever”, and idhmā, “if ever”, are not particles, though some grammarians held them to be (Sībawayh counted idhmā a particle); for Ibn Hishām they are nouns. The maṣdar-making mā, as in bi-mā nasū, “because they forgot” (Q 38:26), and the linking lammā, “when”, which joins one past act to another, are particles, though some held them to be nouns. “In the soundest view”, he adds: these are questions on which the grammarians differ.

Speech (kalām) is “an utterance that conveys a meaning” (lafẓ mufīd): a meaning complete enough that the hearer does not wait for more. Its least form is two nouns, Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”, or a verb and a noun, qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”. The Ājurrūmiyya said “an utterance, compound, that conveys a meaning, by convention”; Ibn Hishām keeps only “conveys a meaning”, which already requires more than one word.

A trap: one written word can be speech. Iḍrib, “hit!”, is a verb with its doer hidden in it, “you”, so it is a verb and a noun, and conveys a full meaning. And a word is not speech by itself: Zaydun alone, or qāma alone, is a word, kalima, and leaves the hearer waiting.

terms.en: the particle: it takes no sign of the noun or the verb
speech: an utterance that conveys a full meaning
an utterance that conveys a meaning
the mā that turns a verb into the sense of a maṣdar: a particle

examples.en: hal, “whether?”, and bal, “rather”: particles
Zaydun qāʾimun, “Zayd is standing”: speech of two nouns
qāma Zaydun, “Zayd stood”: speech of a verb and a noun
iḍrib, “hit!”: one written word, a verb with its hidden doer, and so speech

tasks.prompt: Show that bal is a particle by trying the signs of the noun and of the verb on it.
tasks.answer: It takes no al- or tanwīn, and nothing is said of it, so it is not a noun; it takes no tāʾ of the feminine, no lam and no yāʾ of the woman addressed, so it is not a verb. A word that takes none of these signs is a particle.

tasks.prompt: Which of these is speech (kalām): Zaydun qāʾimun; qāma; iḍrib; ghulāmu Zaydin?
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ — قَامَ — اضْرِبْ — غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ
tasks.answer: Zaydun qāʾimun (two nouns, a full meaning) and iḍrib (a verb with its hidden doer, “you”) are speech. Qāma alone is one word, and ghulāmu Zaydin is a phrase without a full meaning.

tasks.prompt: Which of the four disputed words does Ibn Hishām count as particles, and which as nouns?
tasks.answer: Particles: the maṣdar-making mā and the linking lammā. Not particles (nouns): mahmā and idhmā. He gives this as the soundest view, since the grammarians differ.

quiz.prompt: The particle is known by…
options: taking none of the signs of the noun or the verb
quiz.explanation: Its sign is an absence: hal, bal.

quiz.prompt: Are the particles inflected?
quiz.explanation: “All the particles are mabnī.”

quiz.prompt: For Ibn Hishām, mahmā is…
quiz.explanation: “Not of [the particles] are mahmā and idhmā.”

quiz.prompt: Which of these does the book count as a particle?
quiz.explanation: The maṣdar-making mā and the linking lammā, in the soundest view.

quiz.prompt: Speech (kalām) is…
options: an utterance that conveys a meaning
quiz.explanation: Lafẓ mufīd: a meaning complete enough to rest on.

quiz.prompt: The least that speech is made of is…
options: two nouns, or a verb and a noun
quiz.explanation: Zaydun qāʾimun, qāma Zaydun.

quiz.prompt: Why is iḍrib, “hit!”, speech?
options: It is a verb with its doer hidden in it
quiz.explanation: The doer “you” is hidden in it: a verb and a noun, with a full meaning.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْحَرْفُ فَيُعْرَفُ بِأَنْ لَا يَقْبَلَ شَيْئًا مِنْ عَلَامَاتِ الِاسْمِ وَلَا شَيْئًا مِنْ عَلَامَاتِ الْفِعْلِ، نَحْوُ: هَلْ وَبَلْ، وَلَيْسَ مِنْهُ مَهْمَا وَإِذْمَا، بَلْ مَا الْمَصْدَرِيَّةُ وَلَمَّا الرَّابِطَةُ فِي الْأَصَحِّ. وَجَمِيعُ الْحُرُوفِ مَبْنِيَّةٌ.
text.en: As for the particle, it is known by its not accepting any of the signs of the noun or any of the signs of the verb, as hal “whether?” and bal “rather”. Not among them are mahmā “whatever” and idhmā “if ever”; but the maṣdar-making mā and the linking lammā are, in the soundest view. All the particles are mabnī.

text.original: وَالْكَلَامُ لَفْظٌ مُفِيدٌ، وَأَقَلُّ ائْتِلَافِهِ مِنِ اسْمَيْنِ كَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ فِعْلٍ وَاسْمٍ كَقَامَ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: Speech (kalām) is an utterance that conveys a meaning (lafẓ mufīd). The least it is composed of is two nouns, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”, or a verb and a noun, as qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”.

lessons.title: The four kinds of iʿrāb, and the six nouns
body: The kinds of iʿrāb are four, and the book shows at once where each belongs. Rafʿ and naṣb are shared by noun and verb: Zaydun yaqūmu, “Zayd stands”, both in rafʿ; inna Zaydan lan yaqūma, “Zayd will not stand”, both in naṣb. Jarr belongs to the noun: bi-Zaydin. Jazm belongs to the verb: lam yaqum. Here Ibn Hishām says jarr; in the chapter of the makhfūḍāt he uses khafḍ, the Ājurrūmiyya's word. The two names mean the same.

The original signs are four: the ḍamma for rafʿ, the fatḥa for naṣb, the kasra for jarr, and for jazm “the dropping of a vowel”. Jazm is a loss, not a vowel: yaqūmu loses its ḍamma and becomes lam yaqum. The rest of the chapter lists the words in which other signs stand in for these.

The first of them are the six nouns: abūhu, “his father”, akhūhu, “his brother”, ḥamūhā, “her father-in-law”, hanūhu, “his thing”, fūhu, “his mouth”, and dhū mālin, “possessor of wealth”. They take letters for vowels: the wāw in rafʿ, the alif in naṣb, the yāʾ in jarr: jāʾa abūhu, raʾaytu abāhu, marartu bi-abīhi. The book writes each with what follows it on purpose, to show the condition: they take these letters when they are joined to another word (other than the yāʾ of the speaker); ḥam is the husband's kin, so it is written ḥamūhā, “her father-in-law”; fū without its mīm (not fam); and dhū in the sense of “possessor”, joined to a noun such as mālin.

Two cautions. Without a word after them these nouns take vowels like any noun: inna lahu aban shaykhan kabīran, “he has a father, a very old man” (Q 12:78). And “it is more correct to use han like ghad”, “tomorrow”: with the vowels on its last letter, hanuka, hanaka, hanika, not with letters.

terms.en: the four kinds of iʿrāb: rafʿ, naṣb, jarr, jazm
the original signs: ḍamma, fatḥa, kasra, and the dropping of a vowel
the six nouns, inflected with wāw, alif and yāʾ

examples.arabic: زَيْدٌ يَقُومُ — إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَنْ يَقُومَ
examples.en: Zaydun yaqūmu; inna Zaydan lan yaqūma: rafʿ and naṣb in noun and verb
bi-Zaydin, jarr in the noun; lam yaqum, jazm in the verb
abūhu, abāhu, abīhi: the wāw, the alif and the yāʾ

grid.caption: The six nouns in the three states (p. 4)
head: Noun
Rafʿ (wāw)
Naṣb (alif)

tasks.prompt: Give the state and the sign of each word in brackets: [Zaydun] yaqūmu; inna Zaydan lan [yaqūma]; lam [yaqum].
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ يَقُومُ — إِنَّ زَيْدًا لَنْ يَقُومَ — لَمْ يَقُمْ
tasks.answer: Zaydun: rafʿ, the ḍamma. Yaqūma: naṣb, the fatḥa. Yaqum: jazm, the dropping of the vowel (the ḍamma of yaqūmu).

tasks.prompt: Put fūhu in the three states, and say why the book writes it with -hu.
tasks.answer: Fūhu, fāhu, fīhi. The -hu shows the condition: the six nouns take letters only when joined to a following word; and fū takes them only without its mīm.

tasks.prompt: Why is aban in inna lahu aban shaykhan kabīran in naṣb by a fatḥa, not by an alif?
tasks.answer: It is not joined to a following word, so it is inflected with the vowels like any noun, with tanwīn. The letters belong to the six nouns only when they are muḍāf.

quiz.prompt: Which kinds of iʿrāb are shared by the noun and the verb?
quiz.explanation: Zaydun yaqūmu; inna Zaydan lan yaqūma.

quiz.prompt: Jarr belongs to…
quiz.explanation: Bi-Zaydin; there is no jarr in the verb.

quiz.prompt: The original sign of jazm is…
quiz.explanation: Yaqūmu loses its ḍamma: lam yaqum.

quiz.prompt: The six nouns are put in naṣb with…
quiz.explanation: Raʾaytu abāhu.

quiz.prompt: Which is in jarr?
quiz.explanation: The yāʾ is the sign of jarr in the six nouns.

quiz.prompt: Fū takes these letters only when…
quiz.explanation: Fūhu, fāhu, fīhi; but famun takes vowels.

quiz.prompt: “It is more correct to use han like ghad” means…
options: with the wāw, alif and yāʾ
with the vowels on its last letter
quiz.explanation: Hanuka, hanaka, hanika.

text.original: أَنْوَاعُ الْإِعْرَابِ أَرْبَعَةٌ: رَفْعٌ وَنَصْبٌ فِي اسْمٍ وَفِعْلٍ نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ يَقُومُ، وَإِنَّ زَيْدًا لَنْ يَقُومَ، وَجَرٌّ فِي اسْمٍ نَحْوُ: بِزَيْدٍ، وَجَزْمٌ فِي فِعْلٍ نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَقُمْ. فَيُرْفَعُ بِضَمَّةٍ، وَيُنْصَبُ بِفَتْحَةٍ، وَيُجَرُّ بِكَسْرَةٍ، وَيُجْزَمُ بِحَذْفِ حَرَكَةٍ،
text.en: The kinds of iʿrāb are four: rafʿ and naṣb, in the noun and the verb, as Zaydun yaqūmu “Zayd stands” and inna Zaydan lan yaqūma “Zayd will not stand”; jarr, in the noun, as bi-Zaydin “with Zayd”; and jazm, in the verb, as lam yaqum “he did not stand”. [A word] is put in rafʿ with a ḍamma, in naṣb with a fatḥa, in jarr with a kasra, and in jazm by the dropping of a vowel,

text.original: إِلَّا الْأَسْمَاءَ السِّتَّةَ، وَهِيَ: أَبُوهُ، وَأَخُوهُ، وَحَمُوهَا، وَهَنُوهُ، وَفُوهُ، وَذُو مَالٍ، فَتُرْفَعُ بِالْوَاوِ، وَتُنْصَبُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَتُجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ، وَالْأَفْصَحُ اسْتِعْمَالُ هَنٍ كَغَدٍ.
text.en: except the six nouns, which are abūhu “his father”, akhūhu “his brother”, ḥamūhā “her father-in-law”, hanūhu “his thing”, fūhu “his mouth” and dhū mālin “possessor of wealth”: they are put in rafʿ with the wāw, in naṣb with the alif and in jarr with the yāʾ; and it is more correct to use hanin like ghadin “tomorrow” [with the vowels on its last letter].

lessons.title: The dual, the sound plurals and the diptote
body: The dual, al-Zaydāni, “the two Zayds”, takes the alif in rafʿ and the yāʾ in jarr and naṣb: al-Zaydayni. Three words follow it without being true duals. Kilā and kiltā, “both”, do so only with a pronoun: jāʾa kilāhumā, raʾaytu kilayhimā; with a noun after them they keep the alif in every state. Ithnāni and ithnatāni, “two”, do so “in every case, even when compounded”: ithnā ʿashara shahran, “twelve months” (Q 9:36), in rafʿ, ithnay ʿashara in naṣb and jarr.

The sound masculine plural, al-Zaydūna, takes the wāw in rafʿ and the yāʾ in naṣb and jarr: al-Zaydīna. The book then lists words that are declined like it though they are not true plurals of this kind: ūlū, “possessors”, which has no singular of its own letters; ʿishrūna, “twenty”, to tisʿūna, which are not the plurals of “ten” to “nine”; ʿālamūna, ahlūna, wābilūna; araḍūna and sinūna, whose singulars arḍ and sana are feminine things, not men; banūna, whose singular ibn changes its form; and ʿilliyyūna, a name of the highest place (Q 83:18).

The feminine plural made “with an added alif and tāʾ” is put in naṣb with the kasra, not the fatḥa: khalaqa Allāhu al-samāwāti, “God created the heavens”; aṣṭafā al-banāti, “has He chosen daughters?” (Q 37:153). Both letters must be added: in abyāt, “verses”, the tāʾ belongs to the root (bayt), and in quḍāt, “judges”, the alif does, so these take the fatḥa like other nouns. The same rule holds for ūlātu and for a person named with such a plural.

The diptote (mā lā yanṣarif) takes no tanwīn and is put in jarr with the fatḥa: bi-afḍala minhu, “with one better than him”. The kasra comes back as soon as it takes al- or is joined to a following word: bi-al-afḍali, bi-afḍalikum. What makes a noun a diptote is the subject of a later chapter (lesson 46).

terms.en: the dual: alif in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and jarr
the sound masculine plural: wāw in rafʿ, yāʾ in naṣb and jarr
the plural with added alif and tāʾ: naṣb with the kasra
the diptote: no tanwīn, jarr with the fatḥa

examples.en: al-Zaydāni in rafʿ; al-Zaydayni in naṣb and jarr
al-Zaydūna in rafʿ; al-Zaydīna in naṣb and jarr
khalaqa Allāhu al-samāwāti: naṣb with the kasra
bi-afḍala minhu: jarr with the fatḥa; bi-al-afḍali: the kasra with al-

tasks.prompt: Why is al-samāwāti in khalaqa Allāhu al-samāwāti in naṣb though it ends in a kasra?
tasks.answer: It is a plural with an added alif and tāʾ, the object of khalaqa. Such plurals are put in naṣb with the kasra in place of the fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Kilā in jāʾa kilāhumā and in jāʾa kilā al-rajulayni: is it declined like the dual in both?
tasks.answer: Only in the first, where it is joined to a pronoun (-humā): kilāhumā, kilayhimā. Joined to a noun, as in kilā al-rajulayni, it keeps its alif in every state.

tasks.prompt: Give the jarr of afḍal in three ways: bare, with al-, and joined to -kum.
tasks.answer: Bi-afḍala (with the fatḥa, as a diptote); bi-al-afḍali and bi-afḍalikum (with the kasra, because al- and the iḍāfa bring it back).

quiz.prompt: The dual is put in rafʿ with…
quiz.explanation: Al-Zaydāni.

quiz.prompt: Kilā is declined like the dual when…
options: it is joined to a noun
it is joined to a pronoun
quiz.explanation: Kilāhumā, kilayhimā.

quiz.prompt: The sound masculine plural is put in naṣb with…
quiz.explanation: Raʾaytu al-Zaydīna.

quiz.prompt: ʿIshrūna is declined like the sound masculine plural, but it is…
options: not a true plural of that kind
quiz.explanation: It is not the plural of a singular “ʿishr”; it is attached to the plural.

quiz.prompt: The plural with added alif and tāʾ is put in naṣb with…
quiz.explanation: Khalaqa Allāhu al-samāwāti.

quiz.prompt: The diptote is put in jarr with…
quiz.explanation: Bi-afḍala minhu, unless it has al- or is muḍāf.

quiz.prompt: In bi-afḍalikum, afḍal takes…
options: the kasra, because it is muḍāf
quiz.explanation: Iḍāfa and al- bring the kasra back.

text.original: وَالْمُثَنَّى كَالزَّيْدَانِ فَيُرْفَعُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَيُجَرُّ وَيُنْصَبُ بِالْيَاءِ، وَكِلَا وَكِلْتَا مَعَ الضَّمِيرِ كَالْمُثَنَّى، وَكَذَا اثْنَانِ وَاثْنَتَانِ مُطْلَقًا وَإِنْ رُكِّبَا.
text.en: And the dual, as al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds”: it is put in rafʿ with the alif, and in jarr and naṣb with the yāʾ. kilā and kiltā “both” with a pronoun are like the dual, and so are ithnāni and ithnatāni “two” in every case, even when they are compounded [with ten].

text.original: وَجَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمُ كَالزَّيْدُونَ فَيُرْفَعُ بِالْوَاوِ، وَيُنْصَبُ وَيُجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ، وَأُولُو وَعِشْرُونَ وَأَخَوَاتُهُ، وَعَالَمُونَ، وَأَهْلُونَ، وَوَابِلُونَ، وَأَرَضُونَ، وَسِنُونَ وَبَابُهُ، وَبَنُونَ، وَعِلِّيُّونَ وَشِبْهُهُ كَالْجَمْعِ.
text.en: And the sound masculine plural, as al-Zaydūna: it is put in rafʿ with the wāw, and in naṣb and jarr with the yāʾ. ūlū “possessors”, ʿishrūna “twenty” and its sisters, ʿālamūna “worlds”, ahlūna “families”, wābilūna “heavy rains”, araḍūna “lands”, sinūna “years” and its like, banūna “sons”, and ʿilliyyūna [the highest place] and what resembles it, are like this plural.

text.original: وَأُولَاتُ وَمَا جُمِعَ بِأَلِفٍ وَتَاءٍ مَزِيدَتَيْنِ وَمَا سُمِّيَ بِهِ مِنْهُمَا فَيُنْصَبُ بِالْكَسْرَةِ نَحْوُ: خَلَقَ اللَّهُ السَّمَاوَاتِ، وَأَصْطَفَى الْبَنَاتِ. وَمَا لَا يَنْصَرِفُ فَيُجَرُّ بِالْفَتْحَةِ نَحْوُ: بِأَفْضَلَ مِنْهُ، إِلَّا مَعَ أَلْ نَحْوُ: بِالْأَفْضَلِ، أَوْ بِالْإِضَافَةِ نَحْوُ: بِأَفْضَلِكُمْ.
text.en: ūlātu “possessors (f.)”, what is made plural with an added alif and tāʾ, and what is named with one of these, are put in naṣb with the kasra, as khalaqa Allāhu al-samāwāti “God created the heavens” and aṣṭafā al-banāti “has He chosen daughters?” [37:153]. What takes no tanwīn (mā lā yanṣarif) is put in jarr with the fatḥa, as bi-afḍala minhu “with one better than him”, except with al-, as bi-al-afḍali “with the better one”, or in iḍāfa, as bi-afḍalikum “with the best of you”.

lessons.title: The five patterns, the weak verb and the implied iʿrāb
body: The five patterns (al-amthila al-khamsa) are the forms of the muḍāriʿ that end in a nūn after the alif of the dual, the wāw of the group or the yāʾ of the woman: yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna and tafʿalīna. They are put in rafʿ by keeping the nūn, and in naṣb and jazm by dropping it: fa-in lam tafʿalū wa-lan tafʿalū, “but if you do not, and you will not” (Q 2:24). In that verse the same form, tafʿalū, is in jazm after lam and in naṣb after lan: only the governor tells you which.

The verb with a weak last letter is put in jazm by dropping that letter: lam yaghzu, “he did not raid”, lam yakhsha, “he did not fear”, lam yarmi, “he did not throw”. The vowel left on the letter before (u, a, i) shows which letter has gone.

Then the implied iʿrāb (al-iʿrāb al-taqdīrī): words whose ending cannot be heard. All three vowels are implied in ghulāmī, “my servant”, and in al-fatā, “the young man”, which is called maqṣūr. The kasra and the ḍamma are implied in al-qāḍī, “the judge”, which is called manqūṣ; the ḍamma and the fatḥa in the verb yakhshā; and the ḍamma alone in yadʿū and yaqḍī. The fatḥa shows on the wāw and the yāʾ: inna al-qāḍiya lan yaqḍiya wa-lan yadʿuwa, “the judge will not judge and will not call”.

The commentators give the reason for each. The alif cannot carry a vowel at all, so in al-fatā and yakhshā every vowel is implied. The wāw and the yāʾ can carry one, but the ḍamma and the kasra are heavy on them, so these are implied, while the light fatḥa is spoken. In ghulāmī the letter before the yāʾ must take a kasra to suit the yāʾ, and so it has no room for the vowel of iʿrāb.

terms.en: the five patterns: yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna, tafʿalīna
implied iʿrāb: there, but not heard
a noun ending in alif, as al-fatā
a noun ending in yāʾ after a kasra, as al-qāḍī

fa-in lam tafʿalū wa-lan tafʿalū (Q 2:24): jazm and naṣb by dropping the nūn

tasks.prompt: In fa-in lam tafʿalū wa-lan tafʿalū, give the state of each tafʿalū and its sign.
tasks.answer: The first is in jazm after lam, the second in naṣb after lan. In both the sign is the dropping of the nūn of tafʿalūna.

tasks.prompt: Why is the fatḥa heard in lan yaqḍiya, but the ḍamma not heard in yaqḍī?
tasks.answer: The yāʾ can carry a vowel, but the ḍamma is heavy on it, so in rafʿ the ḍamma is implied. The fatḥa is light, so it is spoken.

tasks.prompt: Which vowels are implied in al-fatā, and why?
tasks.answer: All three, ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra: it ends in an alif, and the alif cannot carry any vowel. It is called maqṣūr.

quiz.prompt: The five patterns are put in rafʿ by…
quiz.explanation: Yafʿalūna, tafʿalīna: the nūn is the sign of rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: In lan tafʿalū, the sign of naṣb is…
quiz.explanation: Naṣb and jazm both drop the nūn.

quiz.prompt: Lam yarmi is in jazm by…
quiz.explanation: Yarmī loses its yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Al-fatā is called…
quiz.explanation: A noun ending in alif.

quiz.prompt: Which vowels are implied in al-qāḍī?
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa is spoken: inna al-qāḍiya.

quiz.prompt: In yakhshā, which vowels are implied?
quiz.explanation: A verb ending in alif: rafʿ and naṣb are both implied.

quiz.prompt: Why are all vowels implied in ghulāmī?
options: The letter before the yāʾ must take a kasra to suit it
quiz.explanation: The kasra of suiting leaves no room for the vowel of iʿrāb.

text.original: وَالْأَمْثِلَةُ الْخَمْسَةُ، وَهِيَ: يَفْعَلَانِ وَيَفْعَلُونَ، وَبِالتَّاءِ فِيهِمَا، وَتَفْعَلِينَ، فَتُرْفَعُ بِثُبُوتِ النُّونِ، وَتُجْزَمُ وَتُنْصَبُ بِحَذْفِهَا نَحْوُ: فَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا وَلَنْ تَفْعَلُوا. وَالْفِعْلُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْآخِرِ فَيُجْزَمُ بِحَذْفِهِ نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَغْزُ، وَلَمْ يَخْشَ، وَلَمْ يَرْمِ.
text.en: And the five patterns (al-amthila al-khamsa), which are yafʿalāni and yafʿalūna, these two with the tāʾ, and tafʿalīna: they are put in rafʿ by keeping the nūn, and in jazm and naṣb by dropping it, as fa-in lam tafʿalū wa-lan tafʿalū “but if you do not, and you will not” [2:24]. The verb with a weak last letter is put in jazm by dropping that letter, as lam yaghzu “he did not raid”, lam yakhsha “he did not fear” and lam yarmi “he did not throw”.

text.original: تُقَدَّرُ جَمِيعُ الْحَرَكَاتِ فِي نَحْوِ: غُلَامِي وَالْفَتَى، وَيُسَمَّى الثَّانِي مَقْصُورًا، وَالْكَسْرَةُ وَالضَّمَّةُ فِي نَحْوِ: الْقَاضِي، وَيُسَمَّى مَنْقُوصًا، وَالضَّمَّةُ وَالْفَتْحَةُ فِي نَحْوِ: يَخْشَى، وَالضَّمَّةُ فِي نَحْوِ: يَدْعُو وَيَقْضِي، وَتَظْهَرُ الْفَتْحَةُ فِي نَحْوِ: إِنَّ الْقَاضِيَ لَنْ يَقْضِيَ وَلَنْ يَدْعُوَ.
text.en: All the vowels are implied in the like of ghulāmī “my servant” and al-fatā “the young man”, and the second is called maqṣūr; the kasra and the ḍamma in the like of al-qāḍī “the judge”, which is called manqūṣ; the ḍamma and the fatḥa in the like of yakhshā “he fears”; and the ḍamma in the like of yadʿū “he calls” and yaqḍī “he judges”. The fatḥa shows in the like of inna al-qāḍiya lan yaqḍiya wa-lan yadʿuwa “the judge will not judge and will not call”.

lessons.title: The muḍāriʿ in rafʿ, and in naṣb by lan, kay, idhan and an
body: “The muḍāriʿ is put in rafʿ when it is free of a governor of naṣb or of jazm”: yaqūmu Zaydun. That is the view of al-Farrāʾ and the Kūfans; the Baṣrans said it is raised by standing where a noun could stand. Ibn Hishām names no governor that is a word; the rafʿ is what the verb has when nothing has entered on it.

Four particles put it in naṣb. Lan negates the future: lan nabraḥa, “we shall not cease” (Q 20:91). Kay gives the purpose, and the book says “the maṣdar-making kay” because kay can also be a particle of jarr, “for”. When the lām comes before it, as in li-kaylā taʾsaw, “so that you do not grieve” (Q 57:23), it can only be the maṣdar-making kay, since one particle of jarr does not come upon another.

Idhan, “then, in that case”, governs only on three conditions: it is placed first in its sentence; the verb is future; and the verb is joined to it, or separated only by an oath: idhan ukrimaka, “then I will honour you”; idhan wa-Allāhi narmiyahum bi-ḥarbin, “then, by God, we will strike them with war”. If idhan is not first (anā idhan, “I then…”) or anything else stands between, the verb stays in rafʿ.

An is the commonest of the four: an yaghfira lī, “that He will forgive me” (Q 26:82). But after a verb of knowing it is not this an: it is anna made light, and the verb after it is in rafʿ: ʿalima an sa-yakūnu minkum marḍā, “He knows that there will be sick ones among you” (Q 73:20). After a verb of supposing both are allowed, and the readers of the Qurʾān read wa-ḥasibū an lā takūna fitnatun (Q 5:71) with takūna and with takūnu.

terms.en: “will not”: naṣb, and negation of the future
the maṣdar-making kay, “so that”, certain after the lām
“then”: governs if first, with a future verb, joined or separated by an oath
the maṣdar-making an, not after a verb of knowing

examples.en: yaqūmu Zaydun: in rafʿ, free of any governor of naṣb or jazm
lan nabraḥa (Q 20:91); li-kaylā taʾsaw (Q 57:23)
idhan ukrimaka, “then I will honour you”
after a verb of knowing: an is anna made light, the verb in rafʿ (Q 73:20)

tasks.prompt: Why is the kay of li-kaylā taʾsaw certainly the maṣdar-making kay?
tasks.answer: Kay can be a particle of jarr or the maṣdar-making particle. Here the lām, a particle of jarr, comes before it, and one particle of jarr does not come upon another; so kay is the maṣdar-making particle, and it puts the verb in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Give the three conditions of idhan, and show them in idhan wa-Allāhi narmiyahum bi-ḥarbin.
tasks.answer: It must be first in its sentence, the verb must be future, and the verb must be joined to it or separated only by an oath. Here idhan is first, narmiya speaks of the future, and only the oath wa-Allāhi stands between them; so narmiyahum is in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why is yakūnu in rafʿ in ʿalima an sa-yakūnu minkum marḍā?
tasks.answer: An comes after a verb of knowing, ʿalima, so it is not the maṣdar-making an but anna made light; it does not put the verb in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: The muḍāriʿ is in rafʿ, in this book, when…

it stands in the place of a noun
quiz.explanation: Yaqūmu Zaydun: the Kūfan view, which Ibn Hishām takes.

quiz.prompt: Lan nabraḥa means…
quiz.explanation: Lan negates the future and gives naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book say “the maṣdar-making kay”?
options: Because kay can also be a particle of jarr
quiz.explanation: Only the maṣdar-making kay gives naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a condition of idhan?
options: That nothing but an oath separates them
That a lām comes before it
quiz.explanation: Idhan needs to be first, with a future verb, joined or separated by an oath.

quiz.prompt: In idhan ukrimaka, ukrimaka is in…
quiz.explanation: All three conditions of idhan are met.

quiz.prompt: After a verb of knowing, an is…
options: anna made light, and the verb is in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: ʿAlima an sa-yakūnu (Q 73:20).

quiz.prompt: After a verb of supposing, the verb after an is…
quiz.explanation: Wa-ḥasibū an lā takūna / takūnu fitnatun (Q 5:71): both are read.

text.original: يُرْفَعُ الْمُضَارِعُ خَالِيًا مِنْ نَاصِبٍ وَجَازِمٍ نَحْوُ: يَقُومُ زَيْدٌ. وَيُنْصَبُ بِلَنْ نَحْوُ: لَنْ نَبْرَحَ، وَبِكَيِ الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ نَحْوُ: لِكَيْلَا تَأْسَوْا،
text.en: The muḍāriʿ is put in rafʿ when it is free of a governor of naṣb or of jazm, as yaqūmu Zaydun “Zayd stands”. It is put in naṣb by lan, as lan nabraḥa “we shall not cease” [20:91]; by the maṣdar-making kay, as li-kaylā taʾsaw “so that you do not grieve” [57:23];

text.original: وَبِإِذَنْ مُصَدَّرَةً، وَهُوَ مُسْتَقْبَلٌ، مُتَّصِلٌ أَوْ مُنْفَصِلٌ بِقَسَمٍ، نَحْوُ: إِذَنْ أُكْرِمَكَ، وَ: إِذَنْ وَاللَّهِ نَرْمِيَهُمْ بِحَرْبٍ. وَبِأَنِ الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ ظَاهِرَةً نَحْوُ: أَنْ يَغْفِرَ لِي، مَا لَمْ تُسْبَقْ بِعِلْمٍ نَحْوُ: عَلِمَ أَنْ سَيَكُونُ مِنْكُمْ مَرْضَى، فَإِنْ سُبِقَتْ بِظَنٍّ فَوَجْهَانِ نَحْوُ: وَحَسِبُوا أَنْ لَا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ.
text.en: by idhan placed first, when [the verb] is future and joined to it or separated from it by an oath, as idhan ukrimaka “then I will honour you” and idhan wa-Allāhi narmiyahum bi-ḥarbin “then, by God, we will strike them with war”; and by the maṣdar-making an, expressed, as an yaghfira lī “that He will forgive me” [26:82], as long as it is not preceded by [a verb of] knowing, as ʿalima an sa-yakūnu minkum marḍā “He knows that there will be sick ones among you” [73:20]. If it is preceded by [a verb of] supposing, both ways are allowed, as wa-ḥasibū an lā takūna fitnatun “and they supposed that there would be no trial” [5:71].

lessons.title: An unseen: after a conjunction, the lām, ḥattā, aw, the fāʾ and the wāw
body: An can govern without being spoken (muḍmara). It is hidden by choice in two places. The first is after a conjunction that joins the verb to “a pure noun”, one that carries no sense of a verb: wa-lubsu ʿabāʾatin wa-taqarra ʿaynī, “and wearing a cloak, with my eye at rest”. Taqarra is joined to the maṣdar lubsu, so it too must stand for a maṣdar, “an taqarra”, and the hidden an puts it in naṣb. The second is after the lām of reason: li-tubayyina li-l-nāsi, “so that you make clear to people” (Q 16:44), where li-an tubayyina could also be said.

The lām has two exceptions. When lā follows it, an must be spoken: liʾallā yaʿlama (Q 57:29), liʾallā yakūna li-l-nāsi (Q 2:150); the commentators explain that this keeps two lāms (li-lā) from meeting. And after the lām that follows a denial with kāna, called the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd), an must be hidden: wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum, “but God would not punish them” (Q 8:33).

It is hidden and nothing else after ḥattā when the verb is future: ḥattā yarjiʿa ilaynā Mūsā, “until Moses returns to us” (Q 20:91); after aw meaning “until”, la-astashilanna al-ṣaʿba aw udrika al-munā, “I will make light of what is hard until I attain my hopes”, or meaning “unless”, kasartu kuʿūbahā aw tastaqīmā, “I broke its knots unless it straightened”; and after the fāʾ of cause and the wāw of accompaniment, when a pure negation or a demand made with a verb comes before them: lā yuqḍā ʿalayhim fa-yamūtū (Q 35:36); wa-lā taṭghaw fīhi fa-yaḥilla, “do not transgress in it, lest [My anger] descend” (Q 20:81).

The book's last example shows why the wāw matters: lā taʾkuli al-samaka wa-tashraba al-labana, “do not eat fish and drink milk”. With tashraba in naṣb the wāw means “with”: what is forbidden is the two together. The grammarians read the same words two other ways: with tashrab in jazm, both are forbidden, each by itself; with tashrabu in rafʿ, the fish is forbidden and the milk allowed. One vowel changes the ruling.

terms.en: an hidden: governing without being spoken
the lām of denial, after mā kāna or lam yakun: an is always hidden after it
the fāʾ of cause, after a negation or a demand
the wāw of accompaniment, “with”

examples.en: li-tubayyina li-l-nāsi (Q 16:44): an hidden by choice after the lām
wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum (Q 8:33): an always hidden after the lām of denial
ḥattā yarjiʿa ilaynā Mūsā (Q 20:91)
lā taʾkuli al-samaka wa-tashraba al-labana: the two together are forbidden

tasks.prompt: What puts tubayyina in naṣb in li-tubayyina li-l-nāsi, and could the governor be spoken?
tasks.answer: An hidden after the lām of reason. It is hidden by choice, so it could be spoken: li-an tubayyina.

tasks.prompt: Why is an spoken in liʾallā yaʿlama, but hidden in wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum?
tasks.arabic: لِئَلَّا يَعْلَمَ — وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ
tasks.answer: After the lām followed by lā, an must be spoken (the commentators: to keep li- and lā from meeting). After the lām of denial, which follows mā kāna, an must be hidden.

tasks.prompt: Read lā taʾkuli al-samaka wa-tashrab- with tashraba, tashrab and tashrabu, and give the meaning of each.
tasks.answer: Tashraba (naṣb, the wāw of “with”, an hidden): do not have the two together. Tashrab (jazm, joined to the prohibition): do not eat fish and do not drink milk. Tashrabu (rafʿ, a new sentence): do not eat fish, while you may drink milk.

quiz.prompt: In wa-lubsu ʿabāʾatin wa-taqarra ʿaynī, what puts taqarra in naṣb?
options: An, hidden after a conjunction joined to a pure noun
quiz.explanation: Taqarra is joined to the maṣdar lubsu, so it stands for an taqarra.

quiz.prompt: After the lām followed by lā, an is…
quiz.explanation: Liʾallā yaʿlama, liʾallā yakūna.

quiz.prompt: After the lām of denial, an is…
quiz.explanation: Wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum (Q 8:33).

quiz.prompt: An is hidden after ḥattā when the verb is…
quiz.explanation: Ḥattā yarjiʿa ilaynā Mūsā (Q 20:91).

quiz.prompt: Aw that puts the verb in naṣb means…
quiz.explanation: Aw udrika al-munā, “until I attain my hopes”.

quiz.prompt: The fāʾ of cause gives naṣb when it comes after…
options: a pure negation or a demand made with a verb
quiz.explanation: Lā yuqḍā ʿalayhim fa-yamūtū; lā taṭghaw fīhi fa-yaḥilla.

quiz.prompt: In lā taʾkuli al-samaka wa-tashraba al-labana, what is forbidden?
options: Each of the two by itself
quiz.explanation: The wāw of accompaniment with naṣb: “do not eat fish with drinking milk”.

text.original: وَمُضْمَرَةً جَوَازًا بَعْدَ عَاطِفٍ مَسْبُوقٍ بِاسْمٍ خَالِصٍ نَحْوُ: وَلُبْسُ عَبَاءَةٍ وَتَقَرَّ عَيْنِي، وَبَعْدَ اللَّامِ نَحْوُ: لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ، إِلَّا فِي نَحْوِ: لِئَلَّا يَعْلَمَ، لِئَلَّا يَكُونَ لِلنَّاسِ، فَتَظْهَرُ لَا غَيْرُ، وَنَحْوِ: وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ، فَتُضْمَرُ لَا غَيْرُ،
text.en: And [an is] implied, by choice, after a conjunction preceded by a pure noun, as wa-lubsu ʿabāʾatin wa-taqarra ʿaynī “and wearing a cloak, with my eye at rest”; and after the lām, as li-tubayyina li-al-nāsi “so that you make clear to people” [16:44], except in the like of liʾallā yaʿlama “so that [they] may know” [57:29] and liʾallā yakūna li-al-nāsi “so that people may not have” [2:150], where it is expressed and nothing else, and in the like of wa-mā kāna Allāhu li-yuʿadhdhibahum “but God would not punish them” [8:33], where it is implied and nothing else;

text.original: كَإِضْمَارِهَا بَعْدَ حَتَّى إِذَا كَانَ مُسْتَقْبَلًا نَحْوُ: حَتَّى يَرْجِعَ إِلَيْنَا مُوسَى، وَبَعْدَ أَوِ الَّتِي بِمَعْنَى إِلَى نَحْوُ: لَأَسْتَسْهِلَنَّ الصَّعْبَ أَوْ أُدْرِكَ الْمُنَى، أَوْ إِلَّا نَحْوُ: وَكُنْتُ إِذَا غَمَزْتُ قَنَاةَ قَوْمٍ * كَسَرْتُ كُعُوبَهَا أَوْ تَسْتَقِيمَا.
text.en: as it is implied after ḥattā when [the verb] is future, as ḥattā yarjiʿa ilaynā Mūsā “until Moses returns to us” [20:91]; and after aw in the sense of ilā “until”, as la-astasʹhilanna al-ṣaʿba aw udrika al-munā “I will surely make light of what is hard until I attain my hopes”, or in the sense of illā “unless”, as wa-kuntu idhā ghamaztu qanāta qawmin / kasartu kuʿūbahā aw tastaqīmā “when I pressed the spear-shaft of a people, I broke its knots unless it straightened”.

text.original: وَبَعْدَ فَاءِ السَّبَبِيَّةِ أَوْ وَاوِ الْمَعِيَّةِ مَسْبُوقَتَيْنِ بِنَفْيٍ مَحْضٍ أَوْ طَلَبٍ بِالْفِعْلِ نَحْوُ: لَا يُقْضَى عَلَيْهِمْ فَيَمُوتُوا، وَيَعْلَمَ الصَّابِرِينَ، وَلَا تَطْغَوْا فِيهِ فَيَحِلَّ، وَلَا تَأْكُلِ السَّمَكَ وَتَشْرَبَ اللَّبَنَ.
text.en: And after the fāʾ of cause (fāʾ al-sababiyya) or the wāw of accompaniment (wāw al-maʿiyya), when they are preceded by a pure negation or by a demand made with a verb, as lā yuqḍā ʿalayhim fa-yamūtū “it is not decreed for them that they should die” [35:36], wa-yaʿlama al-ṣābirīna “and [before] He knows the steadfast” [3:142], wa-lā taṭghaw fīhi fa-yaḥilla “and do not transgress in it, lest [My anger] descend” [20:81] and lā taʾkuli al-samaka wa-tashraba al-labana “do not eat fish and drink milk [together]”.

lessons.title: Jazm in answer to a demand; lam, lammā, the lām and the lā
body: When the fāʾ falls away after a demand and a requital is meant, the verb is in jazm: taʿālaw atlu, “come, I will recite” (Q 6:151). The meaning is “if you come, I will recite”, and the grammarians explain the jazm by that understood condition. Compare the last lesson: with the fāʾ the verb is in naṣb, without it in jazm.

After a prohibition there is a test: jazm is allowed only if “in lā”, “if … not”, can rightly take its place. Lā tadnu mina al-asadi taslam, “do not go near the lion, [and] you will be safe”: “if you do not go near the lion, you will be safe” makes sense, so taslam is in jazm. But lā tadnu mina al-asadi yaʾkulka would mean “if you do not go near the lion, it will eat you”, which is nonsense; so jazm is not allowed there.

Then the governors of jazm of one verb. Lam: lam yalid wa-lam yūlad, “He did not beget and was not begotten” (Q 112:3). Lammā, “not yet”: lammā yaqḍi, “he has not yet done [what He commanded him]” (Q 80:23). The lām of demand: li-yunfiq, “let him spend” (Q 65:7), li-yaqḍi, “let [your Lord] make an end” (Q 43:77). The lā of demand: lā tushrik, “do not associate [anything with God]” (Q 31:13), lā tuʾākhidhnā, “do not take us to task” (Q 2:286).

Why “of demand” (ṭalabiyya) and not “of command” and “of prohibition”? Because a demand made to God is not called a command but a prayer (duʿāʾ): li-yaqḍi ʿalaynā rabbuka and lā tuʾākhidhnā are prayers, and the same lām and lā put the verb in jazm. Note the signs too: the sukūn in yalid, yunfiq, tushrik; the dropping of the weak letter in yaqḍi.

terms.en: the answer of a demand: in jazm when the fāʾ falls away
the lām of demand: command or prayer
the lā of demand: prohibition or prayer
a prayer: a demand made to God

examples.en: taʿālaw atlu (Q 6:151): “if you come, I will recite”
lā tadnu mina al-asadi taslam: “if you do not go near, you will be safe”
lam yalid wa-lam yūlad (Q 112:3)
lā tuʾākhidhnā (Q 2:286): the lā of demand in a prayer

tasks.prompt: Explain the jazm of atlu in taʿālaw atlu.
tasks.answer: It answers a demand (taʿālaw, “come!”) with no fāʾ, and a requital is meant: “if you come, I will recite”. So it is in jazm, by the dropping of its weak last letter (atlū → atlu).

tasks.prompt: Why can one say lā tadnu mina al-asadi taslam, but not lā tadnu mina al-asadi yaʾkulka?
tasks.answer: Jazm after a prohibition needs “in lā” to fit in its place. “If you do not go near the lion, you will be safe” fits; “if you do not go near the lion, it will eat you” does not.

tasks.prompt: In li-yaqḍi ʿalaynā rabbuka, what is the sign of jazm, and why is the lām called “of demand”?
tasks.answer: The dropping of the weak last letter (yaqḍī → yaqḍi). The lām is “of demand” because here the demand is made to God, a prayer, not a command.

quiz.prompt: When the fāʾ falls away after a demand and a requital is meant, the verb is in…
quiz.explanation: Taʿālaw atlu (Q 6:151).

quiz.prompt: Jazm after a prohibition is allowed if…
options: “in lā” can rightly stand in its place
quiz.explanation: Lā tadnu mina al-asadi taslam: “if you do not go near, you will be safe”.

quiz.prompt: Lā tadnu mina al-asadi yaʾkulka is not allowed because…
options: “if you do not go near, it will eat you” is nonsense
quiz.explanation: The test of “in lā” fails.

quiz.prompt: Lammā yaqḍi means…
quiz.explanation: Lammā negates up to now (Q 80:23).

quiz.prompt: The sign of jazm in li-yunfiq is…
quiz.explanation: Yunfiqu becomes li-yunfiq.

quiz.prompt: Lā tuʾākhidhnā is…
options: a prayer, with the lā of demand
quiz.explanation: A demand made to God is called duʿāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Why does the book say “the lām and the lā of demand”?
options: To cover command, prohibition and prayer
Because they come only before nouns
quiz.explanation: Li-yaqḍi ʿalaynā rabbuka is a prayer, not a command.

text.original: فَإِنْ سَقَطَتِ الْفَاءُ بَعْدَ الطَّلَبِ وَقُصِدَ الْجَزَاءُ جُزِمَ نَحْوُ: تَعَالَوْا أَتْلُ. وَشَرْطُ الْجَزْمِ بَعْدَ النَّهْيِ صِحَّةُ حُلُولِ إِنْ لَا مَحَلَّهُ نَحْوُ: لَا تَدْنُ مِنَ الْأَسَدِ تَسْلَمْ، بِخِلَافِ: يَأْكُلْكَ.
text.en: If the fāʾ falls away after a demand and a requital (jazāʾ) is intended, [the verb] is put in jazm, as taʿālaw atlu “come, I will recite” [6:151]. The condition of jazm after a prohibition is that in lā “if … not” can rightly stand in its place, as lā tadnu mina al-asadi taslam “do not go near the lion, [and] you will be safe”, unlike yaʾkulka “it will eat you”.

text.original: وَيُجْزَمُ أَيْضًا بِلَمْ نَحْوُ: لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ، وَلَمَّا نَحْوُ: لَمَّا يَقْضِ، وَبِاللَّامِ وَلَا الطَّلَبِيَّتَيْنِ نَحْوُ: لِيُنْفِقْ، لِيَقْضِ، لَا تُشْرِكْ، لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَا.
text.en: It is also put in jazm by lam, as lam yalid wa-lam yūlad “He did not beget and was not begotten” [112:3]; by lammā, as lammā yaqḍi “he has not yet done” [80:23]; and by the lām and the lā of demand, as li-yunfiq “let him spend” [65:7], li-yaqḍi “let [your Lord] make an end” [43:77], lā tushrik “do not associate [anything with God]” [31:13] and lā tuʾākhidhnā “do not take us to task” [2:286].

lessons.title: What puts two verbs in jazm; the fāʾ in the answer
body: Eleven words put two verbs in jazm: in, idhmā, ayyun, ayna, annā, ayyāna, matā, mahmā, man, mā and ḥaythumā. “The first is called the condition (sharṭ), the second the answer (jawāb) and the requital (jazāʾ)”: in yashaʾ yudhhibkum, “if He wills, He will take you away” (Q 4:133); man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bihi, “whoever does evil will be requited for it” (Q 4:123); mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsihā naʾti, “whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring [better]” (Q 2:106).

Of the eleven only in is a particle; the other ten are nouns, idhmā among them, as the book said in the chapter of the particle (lesson 4). Watch the signs of jazm in the verses: the sukūn in yashaʾ, yudhhib, yaʿmal and nansakh; the dropping of the weak last letter in yujza (from yujzā), nunsi and naʾti.

Some answers cannot follow the particle directly; then they “must be joined with the fāʾ”: wa-in yamsaska bi-khayrin fa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun, “and if He touches you with good, He has power over everything” (Q 6:17). Fa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun is a nominal sentence, and a nominal sentence cannot stand where in could govern it. The commentators list such answers: a nominal sentence, a command or prohibition, a verb with lan, qad or sa-, a verb that does not change such as niʿma or ʿasā. The fāʾ then links the answer to the condition, and the answer is in the place of jazm.

Instead of the fāʾ, the idhā of surprise may link a nominal sentence: wa-in tuṣibhum sayyiʾatun bi-mā qaddamat aydīhim idhā hum yaqnaṭūna, “and if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent before, behold, they despair” (Q 30:36). Idhā hum, “behold, they…”, does what the fāʾ does.

terms.en: the words of condition: in and ten nouns
the condition: the first verb
the answer and the requital: the second verb
the idhā of surprise, “behold”

examples.en: in yashaʾ yudhhibkum (Q 4:133): condition and answer in jazm
man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bihi (Q 4:123)

examples.arabic: وَإِنْ يَمْسَسْكَ بِخَيْرٍ فَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
examples.en: a nominal answer joined with the fāʾ (Q 6:17)
idhā hum yaqnaṭūna (Q 30:36): the idhā of surprise in place of the fāʾ

tasks.prompt: In man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bihi, name the condition and the answer, and the sign of jazm in each.
tasks.answer: Yaʿmal is the condition, in jazm by the sukūn; yujza is the answer, in jazm by the dropping of its weak last letter (yujzā → yujza). Man governs both.

tasks.prompt: Why must the answer in wa-in yamsaska bi-khayrin fa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun take the fāʾ?
tasks.arabic: وَإِنْ يَمْسَسْكَ بِخَيْرٍ فَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
tasks.answer: The answer is a nominal sentence, and a nominal sentence cannot follow in directly, since in governs only verbs. So the fāʾ links it, and the whole answer is in the place of jazm.

tasks.prompt: Which of the eleven is a particle, and why does the book count idhmā with the nouns?
tasks.answer: Only in. In the chapter of the particle the book said that mahmā and idhmā are not particles; so idhmā, like mahmā, is a noun here (Sībawayh had counted it a particle).

quiz.prompt: How many words does the book list that put two verbs in jazm?
quiz.explanation: In, idhmā, ayyun, ayna, annā, ayyāna, matā, mahmā, man, mā, ḥaythumā.

quiz.prompt: The first verb after a word of condition is called…
quiz.explanation: The second is the answer and requital.

quiz.prompt: Which of the eleven is a particle?
quiz.explanation: The others are nouns.

quiz.prompt: In man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bihi, yujza is in jazm by…
quiz.explanation: Yujzā loses its alif.

quiz.prompt: When must the answer take the fāʾ?
options: When it is a muḍāriʿ in jazm
When it cannot follow the word of condition directly
quiz.explanation: As a nominal sentence: fa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun.

quiz.prompt: What may stand in place of the fāʾ before a nominal answer?
quiz.explanation: Idhā hum yaqnaṭūna (Q 30:36).

quiz.prompt: Ayyāna means…
quiz.explanation: A noun of condition for time.

text.original: وَيَجْزِمُ فِعْلَيْنِ: إِنْ، وَإِذْمَا، وَأَيٌّ، وَأَيْنَ، وَأَنَّى، وَأَيَّانَ، وَمَتَى، وَمَهْمَا، وَمَنْ، وَمَا، وَحَيْثُمَا، نَحْوُ: إِنْ يَشَأْ يُذْهِبْكُمْ، مَنْ يَعْمَلْ سُوءًا يُجْزَ بِهِ، مَا نَنْسَخْ مِنْ آيَةٍ أَوْ نُنْسِهَا نَأْتِ. وَيُسَمَّى الْأَوَّلُ شَرْطًا، وَالثَّانِي جَوَابًا وَجَزَاءً.
text.en: Two verbs are put in jazm by in “if”, idhmā “if ever”, ayyun “whichever”, ayna “wherever”, annā “wherever”, ayyāna “whenever”, matā “when”, mahmā “whatever”, man “whoever”, mā “whatever” and ḥaythumā “wherever”, as in yashaʾ yudhhibkum “if He wills, He will take you away” [4:133], man yaʿmal sūʾan yujza bi-hi “whoever does evil will be requited for it” [4:123] and mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsihā naʾti “whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring [better]” [2:106]. The first is called the condition (sharṭ), and the second the answer (jawāb) and the requital (jazāʾ).

text.original: وَإِذَا لَمْ يَصْلُحِ الْجَوَابُ لِمُبَاشَرَةِ الْأَدَاةِ قُرِنَ وُجُوبًا بِالْفَاءِ نَحْوُ: وَإِنْ يَمْسَسْكَ بِخَيْرٍ فَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ، أَوْ بِإِذَا الْفُجَائِيَّةِ نَحْوُ: وَإِنْ تُصِبْهُمْ سَيِّئَةٌ بِمَا قَدَّمَتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ إِذَا هُمْ يَقْنَطُونَ.
text.en: When the answer is not fit to follow the particle directly, it must be joined with the fāʾ, as wa-in yamsaska bi-khayrin fa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīrun “and if He touches you with good, He has power over everything” [6:17], or with the idhā of surprise, as wa-in tuṣibhum sayyiʾatun bi-mā qaddamat aydīhim idhā hum yaqnaṭūna “and if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent before, behold, they despair” [30:36].

lessons.title: The indefinite and the definite; the pronoun
body: The indefinite noun (nakira) is “that which is common to a kind, existing, as rajul, or supposed, as shams”. Rajul, “man”, fits every man there is. Shams, “sun”, fits one thing in the world as we know it, but the word would fit any other sun, if there were one; so it too is indefinite. The definite noun (maʿrifa) is of six kinds, given in order of rank, the most definite first: the pronoun, the proper name, the demonstrative, the relative, the noun with al-, and the noun joined to one of these.

The pronoun (ḍamīr) points to a speaker, one addressed or one absent. It is hidden (mustatir) or visible (bāriz). It is hidden necessarily in aqūmu, “I stand”, and naqūmu, “we stand”: no visible noun can be the doer of these verbs. It is hidden by choice in Zaydun yaqūmu, “Zayd stands”, since a visible noun could take its place (yaqūmu abūhu, “his father stands”).

The visible pronoun is attached (muttaṣil) or separate (munfaṣil). Attached: the tāʾ of qumtu, “I stood”; the kāf of akramaka, “he honoured you”; the hāʾ of ghulāmihi, “his servant”. Separate: anā, anta, huwa, and iyyāya, “me”, for an object put first or cut off from its verb.

The rule is “no separate pronoun where an attached one is possible”: akramtuka, not akramtu iyyāka. Two cases are allowed both ways. With a verb of two objects, both pronouns, as salnīhi, “ask me for it”, the separate salnī iyyāhu is allowed but weaker. With ẓanantukahu, “I thought you [to be] him”, and kuntuhu, “I was him”, Ibn Hishām prefers the separate, ẓanantuka iyyāhu, kuntu iyyāhu; Ibn Mālik preferred the attached. This is one of the places where the two masters differ.

terms.en: the indefinite: common to a kind, existing or supposed
the definite: six kinds, the pronoun first
the hidden pronoun, as in aqūmu
the attached and the separate pronoun

examples.en: rajul, existing; shams, supposed: both indefinite
aqūmu: hidden necessarily; Zaydun yaqūmu: hidden by choice
attached pronouns: the tāʾ, the kāf, the hāʾ
salnīhi, “ask me for it”: the attached form, the better one here

tasks.prompt: Why is shams indefinite, though there is only one sun that we know?
tasks.answer: The indefinite is what is common to a kind, “existing or supposed”. The word shams would fit any other sun if there were one; the kind is supposed, so the word is indefinite.

tasks.prompt: Is the doer hidden necessarily or by choice in naqūmu and in Zaydun yaqūmu? Why?
tasks.answer: In naqūmu necessarily: no visible noun can be the doer of “we stand”. In Zaydun yaqūmu by choice: a visible noun could take the pronoun's place, as yaqūmu abūhu.

tasks.prompt: Find the attached pronoun in each and say whom it points to: qumtu; akramaka; ghulāmihi.
tasks.answer: The tāʾ of qumtu: the speaker (the doer). The kāf of akramaka: the one addressed (the object). The hāʾ of ghulāmihi: one absent (the owner, in jarr by iḍāfa).

quiz.prompt: The indefinite noun is…
options: common to a kind, existing or supposed
quiz.explanation: Rajul, existing; shams, supposed.

quiz.prompt: Which is the most definite of the six?
quiz.explanation: The book lists them in order of rank.

quiz.prompt: In aqūmu, the doer is…
quiz.explanation: No visible noun can be the doer of “I stand”.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun yaqūmu, the doer of yaqūmu is…
quiz.explanation: A visible noun could take its place: yaqūmu abūhu.

quiz.prompt: Which is a separate pronoun?
quiz.explanation: Anā, anta, huwa, iyyāya.

quiz.prompt: The rule for choosing between attached and separate is…
options: no separate where an attached is possible
quiz.explanation: Akramtuka, not akramtu iyyāka.

quiz.prompt: In kuntuhu, “I was him”, Ibn Hishām prefers…
quiz.explanation: He gives the separate “as the stronger”; Ibn Mālik preferred the attached.

text.original: الِاسْمُ ضَرْبَانِ: نَكِرَةٌ، وَهُوَ مَا شَاعَ فِي جِنْسٍ مَوْجُودٍ كَرَجُلٍ، أَوْ مُقَدَّرٍ كَشَمْسٍ، وَمَعْرِفَةٌ، وَهِيَ سِتَّةٌ:
text.en: The noun is of two kinds. Indefinite (nakira), which is that which is common to [the members of] a kind, existing, as rajul “man”, or supposed, as shams “sun”; and definite (maʿrifa), which is of six [kinds]:

text.original: الضَّمِيرُ، وَهُوَ مَا دَلَّ عَلَى مُتَكَلِّمٍ أَوْ مُخَاطَبٍ أَوْ غَائِبٍ، وَهُوَ إِمَّا مُسْتَتِرٌ كَالْمُقَدَّرِ وُجُوبًا فِي نَحْوِ: أَقُومُ وَنَقُومُ، أَوْ جَوَازًا فِي نَحْوِ: زَيْدٌ يَقُومُ، أَوْ بَارِزٌ، وَهُوَ إِمَّا مُتَّصِلٌ كَتَاءِ قُمْتُ وَكَافِ أَكْرَمَكَ وَهَاءِ غُلَامِهِ، أَوْ مُنْفَصِلٌ كَأَنَا وَأَنْتَ وَهُوَ وَإِيَّايَ،
text.en: The pronoun (ḍamīr), which is that which indicates a speaker, one addressed or one absent. It is either hidden (mustatir), as that which is implied necessarily in the like of aqūmu “I stand” and naqūmu “we stand”, or by choice in the like of Zaydun yaqūmu “Zayd stands”; or visible (bāriz), and this is either attached (muttaṣil), as the tāʾ of qumtu “I stood”, the kāf of akramaka “he honoured you” and the hāʾ of ghulāmihi “his servant”, or separate (munfaṣil), as anā “I”, anta “you”, huwa “he” and iyyāya “me”;

text.original: وَلَا فَصْلَ مَعَ إِمْكَانِ الْوَصْلِ، إِلَّا فِي نَحْوِ الْهَاءِ مِنْ سَلْنِيهِ بِمَرْجُوحِيَّةٍ، وَظَنَنْتُكَهُ، وَكُنْتُهُ بِرُجْحَانٍ.
text.en: and there is no separate [pronoun] where the attached is possible, except in the like of the hāʾ of salnīhi “ask me for it”, [where the separate is allowed] as the weaker choice, and of ẓanantukahu “I thought you [to be] him” and kuntuhu “I was him”, [where it is allowed] as the stronger.

lessons.title: The proper name and the demonstrative
body: The proper name (ʿalam) is either personal, the name of one person, as Zayd, or of a kind (jinsī), as Usāma, a name for the lion: a word that names the whole kind and yet behaves as a definite noun. By its form it is a name (ism), as Zayd; a nickname (laqab), which praises or blames, as Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn, “the adornment of the worshippers”, or Quffa, “basket”; or a kunya, made with abū or umm, as Abū ʿAmr and Umm ʿAmr.

When a man has a name and a laqab, the laqab comes after the name. It may always follow the name in its iʿrāb; and if both are single words (not iḍāfas), it may instead be joined to the name by iḍāfa and put in khafḍ: Saʿīdu Kurzin, “Saʿīd Kurz”. With a name of two words, as ʿAbd Allāh, only the first way is open.

The demonstratives (asmāʾ al-ishāra) are dhā for the masculine; dhī, dhih, tī, tih and tā for the feminine; dhāni and tāni for the dual in rafʿ and dhayni and tayni in jarr and naṣb, declined like the dual; and ūlāʾi for the plural of both.

For what is far, the kāf is added: dhāka, “that”; and the lām may come with it: dhālika, as in dhālika khayrun (Q 7:26). The lām is not used in three places: in the dual (dhānika, never with a lām), in the plural for those who say ūlāʾi with the long vowel (ulāʾika), and after the hā of alerting: hādhāka, not hādhālika.

terms.en: the proper name: personal or of a kind
the nickname, praising or blaming
the name with abū or umm
the demonstrative

examples.en: Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn, a laqab; Abū ʿAmr, a kunya
Saʿīdu Kurzin: name and laqab, both single, joined by iḍāfa
dhāni in rafʿ, dhayni in naṣb and jarr
dhālika khayrun (Q 7:26): the far demonstrative with the kāf and the lām

grid.caption: The demonstratives for what is near (p. 11)

Rafʿ
