quiz.explanation: The book says it “is interpreted”; the commentators follow Sībawayh.

text.original: يَجُوزُ فِي نَحْوِ: زَيْدٌ ضَرَبْتُهُ، أَوْ ضَرَبْتُ أَخَاهُ، أَوْ مَرَرْتُ بِهِ، رَفْعُ زَيْدٍ بِالِابْتِدَاءِ، فَالْجُمْلَةُ بَعْدَهُ خَبَرُهُ، وَنَصْبُهُ بِإِضْمَارِ ضَرَبْتُ وَأَهَنْتُ وَجَاوَزْتُ وَاجِبَةِ الْحَذْفِ، فَلَا مَوْضِعَ لِلْجُمْلَةِ بَعْدَهُ.
text.en: In the like of Zaydun ḍarabtuhu “Zayd, I hit him”, or [Zayd,] ḍarabtu akhāhu “I hit his brother”, or [Zayd,] marartu bi-hi “I passed by him”, it is allowed to put Zayd in rafʿ as mubtadaʾ, the sentence after it being its khabar; or to put it in naṣb by an implied ḍarabtu “I hit”, ahantu “I humiliated” or jāwaztu “I passed”, which must be dropped, and then the sentence after it has no place [in the iʿrāb].

text.original: وَيَتَرَجَّحُ النَّصْبُ فِي نَحْوِ: زَيْدًا اضْرِبْهُ، لِلطَّلَبِ، وَنَحْوُ: وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ فَاقْطَعُوا، مُتَأَوَّلٌ، وَفِي نَحْوِ: وَالْأَنْعَامَ خَلَقَهَا لَكُمْ، لِلتَّنَاسُبِ، وَ: أَبَشَرًا مِنَّا وَاحِدًا نَتَّبِعُهُ، وَمَا زَيْدًا رَأَيْتُهُ، لِغَلَبَةِ الْفِعْلِ.
text.en: Naṣb is preferred in the like of Zaydan iḍribhu “Zayd, hit him!”, because of the demand — the like of wa-al-sāriqu wa-al-sāriqatu fa-iqṭaʿū “and the thief, male and female, cut off [their hands]” [5:38] is interpreted [otherwise] —; in the like of wa-al-anʿāma khalaqahā lakum “and the cattle He created for you” [16:5], for the sake of matching [the sentence before]; and in a-basharan minnā wāḥidan nattabiʿuhu “shall we follow a single human being from among us?” [54:24] and mā Zaydan raʾaytuhu “Zayd I did not see”, because the verb predominates [after these particles].

text.original: وَيَجِبُ فِي نَحْوِ: إِنْ زَيْدًا لَقِيتَهُ فَأَكْرِمْهُ، وَهَلَّا زَيْدًا أَكْرَمْتَهُ. وَيَجِبُ الرَّفْعُ فِي نَحْوِ: خَرَجْتُ فَإِذَا زَيْدٌ يَضْرِبُهُ عَمْرٌو، لِامْتِنَاعِهِ. وَيَسْتَوِيَانِ فِي نَحْوِ: زَيْدٌ قَامَ أَبُوهُ وَعَمْرًا أَكْرَمْتُهُ عِنْدَهُ، لِلتَّكَافُؤِ. وَلَيْسَ مِنْهُ: وَكُلُّ شَيْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ فِي الزُّبُرِ، وَأَزَيْدٌ ذُهِبَ بِهِ.
text.en: It is necessary in the like of in Zaydan laqītahu fa-akrimhu “if you meet Zayd, honour him” and hallā Zaydan akramtahu “why did you not honour Zayd?”. Rafʿ is necessary in the like of kharajtu fa-idhā Zaydun yaḍribuhu ʿAmrun “I went out, and there was Zayd, ʿAmr hitting him”, because [naṣb] is impossible. They are equal in the like of Zaydun qāma abūhu wa-ʿAmran akramtuhu ʿindahu “Zayd, his father stood, and ʿAmr I honoured at his house”, because [the two sentences] balance. Not of this [chapter] are wa-kullu shayʾin faʿalūhu fī al-zuburi “and everything they did is in the Scriptures” [54:52] and a-Zaydun dhuhiba bi-hi “was Zayd taken away?”.

lessons.title: Contention (tanāzuʿ)
body: Contention (tanāzuʿ) is two governors before one noun, each needing it: ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtu Zaydan, “Zayd hit me and I hit [him]”. The first verb wants Zayd as its doer, the second as its object; they “contend” for him. Only one can govern him, and the other is given a pronoun or left without.

Either may govern. The Kūfans chose the first, since it came first; then “everything the second needs is put in it as a pronoun”: ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtuhu Zaydun. The Baṣrans chose the second, since it is nearer; then “only its marfūʿ is put in the first as a pronoun”, because a doer cannot be dropped, while an object can simply be left out: jafawnī wa-lam ajfu al-akhillāʾa, “the friends shunned me, and I did not shun [them]”. The wāw of jafawnī is the pronoun of the doer, referring to al-akhillāʾa, which the second verb governs as its object.

Not every pair of verbs is contention. In the verse of Imruʾ al-Qays, kafānī wa-lam aṭlub qalīlun mina al-māli, “a little wealth would have sufficed me, and I did not seek [more]”, qalīlun is governed only by kafānī. If lam aṭlub governed it too, the poet would be saying that he did not seek a little wealth, while his point is that he seeks more than a little; “the meaning would be spoiled”. The object of aṭlub is something else, which the next verse names.

terms.en: contention: two governors before one noun
letting the first governor govern: the Kūfan choice
letting the second governor govern: the Baṣran choice

examples.en: ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtu Zaydan: two verbs contend for Zayd
jafawnī wa-lam ajfu al-akhillāʾa: the second governs; the first takes its doer as a pronoun

examples.arabic: كَفَانِي وَلَمْ أَطْلُبْ قَلِيلٌ مِنَ الْمَالِ
examples.en: not contention: the meaning would be spoiled

tasks.prompt: In ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtu Zaydan, what does each verb want from Zayd?
tasks.answer: Ḍarabanī wants him as its doer (“Zayd hit me”); ḍarabtu wants him as its object (“I hit Zayd”). They contend for the one noun.

tasks.prompt: In jafawnī wa-lam ajfu al-akhillāʾa, which verb governs al-akhillāʾa, and what is the wāw of jafawnī?
tasks.answer: The second, lam ajfu, governs it as its object (the Baṣran choice). The wāw of jafawnī is the pronoun of the first verb's doer, referring to al-akhillāʾa; a doer cannot be dropped, so it is put in as a pronoun.

tasks.prompt: Why is kafānī wa-lam aṭlub qalīlun mina al-māli not contention?
tasks.arabic: كَفَانِي وَلَمْ أَطْلُبْ قَلِيلٌ مِنَ الْمَالِ
tasks.answer: If aṭlub also governed qalīlun, the meaning would be “I did not seek a little wealth”, but the poet means that a little would have been enough had he not sought more. So qalīlun belongs to kafānī alone.

quiz.prompt: Contention is…
options: two governors before one noun that both need it
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtu Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: Which governor did the Kūfans choose?
quiz.explanation: Because it came first.

quiz.prompt: Which governor did the Baṣrans choose?
quiz.explanation: Because it is nearer to the noun.

quiz.prompt: When the second governs, what is put in the first as a pronoun?
quiz.explanation: A doer cannot be dropped; an object can be left out.

quiz.prompt: In jafawnī wa-lam ajfu al-akhillāʾa, the wāw of jafawnī refers to…
quiz.explanation: The pronoun of the doer of the first verb.

quiz.prompt: When the first governs, the second takes…
options: a pronoun for everything it needs
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtuhu Zaydun.

quiz.prompt: Kafānī wa-lam aṭlub qalīlun mina al-māli is not contention because…
quiz.explanation: The poet does not mean that he did not seek a little.

text.original: يَجُوزُ فِي نَحْوِ: ضَرَبَنِي وَضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا، إِعْمَالُ الْأَوَّلِ، وَاخْتَارَهُ الْكُوفِيُّونَ، فَيُضْمَرُ فِي الثَّانِي كُلُّ مَا يَحْتَاجُهُ، أَوِ الثَّانِي، وَاخْتَارَهُ الْبَصْرِيُّونَ، فَيُضْمَرُ فِي الْأَوَّلِ مَرْفُوعُهُ فَقَطْ نَحْوُ: جَفَوْنِي وَلَمْ أَجْفُ الْأَخِلَّاءَ. وَلَيْسَ مِنْهُ: كَفَانِي وَلَمْ أَطْلُبْ قَلِيلٌ مِنَ الْمَالِ، لِفَسَادِ الْمَعْنَى.
text.en: In the like of ḍarabanī wa-ḍarabtu Zaydan “Zayd hit me and I hit [him]” it is allowed to make the first [verb] govern — the Kūfans chose this — and then everything the second needs is put in it as a pronoun; or the second — the Baṣrans chose this — and then only its marfūʿ is put in the first as a pronoun, as jafawnī wa-lam ajfu al-akhillāʾa “the friends shunned me, and I did not shun [them]”. Not of this [chapter] is kafānī wa-lam aṭlub qalīlun mina al-māli “a little wealth sufficed me, and I did not seek [more]”, because the meaning would be spoiled.

lessons.title: The object; the one called
body: The objects (mafʿūlāt) are in naṣb, and there are five: the object (mafʿūl bihi), the absolute object, the object of reason, the object of time and place, and the object of accompaniment. The first is “that on which the act of the doer falls”: ḍarabtu Zaydan, “I hit Zayd”.

The one called (munādā) is a kind of object: yā ʿAbda Allāhi means “I call ʿAbd Allāh”, the particle standing for the verb. It is in naṣb in three cases. When it is a muḍāf: yā ʿAbda Allāhi. When it is like a muḍāf, a word that governs what follows it: yā ḥasanan wajhuhu, “O you whose face is handsome”, where ḥasanan puts wajhuhu in rafʿ; yā ṭāliʿan jabalan, “O you climbing a mountain”, where ṭāliʿan puts jabalan in naṣb; yā rafīqan bi-l-ʿibādi, “O You who are kind to the servants”. And when it is an indefinite not intended, any one at all: the blind man's yā rajulan khudh bi-yadī, “O [some] man, take my hand!”.

“The single definite [one called] is fixed on that with which it is put in rafʿ”: yā Zaydu, with the ḍamma; yā Zaydāni, with the alif; yā Zaydūna, with the wāw; and yā rajulu, said to a particular man, who becomes definite by being called. It is fixed, not inflected, and stands in the place of naṣb.

The pair yā rajulu and yā rajulan is the key to the chapter. Yā rajulu addresses a man in front of you, a definite one: fixed on the ḍamma. Yā rajulan is the call of the blind man, who does not know who is there: any man, indefinite, in naṣb.

terms.en: the object: that on which the doer's act falls
the one called: a kind of object
the indefinite intended, made definite by the call: yā rajulu
like a muḍāf: governing what follows it

examples.en: ḍarabtu Zaydan: the object
yā ḥasanan wajhuhu: like a muḍāf, in naṣb
yā rajulan khudh bi-yadī: the indefinite not intended

examples.arabic: يَا زَيْدُ — يَا زَيْدَانِ — يَا زَيْدُونَ
examples.en: the single definite one called, fixed on its sign of rafʿ

tasks.prompt: Why is the one called counted among the objects?
tasks.answer: Yā stands for the verb “I call”: yā ʿAbda Allāhi is “I call ʿAbd Allāh”. The one called is the object of that verb, so it belongs with the objects.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between yā rajulu and yā rajulan?
tasks.answer: Yā rajulu calls a particular man, made definite by the call: it is fixed on the ḍamma. Yā rajulan calls any man at all, an indefinite not intended, as the blind man does: it is in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why is ḥasanan in naṣb in yā ḥasanan wajhuhu, and what is wajhuhu?
tasks.answer: Ḥasanan is like a muḍāf: it governs the word after it. So the one called is in naṣb. Wajhuhu is in rafʿ, the doer of the adjective ḥasan: “O you whose face is handsome”.

quiz.prompt: How many objects (mafʿūlāt) does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Bihi, muṭlaq, lahu, fīhi and maʿahu.

quiz.prompt: The mafʿūl bihi is…
options: that on which the doer's act falls
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabtu Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: The one called is in naṣb when it is…
quiz.explanation: Yā ʿAbda Allāhi.

quiz.prompt: Yā ṭāliʿan jabalan is in naṣb because ṭāliʿan is…
quiz.explanation: It governs jabalan.

quiz.prompt: Yā Zaydāni is fixed on…
quiz.explanation: The single definite is fixed on its sign of rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: The blind man says yā rajulan because…
options: he calls a man he knows
he calls any man, not a particular one
quiz.explanation: An indefinite not intended is in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Yā rajulu, said to a particular man, is…
quiz.explanation: The indefinite intended becomes definite by the call.

text.original: الْمَفْعُولُ مَنْصُوبٌ، وَهُوَ خَمْسَةٌ: الْمَفْعُولُ بِهِ، وَهُوَ مَا وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ فِعْلُ الْفَاعِلِ كَضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا. وَمِنْهُ الْمُنَادَى، وَإِنَّمَا يُنْصَبُ مُضَافًا كَيَا عَبْدَ اللَّهِ، أَوْ شَبِيهًا بِهِ كَيَا حَسَنًا وَجْهُهُ، وَيَا طَالِعًا جَبَلًا، وَيَا رَفِيقًا بِالْعِبَادِ، أَوْ نَكِرَةً غَيْرَ مَقْصُودَةٍ كَقَوْلِ الْأَعْمَى: يَا رَجُلًا خُذْ بِيَدِي.
text.en: The mafʿūl is manṣūb, and it is of five [kinds]. The mafʿūl bihi, which is that on which the act of the doer falls, as ḍarabtu Zaydan “I hit Zayd”. Of it is the munādā. It is put in naṣb only when it is muḍāf, as yā ʿAbda Allāhi “O ʿAbd Allāh”; or like a muḍāf, as yā ḥasanan wajhuhu “O you whose face is handsome”, yā ṭāliʿan jabalan “O you climbing a mountain” and yā rafīqan bi-al-ʿibādi “O You who are kind to the servants”; or an indefinite not intended, as the blind man's saying yā rajulan khudh bi-yadī “O [some] man, take my hand!”.

text.original: وَالْمُفْرَدُ الْمَعْرِفَةُ يُبْنَى عَلَى مَا يُرْفَعُ بِهِ، كَيَا زَيْدُ، وَيَا زَيْدَانِ، وَيَا زَيْدُونَ، وَيَا رَجُلُ لِمُعَيَّنٍ.
text.en: The single definite [munādā] is fixed on that with which it is put in rafʿ, as yā Zaydu “O Zayd”, yā Zaydāni “O two Zayds”, yā Zaydūna “O Zayds” and yā rajulu “O man”, [said] to a particular one.

lessons.title: Calling with the yāʾ of the speaker; the followers of the one called
body: Calling a noun joined to the yāʾ of the speaker, “my servant”, can be said in six ways: “with the three”, that is, yā ghulāmi, yā ghulāma and yā ghulāmu, the yāʾ dropped; “with the yāʾ, with fatḥa or sukūn”, yā ghulāmiya and yā ghulāmī; and “with the alif”, yā ghulāmā.

Four words go their own way. Yā abati, “O my father”, and yā ummati, “O my mother”, put a tāʾ in place of the yāʾ, as in yā abati (Q 12:4); yā ibna umma, “O son of my mother”, and yā ibna ʿamma, “O son of my uncle”, drop it; all four may be said with fatḥa or with kasra. To add the alif or the yāʾ to the first two (yā abatī) is “ugly”, since the tāʾ already stands for the yāʾ; to the last two it is “weak”.

The followers of a fixed one called (yā Zaydu) have their own rules. An adjective, an emphasis or an explicative noun that is single, or a muḍāf with al-, and a joined noun with al-, may follow its wording, in rafʿ, or its place, in naṣb: yā Zaydu al-ẓarīfu or al-ẓarīfa. A muḍāf without al- follows the place only: yā Zaydu ṣāḥiba ʿAmrin. The adjective of ayy follows its wording only: yā ayyuhā al-nāsu, “O people” (Q 2:21). A badal and a joined noun without al- are treated as if they were called themselves: yā Zaydu Bishru.

The book ends with a famous case: yā Zaydu Zayda al-yaʿmalāti, “O Zayd, Zayd of the swift camels”. You may give the first a ḍamma, as a single proper name, with the second following it as a muḍāf in naṣb; or give both a fatḥa, as if the two Zayds were one name joined to al-yaʿmalāti.

terms.en: the one called joined to the yāʾ of the speaker
the follower of the one called: adjective, emphasis, bayān, badal, joined noun
ayy with hā, to call a noun with al-: its adjective follows its wording

examples.en: yā abati, yā ummati: the tāʾ in place of the yāʾ
yā ibna umma, “O son of my mother”, with fatḥa or kasra
yā ayyuhā al-nāsu (Q 2:21): the adjective of ayy follows its wording
yā Zaydu Zayda al-yaʿmalāti: the first with ḍamma or with fatḥa

tasks.prompt: Give the six ways of calling “my servant”.
tasks.answer: Yā ghulāmi, yā ghulāma, yā ghulāmu (the yāʾ dropped, with the three vowels); yā ghulāmiya and yā ghulāmī (with the yāʾ, with fatḥa or sukūn); yā ghulāmā (with the alif).

tasks.prompt: Why is yā abatī “ugly”?
tasks.answer: The tāʾ of yā abati already stands in place of the yāʾ of the speaker. Adding the yāʾ as well would bring together the substitute and what it replaces.

tasks.prompt: In yā Zaydu al-ẓarīf-, what endings may al-ẓarīf take, and why? And in yā Zaydu ṣāḥib- ʿAmrin?
tasks.answer: Al-ẓarīfu (following the wording of Zaydu) or al-ẓarīfa (following its place, naṣb): a single adjective may follow either. Ṣāḥiba ʿAmrin only in naṣb: a muḍāf without al- follows the place only.

quiz.prompt: In how many ways can “my servant” be called?
quiz.explanation: Three with the yāʾ dropped, two with the yāʾ, one with the alif.

quiz.prompt: In yā abati, the tāʾ stands for…
quiz.explanation: So adding the yāʾ again is ugly.

quiz.prompt: Yā ibna umma may be said…
quiz.explanation: Yā ibna umma, yā ibna ummi.

quiz.prompt: Adding the alif or yāʾ to yā ibna umm- is…
quiz.explanation: To the first two, abati and ummati, it is ugly.

quiz.prompt: A follower that is a muḍāf without al- follows the one called…
quiz.explanation: Yā Zaydu ṣāḥiba ʿAmrin.

quiz.prompt: The adjective of ayy, as in yā ayyuhā al-nāsu, follows…
quiz.explanation: Al-nāsu is in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: A badal of the one called is treated…
options: as if it were called itself
quiz.explanation: Yā Zaydu Bishru.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: وَتَقُولُ: يَا غُلَامِ بِالثَّلَاثِ، وَبِالْيَاءِ فَتْحًا وَإِسْكَانًا، وَبِالْأَلِفِ، وَيَا أَبَتِ، وَيَا أُمَّتِ، وَيَا ابْنَ أُمَّ، وَيَا ابْنَ عَمَّ، بِالْفَتْحِ وَالْكَسْرِ، وَإِلْحَاقُ الْأَلِفِ أَوِ الْيَاءِ لِلْأَوَّلَيْنِ قَبِيحٌ، وَلِلْآخِرَيْنِ ضَعِيفٌ.
text.en: Section. You say yā ghulāmi “O my servant” with the three [vowels on the mīm], with the yāʾ, with fatḥa or sukūn, and with the alif; and yā abati “O my father”, yā ummati “O my mother”, yā ibna umma “O son of my mother” and yā ibna ʿamma “O son of my uncle”, with fatḥa and kasra. Adding the alif or the yāʾ to the first two is ugly, and to the last two weak.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: وَيَجْرِي مَا أُفْرِدَ أَوْ أُضِيفَ مَقْرُونًا بِأَلْ مِنْ نَعْتِ الْمَبْنِيِّ وَتَأْكِيدِهِ وَبَيَانِهِ وَنَسَقِهِ الْمَقْرُونِ بِأَلْ عَلَى لَفْظِهِ أَوْ مَحَلِّهِ، وَمَا أُضِيفَ مُجَرَّدًا عَلَى مَحَلِّهِ، وَنَعْتُ أَيٍّ عَلَى لَفْظِهِ، وَالْبَدَلُ وَالنَّسَقُ الْمُجَرَّدُ كَالْمُنَادَى الْمُسْتَقِلِّ مُطْلَقًا. وَلَكَ فِي نَحْوِ: يَا زَيْدُ زَيْدَ الْيَعْمَلَاتِ، فَتْحُهُمَا أَوْ ضَمُّ الْأَوَّلِ.
text.en: Section. The naʿt of the mabnī [munādā], its tawkīd and its bayān, when single or muḍāf with al-, and its nasaq [ʿaṭf] joined with al-, follow its wording or its place; what is muḍāf without al- follows its place; the naʿt of ayy follows its wording; and the badal and the nasaq without al- are like an independent munādā in every case. In the like of yā Zaydu Zayda al-yaʿmalāti “O Zayd, Zayd of the swift camels” you may give both a fatḥa, or the first a ḍamma.

lessons.title: Shortening the name called; calling for help; lamenting
body: A definite one called may be shortened (tarkhīm): its end is dropped to lighten it. A word ending in the tāʾ of the feminine may be shortened always, name or not, long or short: yā Ṭalḥa for Ṭalḥatu, yā thuba, “O company”, for thubatu. Others only on three conditions: the word is fixed on the ḍamma (a single word), it is a proper name, and it has more than three letters: yā Jaʿfa, for Jaʿfar. What is left may keep its own vowel, yā Jaʿfa, or take the ḍamma, as if it were a whole name, yā Jaʿfu.

Two letters are dropped where a long vowel or an added letter stands before the last, in a name of more than three letters: Salmān, Manṣūr, Miskīn become yā Salma, yā Manṣu, yā Miski. From a compound name such as Maʿdī Karib the second word is dropped: yā Maʿdī.

One who calls for help (al-mustaghīth) says yā la-llāhi li-l-muslimīna, “O God, [help] for the Muslims!”. The one called for help takes a lām with fatḥa, la-llāhi; the one helped a lām with kasra, li-l-muslimīna. A second one called for help, joined by wa- without a new yā, takes the kasra. An alif at the end may replace the lām, yā Zaydā li-ʿAmrin, and the same form calls out in wonder: yā qawmi li-l-ʿajabi al-ʿajībi, “O my people, for the wondrous wonder!”.

One who laments (al-nādib) calls with wā and an alif at the end: wā Zaydā, “alas, Zayd!”; wā amīra al-muʾminīnāh, “alas, Commander of the Faithful!”; wā raʾsāh, “alas, my head!”, said of pain. In a pause a hāʾ may be added after the alif, as in the last two.

terms.en: shortening the name called by dropping its end
the one called for help, with a lām with fatḥa
the one lamented, with wā and a final alif
the hāʾ of the pause, after the alif of lament

examples.en: yā Ṭalḥa, yā thuba: a word with the tāʾ, shortened always
yā Jaʿfa, for Jaʿfar: a name of more than three letters
yā la-llāhi li-l-muslimīna: lām with fatḥa, lām with kasra
wā Zaydā; wā raʾsāh: lament, with the hāʾ of the pause

tasks.prompt: Why may thuba be shortened, though it is not a name and has only three letters with its tāʾ?
tasks.answer: A word ending in the tāʾ of the feminine may be shortened in every case; the three conditions (fixed on the ḍamma, a proper name, more than three letters) apply only to words without the tāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Give the two ways of shortening Jaʿfar, and explain the difference.
tasks.answer: Yā Jaʿfa keeps the fāʾ's own vowel, as if the dropped rāʾ were still meant; yā Jaʿfu gives it the ḍamma, as if Jaʿf were the whole name.

tasks.prompt: In yā la-llāhi li-l-muslimīna, why does the first lām have a fatḥa and the second a kasra?
tasks.answer: The lām of the one called for help takes a fatḥa, to tell it from the lām of the one for whom help is sought, which keeps its usual kasra.

quiz.prompt: Tarkhīm is…
options: adding an alif to the one called
dropping the end of a definite one called to lighten it
quiz.explanation: Yā Ṭalḥa, yā Jaʿfa.

quiz.prompt: A word with the tāʾ of the feminine may be shortened…
options: only if it is a name
only if it has four letters
quiz.explanation: Yā thuba, though thuba is not a name.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT a condition for shortening a word without the tāʾ?
options: That it is a proper name
That it ends in a hamza
That it has more than three letters
That it is fixed on the ḍamma
quiz.explanation: The three conditions are ḍamma, name, more than three letters.

quiz.prompt: From Manṣūr, tarkhīm drops…
quiz.explanation: A long vowel before the last letter goes with it.

quiz.prompt: In istighātha, the lām of the one called for help has…
quiz.explanation: Yā la-llāhi.

quiz.prompt: Wā Zaydā is…
quiz.explanation: Wā and the alif of lament.

quiz.prompt: The hāʾ in wā raʾsāh is…
quiz.explanation: It may be added in a pause.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: وَيَجُوزُ تَرْخِيمُ الْمُنَادَى الْمَعْرِفَةِ، وَهُوَ حَذْفُ آخِرِهِ تَخْفِيفًا، فَذُو التَّاءِ مُطْلَقًا كَيَا طَلْحَ وَيَا ثُبَ، وَغَيْرُهُ بِشَرْطِ ضَمِّهِ وَعَلَمِيَّتِهِ وَمُجَاوَزَتِهِ ثَلَاثَةَ أَحْرُفٍ كَيَا جَعْفَ، ضَمًّا وَفَتْحًا، وَيُحْذَفُ مِنْ نَحْوِ: سَلْمَانَ وَمَنْصُورٍ وَمِسْكِينٍ حَرْفَانِ، وَمِنْ نَحْوِ: مَعْدِي كَرِبَ الْكَلِمَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ.
text.en: Section. The definite munādā may be shortened (tarkhīm), which is dropping its end to lighten it: what has the tāʾ, in every case, as yā Ṭalḥa “O Ṭalḥa” and yā thuba “O company”; and others on condition that it has a ḍamma, is a proper name and has more than three letters, as yā Jaʿfa “O Jaʿfar”, with ḍamma or fatḥa. Two letters are dropped from the like of Salmān, Manṣūr and Miskīn, and the second word from the like of Maʿdī Karib.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: وَيَقُولُ الْمُسْتَغِيثُ: يَا لَلَّهِ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ، بِفَتْحِ لَامِ الْمُسْتَغَاثِ إِلَّا فِي الْمَعْطُوفِ الَّذِي لَمْ يَتَكَرَّرْ مَعَهُ يَا، وَنَحْوُ: يَا زَيْدَا لِعَمْرٍو، وَيَا قَوْمِ لِلْعَجَبِ الْعَجِيبِ. وَالنَّادِبُ: وَا زَيْدَا، وَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَاهْ، وَا رَأْسَاهْ، وَلَكَ إِلْحَاقُ الْهَاءِ وَقْفًا.
text.en: Section. The one who calls for help says yā la-Allāhi li-al-muslimīna “O God, [help] for the Muslims!”, with fatḥa on the lām of the one called for help, except in a ʿaṭf with which yā is not repeated; and the like of yā Zaydā li-ʿAmrin “O Zayd, for ʿAmr!” and yā qawmi li-al-ʿajabi al-ʿajībi “O my people, for the wondrous wonder!”. The one who laments says wā Zaydā “alas, Zayd!”, wā amīra al-muʾminīnāh “alas, Commander of the Faithful!” and wā raʾsāh “alas, my head!”; and you may add the hāʾ in the pause.

lessons.title: The absolute object and the object of reason
body: The absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) is “the maṣdar that is an extra (faḍla), on which a governor of its own wording is brought to bear”: ḍarabtu ḍarban, “I hit a hitting”; or a governor of its meaning: qaʿadtu julūsan, “I sat a sitting”, where qaʿada and julūs mean the same with other letters. “Extra” means that the sentence is complete without it: it adds emphasis, the kind of act, or its number.

Other words can take its place: the instrument, ḍarabtuhu sawṭan, “I hit him a whip-stroke”; a number, fa-jlidūhum thamānīna jaldatan, “then flog them eighty lashes” (Q 24:4); kull, fa-lā tamīlū kulla al-mayli, “so do not incline wholly” (Q 4:129); and baʿḍ, baʿḍa al-aqāwīli, “some sayings” (Q 69:44). “Not of it is wa-kulā minhā raghadan” (Q 2:35): raghadan, “freely”, looks like one, but the commentators take it as a ḥāl.

The object of reason (mafʿūl lahu) is “the maṣdar that gives the reason for an event with which it shares the time and the doer”: qumtu ijlālan laka, “I stood out of respect for you”. The respect and the standing are mine, and at the same moment.

If one of the conditions is missing, the reason is put in jarr by a particle of reason, usually the lām. Not a maṣdar: khalaqa lakum, “He created for you” (Q 2:29). Not the same doer: wa-innī la-taʿrūnī li-dhikrāki hizzatun, “a trembling comes over me at the thought of you”: the remembering is mine, the coming over is the trembling's. Not the same time: fa-jiʾtu wa-qad naḍḍat li-nawmin thiyābahā, “I came when she had put off her clothes for sleep”: the undressing came before the sleep.

terms.en: the absolute object: a maṣdar of the verb's wording or meaning
an extra: a word the sentence is complete without
the object of reason: a maṣdar sharing the time and the doer

examples.en: of its own wording; of its meaning
a number in the place of the maṣdar (Q 24:4)
qumtu ijlālan laka: the object of reason
the doer differs, so the reason takes the lām

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of ḍarban in ḍarabtu ḍarban and of julūsan in qaʿadtu julūsan.
tasks.answer: Both are absolute objects in naṣb. Ḍarban is governed by a verb of its own letters (ḍaraba); julūsan by a verb of its meaning with other letters (qaʿada).

tasks.prompt: What stands in the place of the maṣdar in fa-jlidūhum thamānīna jaldatan, and in fa-lā tamīlū kulla al-mayli?
tasks.arabic: فَاجْلِدُوهُمْ ثَمَانِينَ جَلْدَةً — فَلَا تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ
tasks.answer: A number, thamānīna, joined by its tamyīz to the maṣdar jalda; and kull, joined to the maṣdar al-mayl. Each is in naṣb in the place of the absolute object.

tasks.prompt: Why does the reason take the lām in li-dhikrāki, but not in qumtu ijlālan laka?
tasks.answer: In qumtu ijlālan laka the maṣdar shares the time and the doer of the verb, so it is a mafʿūl lahu in naṣb. In li-dhikrāki the doer differs (the remembering is the poet's, the coming over is the trembling's), so a condition is missing and the reason takes the lām.

quiz.prompt: The absolute object is…
options: a maṣdar governed by a verb of its wording or meaning
quiz.explanation: Ḍarabtu ḍarban; qaʿadtu julūsan.

quiz.prompt: In qaʿadtu julūsan, julūsan is governed by a verb…
quiz.explanation: Qaʿada and julūs mean the same.

quiz.prompt: In ḍarabtuhu sawṭan, sawṭan stands for the maṣdar as…
quiz.explanation: “A whip-stroke.”

quiz.prompt: Raghadan in wa-kulā minhā raghadan is…
options: not an absolute object, as the book says
quiz.explanation: The commentators take it as a ḥāl.

quiz.prompt: The object of reason shares with its verb…
quiz.explanation: Qumtu ijlālan laka.

quiz.prompt: In khalaqa lakum, the reason takes the lām because…
quiz.explanation: Lakum is a pronoun, not a maṣdar.

quiz.prompt: In naḍḍat li-nawmin thiyābahā, which condition is missing?
quiz.explanation: She undressed before the sleep.

text.original: وَالْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ، وَهُوَ الْمَصْدَرُ الْفَضْلَةُ الْمُسَلَّطُ عَلَيْهِ عَامِلٌ مِنْ لَفْظِهِ كَضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبًا، أَوْ مِنْ مَعْنَاهُ كَقَعَدْتُ جُلُوسًا، وَقَدْ يَنُوبُ عَنْهُ غَيْرُهُ كَضَرَبْتُهُ سَوْطًا، فَاجْلِدُوهُمْ ثَمَانِينَ جَلْدَةً، فَلَا تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ، بَعْضَ الْأَقَاوِيلِ. وَلَيْسَ مِنْهُ: وَكُلَا مِنْهَا رَغَدًا.
text.en: And the mafʿūl muṭlaq, which is the maṣdar that is an extra (faḍla), on which a governor of its own wording is brought to bear, as ḍarabtu ḍarban “I hit a hitting”, or [one] of its meaning, as qaʿadtu julūsan “I sat a sitting”. Something else may take its place, as ḍarabtuhu sawṭan “I hit him a whip[-stroke]”, fa-ijlidūhum thamānīna jaldatan “then flog them eighty lashes” [24:4], fa-lā tamīlū kulla al-mayli “so do not incline wholly” [4:129] and baʿḍa al-aqāwīli “some sayings” [69:44]. Not of it is wa-kulā minhā raghadan “and eat of it freely” [2:35].

text.original: وَالْمَفْعُولُ لَهُ، وَهُوَ الْمَصْدَرُ الْمُعَلِّلُ لِحَدَثٍ شَارَكَهُ وَقْتًا وَفَاعِلًا كَقُمْتُ إِجْلَالًا لَكَ، فَإِنْ فَقَدَ الْمُعَلِّلُ شَرْطًا جُرَّ بِحَرْفِ التَّعْلِيلِ نَحْوُ: خَلَقَ لَكُمْ، وَ: وَإِنِّي لَتَعْرُونِي لِذِكْرَاكِ هِزَّةٌ، وَ: فَجِئْتُ وَقَدْ نَضَّتْ لِنَوْمٍ ثِيَابَهَا.
text.en: And the mafʿūl lahu, which is the maṣdar that gives the reason for an event with which it shares the time and the doer, as qumtu ijlālan laka “I stood out of respect for you”. If the [word] giving the reason lacks a condition, it is put in jarr by a particle of reason, as khalaqa lakum “He created for you” [2:29], wa-innī la-taʿrūnī li-dhikrāki hizzatun “and a trembling comes over me at the thought of you” and fa-jiʾtu wa-qad naḍḍat li-nawmin thiyābahā “and I came when she had put off her clothes for sleep”.

lessons.title: The object of time and place; the object of accompaniment
body: The object of time and place (mafʿūl fīhi, also called ẓarf) is a word governed “in the sense of fī”, “in”. Any noun of time can be one, definite or not: ṣumtu yawma al-khamīsi, “I fasted on Thursday”; ṣumtu ḥīnan, “a while”; usbūʿan, “a week”.

A noun of place can be one only if it is vague (mubham): the six directions, al-amām, al-fawq, al-yamīn and their opposites, behind, below and on the left; words like them, ʿinda, “at”, and ladā, “with”; the measures, as al-farsakh, “the parasang”; and a noun of place formed from the maṣdar of its own governor: qaʿadtu maqʿada Zaydin, “I sat in Zayd's seat”. A place with its own bounds, as al-dār, “the house”, or al-masjid, is not a ẓarf: one says ṣallaytu fī al-masjidi, with fī spoken.

The object of accompaniment (mafʿūl maʿahu) is “an extra noun after a wāw by which accompaniment is meant expressly”, coming after a verb or a word with a verb's letters and meaning: sirtu wa-l-Nīla, “I travelled along the Nile”; anā sāʾirun wa-l-Nīla. The Nile did not travel; the wāw means “with”, and the noun is in naṣb. Without a verb before it, as in kullu rajulin wa-ḍayʿatuhu (lesson 17), there is no mafʿūl maʿahu.

Sometimes the naṣb is necessary, because joining by “and” is impossible or spoils the sense: lā tanha ʿani al-qabīḥi wa-ityānahu, “do not forbid what is ugly while doing it”, since joining would mean “do not forbid its doing”; qumtu wa-Zaydan, since joining to the pronoun of qumtu would need anā first; marartu bika wa-Zaydan, since joining to a pronoun in jarr would need bi- again. It is preferred in kun anta wa-Zaydan ka-l-akhi, “be, you with Zayd, like a brother”, since the command kun cannot govern Zayd; and it is weak in qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, where joining is natural.

terms.en: the object of time and place (ẓarf), in the sense of fī
vague: a place without bounds of its own, as the directions
the object of accompaniment, after the wāw of “with”

examples.en: ṣumtu yawma al-khamīsi: a noun of time in naṣb
qaʿadtu maqʿada Zaydin: a place formed from the governor's maṣdar
sirtu wa-l-Nīla: the object of accompaniment
naṣb necessary: joining would spoil the sense

tasks.prompt: Which of these can be a ẓarf in naṣb, and which need fī: yawma al-khamīsi; al-masjidi; al-amāma; maqʿada Zaydin?
tasks.answer: Yawma al-khamīsi (a time), al-amāma (a direction) and maqʿada Zaydin (a place formed from the maṣdar of qaʿadtu) can be in naṣb as ẓarfs. Al-masjidi is a bounded place, so it needs fī: fī al-masjidi.

tasks.prompt: Why is the naṣb necessary in lā tanha ʿani al-qabīḥi wa-ityānahu?
tasks.answer: Joining ityānahu to al-qabīḥi would mean “do not forbid what is ugly and do not forbid doing it”, which spoils the sense. The meaning is “do not forbid it while doing it”: the wāw is “with”, so ityānahu is a mafʿūl maʿahu in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why is the naṣb preferred in kun anta wa-Zaydan ka-l-akhi?
tasks.answer: Joining Zayd to anta would make him governed by the command kun, which addresses only the one present. So the wāw is better taken as “with”, and Zaydan as the object of accompaniment.

quiz.prompt: The mafʿūl fīhi is governed in the sense of…
quiz.explanation: It is also called the ẓarf.

quiz.prompt: Which noun of place can be a ẓarf in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: Only vague places: the directions, ʿinda, ladā, measures.

quiz.prompt: In qaʿadtu maqʿada Zaydin, maqʿada is a ẓarf because…
options: it is formed from the maṣdar of its governor
quiz.explanation: Qaʿada governs maqʿad, from the same root.

quiz.prompt: The mafʿūl maʿahu comes after…
quiz.explanation: Sirtu wa-l-Nīla.

quiz.prompt: In qumtu wa-Zaydan, the naṣb is necessary because…
options: joining to the pronoun of qumtu would need anā
quiz.explanation: In the soundest view, as the book says.

quiz.prompt: In qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, the naṣb of ʿAmr would be…
quiz.explanation: Joining is natural: both stood.

quiz.prompt: In anā sāʾirun wa-l-Nīla, what comes before the wāw?
options: a word with a verb's letters and meaning
quiz.explanation: Sāʾir has the letters and meaning of sāra.

text.original: وَالْمَفْعُولُ فِيهِ، وَهُوَ مَا سُلِّطَ عَلَيْهِ عَامِلٌ عَلَى مَعْنَى فِي مِنِ اسْمِ زَمَانٍ كَصُمْتُ يَوْمَ الْخَمِيسِ، أَوْ حِينًا، أَوْ أُسْبُوعًا، أَوِ اسْمِ مَكَانٍ مُبْهَمٍ، وَهُوَ الْجِهَاتُ السِّتُّ كَالْأَمَامِ وَالْفَوْقِ وَالْيَمِينِ وَعَكْسِهِنَّ، وَنَحْوُهُنَّ كَعِنْدَ وَلَدَى، وَالْمَقَادِيرُ كَالْفَرْسَخِ، وَمَا صِيغَ مِنْ مَصْدَرِ عَامِلِهِ كَقَعَدْتُ مَقْعَدَ زَيْدٍ.
text.en: And the mafʿūl fīhi, which is that on which a governor is brought to bear in the sense of fī “in”: a noun of time, as ṣumtu yawma al-khamīsi “I fasted on Thursday”, or ḥīnan “a while”, or usbūʿan “a week”; or a vague noun of place, which is the six directions, as al-amām “in front”, al-fawq “above” and al-yamīn “on the right”, and their opposites, and what is like them, as ʿinda “at” and ladā “with”; and the measures, as al-farsakh “the parasang”; and what is formed from the maṣdar of its governor, as qaʿadtu maqʿada Zaydin “I sat in Zayd's seat”.

text.original: وَالْمَفْعُولُ مَعَهُ، وَهُوَ اسْمٌ فَضْلَةٌ بَعْدَ وَاوٍ أُرِيدَ بِهَا التَّنْصِيصُ عَلَى الْمَعِيَّةِ، مَسْبُوقَةٍ بِفِعْلٍ أَوْ مَا فِيهِ حُرُوفُهُ وَمَعْنَاهُ، كَسِرْتُ وَالنِّيلَ، وَأَنَا سَائِرٌ وَالنِّيلَ.
text.en: And the mafʿūl maʿahu, which is an extra noun after a wāw by which accompaniment is meant expressly, preceded by a verb or by what has its letters and its meaning, as sirtu wa-al-nīla “I travelled along the Nile” and anā sāʾirun wa-al-nīla “I am travelling along the Nile”.

text.original: وَقَدْ يَجِبُ كَقَوْلِكَ: لَا تَنْهَ عَنِ الْقَبِيحِ وَإِتْيَانَهُ، وَمِنْهُ: قُمْتُ وَزَيْدًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِكَ وَزَيْدًا، عَلَى الْأَصَحِّ فِيهِمَا. وَيَتَرَجَّحُ فِي نَحْوِ: كُنْ أَنْتَ وَزَيْدًا كَالْأَخِ، وَيَضْعُفُ فِي نَحْوِ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو.
text.en: It is sometimes necessary, as your saying lā tanha ʿani al-qabīḥi wa-ityānahu “do not forbid what is ugly while doing it”; and of this are qumtu wa-Zaydan “I stood with Zayd” and marartu bi-ka wa-Zaydan “I passed by you with Zayd”, in the soundest view of both. It is preferred in the like of kun anta wa-Zaydan ka-al-akhi “be, you with Zayd, like a brother”, and weak in the like of qāma Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun “Zayd and ʿAmr stood”.

lessons.title: The ḥāl
body: The ḥāl is “an extra adjective that comes in answer to ‘how?’”: ḍarabtu al-liṣṣa maktūfan, “I beat the thief bound”. How was the thief when I beat him? Bound. It is an adjective (waṣf), a word made from a verb, as maktūf from katafa; this sets it apart from the tamyīz of the next lesson, which is a noun that is not made from a verb.

“Its condition is to be indefinite”: it tells a passing state, not who someone is. Its owner (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl), the one whose state it tells, is normally definite. The book gives four kinds of owner, each with a verse or a verse of poetry. Definite: khushshaʿan abṣāruhum yakhrujūna, “with downcast eyes they will come out” (Q 54:7), the owner being the pronoun of yakhrujūna. Made particular: fī arbaʿati ayyāmin sawāʾan (Q 41:10), the owner arbaʿati ayyāmin, made particular by iḍāfa.

General: mā ahlaknā min qaryatin illā lahā mundhirūna, “We destroyed no town but it had warners” (Q 26:208), where the sentence lahā mundhirūna is a ḥāl of qaryatin, which is general after the negation. And placed after the ḥāl: li-Mayyata mūḥishan ṭalalu, “Mayya has a ruin, desolate”, where the owner ṭalalu is indefinite but comes after its ḥāl.

That last verse teaches a rule. Had the poet said ṭalalun mūḥishun, mūḥishun would be an adjective (naʿt) following its noun. But an adjective may not come before its noun; so when the description is put first, it becomes a ḥāl and takes the naṣb: mūḥishan.

terms.en: an extra adjective answering “how?”
the owner of the ḥāl: the one whose state it tells
an adjective, made from a verb

examples.en: ḍarabtu al-liṣṣa maktūfan: “how?” bound
the owner definite: the pronoun of yakhrujūna (Q 54:7)
the owner made particular by iḍāfa (Q 41:10)
the owner placed after its ḥāl

tasks.prompt: Find the ḥāl and its owner in ḍarabtu al-liṣṣa maktūfan.
tasks.answer: Maktūfan is the ḥāl, indefinite, in naṣb; its owner is al-liṣṣa, definite. It answers “how was the thief?”: bound.

tasks.prompt: In fī arbaʿati ayyāmin sawāʾan, the owner arbaʿati ayyāmin is indefinite. Why is the ḥāl allowed?
tasks.answer: An indefinite owner is allowed if it is made particular. Arbaʿati is made particular by its iḍāfa to ayyāmin, so it may own the ḥāl sawāʾan.

tasks.prompt: Why is it mūḥishan, in naṣb, in li-Mayyata mūḥishan ṭalalu?
tasks.answer: The description comes before its noun ṭalalu. An adjective may not come before its noun, so it cannot be a naʿt; it becomes a ḥāl, in naṣb, with ṭalalu as its owner placed after it.

quiz.explanation: A definite owner, the doer of yakhrujūna.

quiz.explanation: An adjective may not precede its noun.

options: A noun in jarr by min alone
quiz.explanation: Definite, particular, general, placed after.

text.original: وَالْحَالُ، وَهُوَ وَصْفٌ فَضْلَةٌ يَقَعُ فِي جَوَابِ كَيْفَ، كَضَرَبْتُ اللِّصَّ مَكْتُوفًا. وَشَرْطُهَا التَّنْكِيرُ، وَصَاحِبِهَا التَّعْرِيفُ أَوِ التَّخْصِيصُ أَوِ التَّعْمِيمُ أَوِ التَّأْخِيرُ، نَحْوُ: خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ يَخْرُجُونَ، وَ: فِي أَرْبَعَةِ أَيَّامٍ سَوَاءً، وَ: مَا أَهْلَكْنَا مِنْ قَرْيَةٍ إِلَّا لَهَا مُنْذِرُونَ، وَ: لِمَيَّةَ مُوحِشًا طَلَلُ.
text.en: And the ḥāl, which is an extra adjective that comes in answer to “how?”, as ḍarabtu al-liṣṣa maktūfan “I beat the thief bound”. Its condition is to be indefinite, and that of its owner (ṣāḥib) to be definite, made particular, general or placed after it, as khushshaʿan abṣāruhum yakhrujūna “with downcast eyes they will come out” [54:7], fī arbaʿati ayyāmin sawāʾan “in four days, equal [for those who ask]” [41:10], mā ahlaknā min qaryatin illā lahā mundhirūna “We destroyed no town but it had warners” [26:208] and li-Mayyata mūḥishan ṭalalu “Mayya has a ruin, desolate”.

lessons.title: The tamyīz
body: The tamyīz is “an extra, indefinite, non-derived noun that explains what is vague among things”. Most often it follows a measure, jarībun nakhlan, “an acre of palms”, ṣāʿun tamran, “a ṣāʿ of dates”, manawāni ʿasalan, “two manns of honey”; or a number, aḥada ʿashara kawkaban, “eleven stars” (Q 12:4), and so on up to tisʿun wa-tisʿūna naʿjatan, “ninety-nine ewes” (Q 38:23); or the asking kam, kam ʿabdan malakta, “how many slaves have you owned?”.

The kam that tells of a great number (al-khabariyya) takes its tamyīz in jarr, not naṣb: singular, as after a hundred, “how many a slave I have owned!”; or plural, as after ten and below. And when the asking kam is itself put in jarr by a particle, as in “for how many dirhams…?”, its tamyīz may be in jarr or in naṣb.

A tamyīz may also explain a relation (nisba) rather than a thing. Often it is “turned” from another part of the sentence: ishtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban, “the head is aflame with grey hair” (Q 19:4), from “the grey hair of the head is aflame”, turned from the doer; wa-fajjarnā al-arḍa ʿuyūnan, “We made the earth burst forth with springs” (Q 54:12), from “the springs of the earth”, turned from the object; anā aktharu minka mālan, “I have more wealth than you” (Q 18:34), from “my wealth is more”, turned from the subject. Or it is not turned: imtalaʾa al-ināʾu māʾan, “the vessel was filled with water”.

The ḥāl and the tamyīz may also only emphasize, saying again what is already said: wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīna, “do not go about the earth making mischief” (Q 2:60), where ʿathā already means to make mischief; and biʾsa al-faḥlu faḥluhum faḥlā, “how bad a stallion is their stallion, as a stallion!”. The last is “against Sībawayh”, who did not allow a tamyīz where the doer of niʿma or biʾsa is spoken.

terms.en: an indefinite, non-derived noun that explains a vagueness
the tamyīz of a relation, often turned from doer, object or subject
the kam that tells of a great number: its tamyīz in jarr
turned: a tamyīz moved from another part of the sentence

examples.en: after a measure: an acre of palms, a ṣāʿ of dates
kam ʿabdan malakta: the tamyīz of the asking kam
ishtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban (Q 19:4): turned from the doer
a ḥāl of emphasis (Q 2:60)

tasks.prompt: Find the tamyīz and what it explains: aḥada ʿashara kawkaban; manawāni ʿasalan; kam ʿabdan malakta.
tasks.arabic: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا — مَنَوَانِ عَسَلًا — كَمْ عَبْدًا مَلَكْتَ
tasks.answer: Kawkaban explains the number eleven; ʿasalan explains the measure “two manns”; ʿabdan explains the asking kam. All three are indefinite, non-derived nouns in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: From what has the tamyīz been turned in wa-fajjarnā al-arḍa ʿuyūnan and in anā aktharu minka mālan?
tasks.arabic: وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا — أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مَالًا
tasks.answer: In the first from the object: “We made the springs of the earth burst forth”. In the second from the subject: “my wealth is more than yours”.

tasks.prompt: How does the tamyīz of the telling kam differ from that of the asking kam?
tasks.answer: The asking kam takes its tamyīz in naṣb, singular (kam ʿabdan malakta?). The telling kam takes it in jarr, singular like the tamyīz of a hundred or plural like that of ten and below.

text.original: وَالتَّمْيِيزُ، وَهُوَ اسْمٌ فَضْلَةٌ نَكِرَةٌ جَامِدٌ مُفَسِّرٌ لِمَا انْبَهَمَ مِنَ الذَّوَاتِ، وَأَكْثَرُ وُقُوعِهِ بَعْدَ الْمَقَادِيرِ كَجَرِيبٍ نَخْلًا، وَصَاعٍ تَمْرًا، وَمَنَوَيْنِ عَسَلًا، وَالْعَدَدِ نَحْوُ: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا إِلَى تِسْعٍ وَتِسْعِينَ نَعْجَةً، وَمِنْهُ تَمْيِيزُ كَمِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِيَّةِ نَحْوُ: كَمْ عَبْدًا مَلَكْتَ؟
text.en: And the tamyīz, which is an extra, indefinite, non-derived (jāmid) noun that explains what is vague among things. It mostly comes after measures, as jarībin nakhlan “an acre of palms”, ṣāʿin tamran “a ṣāʿ of dates” and manawayni ʿasalan “two manns of honey”, and after number, as aḥada ʿashara kawkaban “eleven stars” [12:4] up to tisʿin wa-tisʿīna naʿjatan “ninety-nine ewes” [38:23]; and of it is the tamyīz of the interrogative kam, as kam ʿabdan malakta “how many slaves have you owned?”.

text.original: فَأَمَّا تَمْيِيزُ الْخَبَرِيَّةِ فَمَجْرُورٌ، مُفْرَدٌ كَتَمْيِيزِ الْمِائَةِ وَمَا فَوْقَهَا، أَوْ مَجْمُوعٌ كَتَمْيِيزِ الْعَشَرَةِ وَمَا دُونَهَا، وَلَكَ فِي تَمْيِيزِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِيَّةِ الْمَجْرُورَةِ بِالْحَرْفِ جَرٌّ وَنَصْبٌ.
text.en: As for the tamyīz of the declarative [kam], it is majrūr: singular, like the tamyīz of a hundred and what is above it, or plural, like the tamyīz of ten and what is below it. With the interrogative [kam] that is put in jarr by a particle, its tamyīz may be in jarr or in naṣb.

text.original: وَيَكُونُ التَّمْيِيزُ مُفَسِّرًا لِلنِّسْبَةِ مُحَوَّلًا كَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا، وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا، وَأَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنْكَ مَالًا، أَوْ غَيْرَ مُحَوَّلٍ نَحْوُ: امْتَلَأَ الْإِنَاءُ مَاءً.
text.en: The tamyīz may explain a relation (nisba), either turned [from another part of the sentence], as ishtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban “the head is aflame with grey hair” [19:4], wa-fajjarnā al-arḍa ʿuyūnan “and We made the earth burst forth with springs” [54:12] and anā aktharu minka mālan “I have more wealth than you” [18:34], or not turned, as imtalaʾa al-ināʾu māʾan “the vessel was filled with water”.

text.original: وَقَدْ يُؤَكِّدَانِ نَحْوُ: وَلَا تَعْثَوْا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ، وَقَوْلِهِ: مِنْ خَيْرِ أَدْيَانِ الْبَرِيَّةِ دِينَا، وَمِنْهُ: بِئْسَ الْفَحْلُ فَحْلُهُمْ فَحْلَا، خِلَافًا لِسِيبَوَيْهِ.
text.en: The two [the ḥāl and the tamyīz] may emphasize, as wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīna “and do not go about the earth making mischief” [2:60], and the poet's saying min khayri adyāni al-bariyyati dīnā “of the best religions of mankind, as a religion”; and of it is biʾsa al-faḥlu faḥluhum faḥlā “how bad a stallion is their stallion, as a stallion”, against Sībawayh.

lessons.title: The excepted (mustathnā)
body: The excepted after illā, “from complete affirmative speech”, is in naṣb: fa-sharibū minhu illā qalīlan minhum, “they drank of it, except a few of them” (Q 2:249). “Complete” means that the one it is taken from (al-mustathnā minhu) is named; “affirmative” that there is no negation, prohibition or question.

If the speech is complete but not affirmative, the rule depends on whether the excepted is of the same kind. If it is (muttaṣil, connected), it is better made a badal of the one it is taken from, in the same state: mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum, “they would not have done it, except a few of them” (Q 4:66), qalīlun following the wāw of faʿalūhu; the naṣb is allowed, and was read by Ibn ʿĀmir. If it is not (munqaṭiʿ, disconnected), the naṣb is preferred among the Banū Tamīm and necessary among the people of the Ḥijāz: mā lahum bihi min ʿilmin illā ittibāʿa al-ẓanni, “they have no knowledge of it, only the following of conjecture” (Q 4:157), conjecture being no kind of knowledge.

If the excepted comes before what it is taken from, it is in naṣb in either case: wa-mā liya illā āla Aḥmada shīʿatun, “I have no party but the family of Aḥmad”. And if the speech is not complete, with nothing named to take from, the excepted takes whatever ending the governor before illā requires, as if illā were not there: wa-mā Muḥammadun illā rasūlun (Q 3:144). This is called the “emptied” exception (mufarragh): the governor has been emptied for the word after illā.

Other words of exception: ghayr and siwā put the excepted in khafḍ, by iḍāfa, and themselves take the ending that the noun after illā would have taken: qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin. Khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā put it in naṣb, as verbs, or in khafḍ, as particles. Mā khalā, mā ʿadā, laysa and lā yakūnu put it only in naṣb, since they are verbs: the mā before khalā and ʿadā can only stand before a verb.

terms.en: the excepted
connected (of the same kind) and disconnected exception
the emptied exception: nothing named to take from
what the excepted is taken from

examples.en: complete and affirmative: naṣb (Q 2:249)
complete, negative, connected: badal preferred (Q 4:66)

examples.en: disconnected: naṣb (Q 4:157)

tasks.prompt: Why is qalīlan in naṣb in fa-sharibū minhu illā qalīlan minhum, but qalīlun in rafʿ in mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum?
tasks.arabic: فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ — مَا فَعَلُوهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ مِنْهُمْ
tasks.answer: The first is complete and affirmative, so the excepted is in naṣb. The second is complete but negative, and the few are of the same kind as those who did not do it, so the better way is a badal of the wāw of faʿalūhu, in rafʿ like it.

tasks.prompt: Why is ittibāʿa in naṣb in mā lahum bihi min ʿilmin illā ittibāʿa al-ẓanni?
tasks.arabic: مَا لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا اتِّبَاعَ الظَّنِّ
tasks.answer: The exception is disconnected: following conjecture is not a kind of knowledge. With a disconnected exception the naṣb is necessary in the usage of the Ḥijāz, which the Qurʾān follows here.

tasks.prompt: What is the iʿrāb of ghayr in qāma al-qawmu ghayra Zaydin, and why?
tasks.answer: Ghayra is in naṣb, the ending the noun after illā would have in qāma al-qawmu illā Zaydan (complete and affirmative); Zaydin is in khafḍ by iḍāfa to it.

quiz.prompt: After illā in complete affirmative speech, the excepted is in…
quiz.explanation: Fa-sharibū minhu illā qalīlan minhum.

quiz.prompt: In complete negative speech with a connected exception, the better way is…
quiz.explanation: Mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum (Q 4:66).

quiz.prompt: A disconnected (munqaṭiʿ) exception is one where the excepted…
options: is not of the kind of what it is taken from
quiz.explanation: Conjecture is not knowledge (Q 4:157).

quiz.prompt: Among the people of the Ḥijāz, a disconnected excepted is…
quiz.explanation: The Banū Tamīm prefer naṣb but allow the badal.

quiz.prompt: In wa-mā Muḥammadun illā rasūlun, the exception is…
quiz.explanation: Nothing is named to take from; rasūlun is the predicate.

quiz.prompt: Ghayr and siwā put the excepted in…
quiz.explanation: By iḍāfa; ghayr itself takes the ending of the noun after illā.

quiz.prompt: After mā ʿadā, the excepted is…
quiz.explanation: Mā can only come before a verb here.

text.original: وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى بِإِلَّا مِنْ كَلَامٍ تَامٍّ مُوجَبٍ نَحْوُ: فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ. فَإِنْ فُقِدَ الْإِيجَابُ تَرَجَّحَ الْبَدَلُ فِي الْمُتَّصِلِ نَحْوُ: مَا فَعَلُوهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلٌ مِنْهُمْ، وَالنَّصْبُ فِي الْمُنْقَطِعِ عِنْدَ بَنِي تَمِيمٍ، وَوَجَبَ عِنْدَ الْحِجَازِيِّينَ، نَحْوُ: مَا لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا اتِّبَاعَ الظَّنِّ،
text.en: And the mustathnā by illā from complete affirmative speech, as fa-sharibū minhu illā qalīlan minhum “they drank of it, except a few of them” [2:249]. If [the speech] is not affirmative, the badal is preferred in the connected [exception], as mā faʿalūhu illā qalīlun minhum “they would not have done it, except a few of them” [4:66], and naṣb in the disconnected among the Banū Tamīm, while among the people of the Ḥijāz it is necessary, as mā lahum bi-hi min ʿilmin illā ittibāʿa al-ẓanni “they have no knowledge of it, only the following of conjecture” [4:157];

text.original: مَا لَمْ يَتَقَدَّمْ فِيهِمَا فَالنَّصْبُ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ: وَمَا لِيَ إِلَّا آلَ أَحْمَدَ شِيعَةٌ * وَمَا لِيَ إِلَّا مَذْهَبَ الْحَقِّ مَذْهَبُ. أَوْ فُقِدَ التَّمَامُ فَعَلَى حَسَبِ الْعَوَامِلِ نَحْوُ: وَمَا مُحَمَّدٌ إِلَّا رَسُولٌ، وَيُسَمَّى مُفَرَّغًا.
text.en: as long as [the mustathnā] does not come first in either, for then [it takes] naṣb, as the poet's saying wa-mā liya illā āla Aḥmada shīʿatun / wa-mā liya illā madhhaba al-ḥaqqi madhhabu “I have no party but the family of Aḥmad, and I have no way but the way of the truth”. If [the speech] is not complete, [the mustathnā takes its iʿrāb] according to the governors, as wa-mā Muḥammadun illā rasūlun “Muḥammad is only a messenger” [3:144]; and it is called emptied (mufarragh).

text.original: وَالْمُسْتَثْنَى بِغَيْرٍ وَسِوًى خَافِضَيْنِ مُعْرَبَيْنِ بِإِعْرَابِ الِاسْمِ الَّذِي بَعْدَ إِلَّا، وَبِخَلَا وَعَدَا وَحَاشَا نَوَاصِبَ وَخَوَافِضَ، وَبِمَا خَلَا وَبِمَا عَدَا وَلَيْسَ وَلَا يَكُونُ نَوَاصِبَ.
text.en: The mustathnā by ghayr and siwan: these two put it in khafḍ and are inflected with the iʿrāb of the noun after illā. By khalā, ʿadā and ḥāshā: these put it in naṣb or in khafḍ. And by mā khalā, mā ʿadā, laysa and lā yakūnu: these put it in naṣb.

lessons.title: The words in khafḍ: by a particle and by iḍāfa
body: “A noun is put in khafḍ either by a particle or by iḍāfa.” The particles are of two kinds. Some go both with an explicit noun and with a pronoun: min, ilā, ʿan, ʿalā, fī, the lām and the bāʾ (the bāʾ for an oath and for its other meanings): minhu, ilayka, bihi. Others go only with an explicit noun: rubba, mudh, mundhu, the kāf, ḥattā, and the wāw and the tāʾ of the oath. One says bihi la-afʿalanna, swearing by a pronoun with the bāʾ, but never with the wāw.

Iḍāfa of meaning (maʿnawiyya) joins a noun to another “in the sense of” a particle: of the lām, ghulāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's servant”, a servant belonging to Zayd; of min, khātamu ḥadīdin, “a ring of iron”, a ring made from iron; of fī, makru al-layli, “scheming by night” (Q 34:33), scheming in the night. It is called “of meaning” because it does something to the meaning: it makes the first noun definite, if the second is definite, or particular, if the second is indefinite.

Iḍāfa of wording (lafẓiyya) joins an adjective to the word it governs: bāligha al-kaʿbati, “reaching the Kaʿba” (Q 5:95); muʿṭī al-qadri, “one who gives the cooking-pot”; ḥasanu al-wajhi, “handsome of face”. It is called “of wording” because it only lightens the word, taking away its tanwīn or nūn; it does not make it definite. In the verse, hadyan bāligha al-kaʿbati, the adjective of an indefinite hadyan is still indefinite after its iḍāfa.

Iḍāfa never goes with tanwīn, nor with the nūn of the dual or plural, and not with al-. The only exception is in iḍāfa of wording: al- may stand on the first word when it is a dual or plural, al-ḍāribā Zaydin, al-ḍāribū Zaydin; or when the second word has al-, al-ḍāribu al-rajuli, or is joined to one that has it, al-ḍāribu raʾsi al-rajuli, or to a pronoun of one that has it, al-rajulu al-ḍāribu ghulāmihi.

terms.en: the particles of khafḍ (jarr)
iḍāfa of meaning: makes definite or particular
iḍāfa of wording: only lightens

examples.en: in the sense of the lām and of min
makri al-layli (Q 34:33): in the sense of fī
iḍāfa of wording: an adjective joined to what it governs
al-ḍāribū Zaydin: al- with iḍāfa, allowed in a plural

diagram.caption: What puts a noun in khafḍ (p. 33)

tasks.prompt: In what sense is each iḍāfa: ghulāmu Zaydin; khātamu ḥadīdin; makru al-layli?
tasks.arabic: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ — خَاتَمُ حَدِيدٍ — مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ
tasks.answer: Ghulāmu Zaydin: of the lām, “a servant belonging to Zayd”. Khātamu ḥadīdin: of min, “a ring made of iron”. Makru al-layli: of fī, “scheming in the night”.

tasks.prompt: How does the verse hadyan bāligha al-kaʿbati show that iḍāfa of wording does not make a word definite?
tasks.answer: Bāligha al-kaʿbati describes hadyan, which is indefinite; an adjective agrees with its noun in definiteness. So bāligha is still indefinite, though it is joined to the definite al-kaʿbati.

tasks.prompt: Why may one say al-ḍāribū Zaydin, though iḍāfa does not go with al-?
tasks.answer: It is iḍāfa of wording, and the first word is a plural that has lost its nūn by the iḍāfa: in that case al- is allowed. In iḍāfa of meaning al- is never allowed on the first word.

quiz.prompt: Which particle of khafḍ goes only with an explicit noun?
quiz.explanation: Rubba, mudh, mundhu, the kāf, ḥattā, and the wāw and tāʾ of oath.

quiz.prompt: Khātamu ḥadīdin is an iḍāfa in the sense of…
quiz.explanation: A ring made of iron.

quiz.prompt: Makru al-layli is an iḍāfa in the sense of…
quiz.explanation: Scheming in the night (Q 34:33).

quiz.prompt: Iḍāfa of meaning is called so because it…
options: makes the first noun definite or particular
quiz.explanation: It does something to the meaning.

quiz.prompt: Ḥasanu al-wajhi is an iḍāfa of…
quiz.explanation: An adjective joined to what it governs.

quiz.prompt: Iḍāfa of wording…
options: is in the sense of fī
only lightens, taking away tanwīn or nūn
quiz.explanation: Hadyan bāligha al-kaʿbati stays indefinite.

quiz.prompt: Al- on the first word of an iḍāfa is allowed in…
quiz.explanation: Only in iḍāfa of wording, in the cases the book lists.

text.original: يُخْفَضُ الِاسْمُ إِمَّا بِحَرْفٍ مُشْتَرَكٍ، وَهُوَ مِنْ، وَإِلَى، وَعَنْ، وَعَلَى، وَفِي، وَاللَّامُ، وَالْبَاءُ لِلْقَسَمِ وَغَيْرِهَا، أَوْ مُخْتَصٍّ بِالظَّاهِرِ، وَهُوَ رُبَّ، وَمُذْ، وَمُنْذُ، وَالْكَافُ، وَحَتَّى، وَوَاوُ الْقَسَمِ وَتَاؤُهُ.
text.en: A noun is put in khafḍ either by a particle shared [by the explicit noun and the pronoun], which is min “from”, ilā “to”, ʿan “away from”, ʿalā “on”, fī “in”, the lām, and the bāʾ, [this last] for oath and for other [meanings]; or by one reserved for the explicit noun, which is rubba “many a”, mudh and mundhu “since”, the kāf, ḥattā “until”, and the wāw and the tāʾ of oath.

text.original: أَوْ بِإِضَافَةٍ إِلَى اسْمٍ عَلَى مَعْنَى اللَّامِ كَغُلَامِ زَيْدٍ، أَوْ مِنْ كَخَاتَمِ حَدِيدٍ، أَوْ فِي كَمَكْرِ اللَّيْلِ، وَتُسَمَّى مَعْنَوِيَّةً؛ لِأَنَّهَا لِلتَّعْرِيفِ أَوِ التَّخْصِيصِ.
text.en: Or by iḍāfa to a noun in the sense of the lām, as ghulāmi Zaydin “Zayd's servant”, or of min, as khātami ḥadīdin “a ring of iron”, or of fī, as makri al-layli “scheming by night” [34:33]; and it is called iḍāfa of meaning (maʿnawiyya), because it serves to make definite or particular.

text.original: وَبِإِضَافَةِ الْوَصْفِ إِلَى مَعْمُولِهِ كَبَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ، وَمُعْطِي الْقَدْرِ، وَحَسَنِ الْوَجْهِ، وَتُسَمَّى لَفْظِيَّةً؛ لِأَنَّهَا لِمُجَرَّدِ التَّخْفِيفِ. وَلَا تُجَامِعُ الْإِضَافَةُ تَنْوِينًا، وَلَا نُونًا تَالِيَةً لِلْإِعْرَابِ مُطْلَقًا، وَلَا أَلْ، إِلَّا فِي نَحْوِ: الضَّارِبَا زَيْدٍ، وَالضَّارِبُو زَيْدٍ، وَالضَّارِبِ الرَّجُلِ، وَالضَّارِبِ رَأْسِ الرَّجُلِ، وَالرَّجُلِ الضَّارِبِ غُلَامِهِ.
text.en: And by the iḍāfa of an adjective to what it governs, as bāligha al-kaʿbati “reaching the Kaʿba” [5:95], muʿṭī al-qadri “one who gives the cooking-pot” and ḥasani al-wajhi “handsome of face”; and it is called iḍāfa of wording (lafẓiyya), because it serves only to lighten. Iḍāfa does not go together with tanwīn, nor with a nūn that follows the iʿrāb, in any case, nor with al-, except in the like of al-ḍāribā Zaydin “the two who hit Zayd”, al-ḍāribū Zaydin “those who hit Zayd”, al-ḍāribi al-rajuli “the one who hits the man”, al-ḍāribi raʾsi al-rajuli “the one who hits the man's head” and al-rajuli al-ḍāribi ghulāmihi “the man who hits his servant”.

parts.title: What governs as its verb governs

lessons.title: What works like its verb: the noun of a verb and the maṣdar
body: “Seven govern as their verb governs”: the noun of a verb, the maṣdar, the active participle, the intensive form, the passive participle, the resembling adjective and the elative. The first is the noun of a verb (ism al-fiʿl), a word with a verb's meaning: hayhāta, “it is far” (baʿuda), a past; ṣah, “be silent!” (uskut), a command; way, “I wonder!” (aʿjabu), a present.

It has its rules. It is not dropped, and it does not come after what it governs; kitāba Allāhi ʿalaykum, “[this is] God's decree for you” (Q 4:24), “is interpreted”, since otherwise kitāba would be governed by ʿalaykum placed after it. Its pronoun never shows: ṣah is said to one or to many. A muḍāriʿ may be put in jazm in answer to one that demands: makānaki tuḥmadī aw tastarīḥī, “[keep to] your place: you will be praised or have rest”. But it is not put in naṣb after the fāʾ in answer to it.

The maṣdar, ḍarb, “hitting”, or ikrām, “honouring”, governs like its verb “if a verb with an or mā can stand in its place”: aʿjabanī ḍarbuka Zaydan, “your hitting Zayd pleased me”, is “that you hit Zayd”. And on seven conditions: it is not a diminutive, not a pronoun, not limited to one act (ḍarbatan), not described before it governs, not dropped, not separated from what it governs, and not placed after it.

It governs most often as a muḍāf: joined to its doer, wa-lawlā dafʿu Allāhi al-nāsa, “were it not for God's repelling people” (Q 2:251); or to its object, with the doer after it, alā inna ẓulma nafsihi al-marʾu bayyinun, “a man's wronging himself is plain”. With tanwīn it is “more regular”, closest to the verb: aw iṭʿāmun fī yawmin dhī masghabatin yatīman, “or feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan” (Q 90:14–15). With al- it is “irregular”: wa-kayfa al-tawaqqī ẓahra mā anta rākibuhu.

terms.en: the noun of a verb: a word with a verb's meaning and work
the maṣdar that governs, when an or mā with a verb could replace it
the seven that govern as their verb governs

examples.en: hayhāta (past), ṣah (command), way (present): nouns of verbs
jazm in answer to a noun of a verb that demands
the maṣdar as muḍāf to its doer, with its object in naṣb (Q 2:251)

examples.arabic: أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ يَتِيمًا
examples.en: the maṣdar with tanwīn (Q 90:14–15)

tasks.prompt: Give the verb whose meaning each noun of a verb carries, and its time: hayhāta; ṣah; way.
tasks.answer: Hayhāta: baʿuda, “it is far”, a past. Ṣah: uskut, “be silent!”, a command. Way: aʿjabu, “I wonder”, a present.

tasks.prompt: In wa-lawlā dafʿu Allāhi al-nāsa, what does the maṣdar dafʿ govern?
tasks.answer: It is joined to its doer, Allāhi, in khafḍ by iḍāfa, and puts its object al-nāsa in naṣb, as its verb would: “that God repels people”.

tasks.prompt: Why can ḍarbatan, “one hit”, not govern like its verb?
tasks.answer: It is limited to one act (maḥdūd), and the maṣdar governs only if it is not limited. Ḍarbatan cannot be replaced by an with a verb in the same sense.

quiz.prompt: How many words does the book say govern as their verb governs?
quiz.explanation: Noun of a verb, maṣdar, two participles, intensive, resembling adjective, elative.

quiz.prompt: Ṣah means…
quiz.explanation: A noun of a verb in the sense of uskut.

quiz.prompt: The pronoun of a noun of a verb…
quiz.explanation: Ṣah is said to one or to many.

quiz.prompt: In answer to a noun of a verb that demands, the muḍāriʿ may be…
options: in jazm, but not in naṣb
quiz.explanation: Makānaki tuḥmadī aw tastarīḥī.

quiz.prompt: The maṣdar governs if…
options: a verb with an or mā can stand in its place
it comes after what it governs
quiz.explanation: Aʿjabanī ḍarbuka Zaydan = an ḍarabta Zaydan.

quiz.prompt: The maṣdar governs most regularly…
quiz.explanation: With tanwīn it is closest to the verb.

quiz.prompt: In alā inna ẓulma nafsihi al-marʾu bayyinun, al-marʾu is…
quiz.arabic: أَلَا إِنَّ ظُلْمَ نَفْسِهِ الْمَرْءُ بَيِّنٌ
options: the doer of the maṣdar, in rafʿ
quiz.explanation: The maṣdar is joined to its object, nafsihi, and its doer follows in rafʿ.

text.original: يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ سَبْعَةٌ: اسْمُ الْفِعْلِ، كَهَيْهَاتَ، وَصَهْ، وَوَيْ، بِمَعْنَى بَعُدَ وَاسْكُتْ وَأَعْجَبُ، وَلَا يُحْذَفُ، وَلَا يَتَأَخَّرُ عَنْ مَعْمُولِهِ، وَ«كِتَابَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ» مُتَأَوَّلٌ، وَلَا يَبْرُزُ ضَمِيرُهُ، وَيُجْزَمُ الْمُضَارِعُ فِي جَوَابِ الطَّلَبِيِّ مِنْهُ نَحْوُ: مَكَانَكِ تُحْمَدِي أَوْ تَسْتَرِيحِي، وَلَا يُنْصَبُ.
text.en: Seven [kinds of word] govern as their verb governs. The verbal noun (ism al-fiʿl), as hayhāta, ṣah and way, in the sense of baʿuda “it is far”, uskut “be silent!” and aʿjabu “I wonder”. It is not dropped and does not come after what it governs — kitāba Allāhi ʿalaykum “[this is] God's decree for you” [4:24] is interpreted [otherwise] —, and its pronoun does not appear. The muḍāriʿ is put in jazm in answer to one of them that expresses a demand, as makānaki tuḥmadī aw tastarīḥī “[keep to] your place: you will be praised or have rest”, but it is not put in naṣb.

text.original: وَالْمَصْدَرُ، كَضَرْبٍ وَإِكْرَامٍ، إِنْ حَلَّ مَحَلَّهُ فِعْلٌ مَعَ أَنْ أَوْ مَا، وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مُصَغَّرًا، وَلَا مُضْمَرًا، وَلَا مَحْدُودًا، وَلَا مَنْعُوتًا قَبْلَ الْعَمَلِ، وَلَا مَحْذُوفًا، وَلَا مَفْصُولًا مِنَ الْمَعْمُولِ بِهِ، وَلَا مُؤَخَّرًا عَنْهُ.
text.en: The maṣdar, as ḍarb “hitting” and ikrām “honouring”, if a verb with an or mā can stand in its place, and it is not diminutive, nor a pronoun, nor limited [to one act], nor described before it governs, nor dropped, nor separated from what it governs, nor placed after it.

text.original: وَإِعْمَالُهُ مُضَافًا أَكْثَرُ نَحْوُ: وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النَّاسَ، وَنَحْوُ: أَلَا إِنَّ ظُلْمَ نَفْسِهِ الْمَرْءُ بَيِّنٌ، وَمُنَوَّنًا أَقْيَسُ نَحْوُ: أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ يَتِيمًا، وَبِأَلْ شَاذٌّ نَحْوُ: وَكَيْفَ التَّوَقِّي ظَهْرَ مَا أَنْتَ رَاكِبُهُ.
text.en: It governs more often when muḍāf, as wa-lawlā dafʿu Allāhi al-nāsa “and were it not for God's repelling people” [2:251] and as alā inna ẓulma nafsihi al-marʾu bayyinun “indeed, a man's wronging himself is plain”; with tanwīn it is more regular, as aw iṭʿāmun fī yawmin dhī masghabatin yatīman “or feeding, on a day of hunger, an orphan” [90:14–15]; and with al- it is irregular, as wa-kayfa al-tawaqqī ẓahra mā anta rākibuhu “and how can one be wary of the back of what one is riding?”.

lessons.title: The active participle, the intensive form and the passive participle
body: The active participle, ḍārib, “hitting”, mukrim, “honouring”, governs like its verb. With al- it governs in every case: jāʾa al-ḍāribu Zaydan, “the one who hit Zayd came”, whatever the time. Without al- it needs two conditions: it must mean the present or the future, and it must lean (iʿtimād) on something before it: a negation, mā ḍāribun Zaydun ʿAmran; a question, a-ḍāribun Zaydun ʿAmran?; a word of which it is the predicate, Zaydun ḍāribun ʿAmran, “Zayd is hitting ʿAmr”; or a word it describes, marartu bi-rajulin ḍāribin ʿAmran.

Two verses seem to break the rule, and the book explains them. Wa-kalbuhum bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi, “and their dog stretching its forelegs” (Q 18:18), speaks of the past, yet bāsiṭun governs dhirāʿayhi: it is “the telling of a past state”, as if the hearer saw it now; al-Kisāʾī, against whom Ibn Hishām writes, let a participle of the past govern. And in khabīrun banū Lihbin, “the Banū Lihb are expert”, khabīr does not lean on anything: it is a predicate put before its subject, and khabīr is used for many, like ẓahīr, “helper”; al-Akhfash, who let the bare participle govern without leaning, read banū as its doer.

The intensive form (mithāl, later books say ṣīghat al-mubālagha) is a participle turned for intensity from fāʿil to faʿʿāl, faʿūl or mifʿāl, which govern often, or to faʿīl and faʿil, which govern seldom: ammā al-ʿasala fa-anā sharrābun, “as for honey, I am a great drinker of it”, where sharrāb governs al-ʿasala put before it.

The passive participle, maḍrūb, “hit”, mukram, “honoured”, governs as its passive verb does, on the same conditions as the active: Zaydun maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu, “Zayd, his servant is beaten”, where ghulāmuhu is the deputy of the doer, in rafʿ.

terms.en: the active participle: governs like its active verb
leaning on a negation, a question, a subject or a described noun
telling a past state as if it were present
the intensive form: faʿʿāl, faʿūl, mifʿāl, faʿīl, faʿil

examples.en: Zaydun ḍāribun ʿAmran: the participle leans on its subject (ḍārib from the engine)
wa-kalbuhum bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi (Q 18:18): the telling of a past state
the intensive sharrāb governs al-ʿasala
the passive participle with its deputy (maḍrūb from the engine)

tasks.prompt: Why does ḍāribun govern ʿAmran in Zaydun ḍāribun ʿAmran, and what two conditions are met?
tasks.answer: It is a bare active participle, so it needs two conditions: it means the present or the future (“is hitting, will hit”), and it leans on a word of which it is the predicate, Zaydun. So it puts ʿAmran in naṣb as its object.

tasks.prompt: How does Ibn Hishām explain bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi, which speaks of the past?
tasks.answer: As the telling of a past state (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl): the verse shows the scene as if it were present, so the participle has the present meaning it needs. Al-Kisāʾī instead allowed a participle of the past to govern.

tasks.prompt: In Zaydun maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu, what is ghulāmuhu, and why?
tasks.answer: The deputy of the doer, in rafʿ. Maḍrūb, the passive participle, governs as its passive verb would (ḍuriba ghulāmuhu), and it leans on its subject Zaydun.

quiz.explanation: Against al-Kisāʾī.

quiz.explanation: Faʿʿāl, faʿūl and mifʿāl govern often.

quiz.explanation: Zaydun maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu.

text.original: وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ، كَضَارِبٍ وَمُكْرِمٍ، فَإِنْ كَانَ بِأَلْ عَمِلَ مُطْلَقًا، أَوْ مُجَرَّدًا فَبِشَرْطَيْنِ: كَوْنُهُ حَالًا أَوِ اسْتِقْبَالًا، وَاعْتِمَادُهُ عَلَى نَفْيٍ، أَوِ اسْتِفْهَامٍ، أَوْ مُخْبَرٍ عَنْهُ، أَوْ مَوْصُوفٍ.
text.en: The active participle, as ḍārib “hitting” and mukrim “honouring”. If it has al-, it governs in every case; if it is bare, on two conditions: that it is for the present or the future, and that it leans on a negation, a question, [a word] of which it is the khabar, or [a word] it describes.

text.original: وَ«كَلْبُهُمْ بَاسِطٌ ذِرَاعَيْهِ» عَلَى حِكَايَةِ الْحَالِ، خِلَافًا لِلْكِسَائِيِّ، وَ«خَبِيرٌ بَنُو لِهْبٍ» عَلَى التَّقْدِيمِ وَالتَّأْخِيرِ، وَتَقْدِيرُ خَبِيرٍ كَظَهِيرٍ، خِلَافًا لِلْأَخْفَشِ.
text.en: kalbuhum bāsiṭun dhirāʿayhi “and their dog stretching its forelegs” [18:18] is the telling of a past state, against al-Kisāʾī; and khabīrun banū Lihbin “the Banū Lihb are expert” is by putting first what comes later, khabīr being taken like ẓahīr “helper” [which is said of many], against al-Akhfash.

text.original: وَالْمِثَالُ، وَهُوَ مَا حُوِّلَ لِلْمُبَالَغَةِ مِنْ فَاعِلٍ إِلَى فَعَّالٍ أَوْ فَعُولٍ أَوْ مِفْعَالٍ بِكَثْرَةٍ، أَوْ فَعِيلٍ أَوْ فَعِلٍ بِقِلَّةٍ، نَحْوُ: أَمَّا الْعَسَلَ فَأَنَا شَرَّابٌ.
text.en: The intensive form (mithāl), which is what is turned, for intensity, from fāʿil into faʿʿāl, faʿūl or mifʿāl, often, or faʿīl or faʿil, seldom, as ammā al-ʿasala fa-anā sharrābun “as for honey, I am a great drinker [of it]”.

text.original: وَاسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ، كَمَضْرُوبٍ وَمُكْرَمٍ، وَيَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ، وَهُوَ كَاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ.
text.en: The passive participle, as maḍrūb “hit” and mukram “honoured”; it governs as its verb governs, and it is like the active participle.

lessons.title: The resembling adjective and the elative
body: The resembling adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha) is “likened to the active participle of a verb that takes one object”: an adjective, “formed not for preference, to convey permanence”, as ḥasan, “handsome”, ẓarīf, “witty”, ṭāhir, “pure”, ḍāmir, “lean”. The last two look like active participles, but they name a lasting quality, so they belong here. Unlike the participle it names a state, not an act, and it is likened to the participle only because it too takes a noun after it.

Two limits: what it governs never comes before it, and it is never a stranger: it must belong to the one described, as wajhuhu, “his face”, belongs to Zayd. Then the noun after it can take every state. Rafʿ, as its doer (or a badal): Zaydun ḥasanun wajhuhu. Naṣb, as a tamyīz, ḥasanun wajhan, or by likeness to an object, ḥasanun al-wajha, the second being the only way when the noun is definite. Khafḍ, by iḍāfa: ḥasanu al-wajhi.

The elative (ism al-tafḍīl), as akram, “more noble”, says that two share a quality and one exceeds. Used with min, or joined to an indefinite, it stays singular and masculine whatever it describes: Hindun afḍalu min ʿAmrin. With al- it agrees with its noun. Joined to a definite, both ways are allowed.

The elative never puts an object in naṣb, and mostly does not put a visible noun in rafʿ, “except in the question of the kohl”: mā raʾaytu rajulan aḥsana fī ʿaynihi al-kuḥlu minhu fī ʿayni Zaydin, “I have not seen a man in whose eye kohl is finer than in the eye of Zayd”. There aḥsana raises al-kuḥlu, because the sentence is negated and compares the kohl with itself in two places.

terms.en: the resembling adjective: a lasting quality
permanence: what the resembling adjective conveys
the elative: sharing a quality and exceeding in it
the question of the kohl: where the elative raises a visible noun

examples.en: Zaydun ḥasanun wajhuhu: the noun after it in rafʿ, as its doer
ḥasanu al-wajhi: in khafḍ, by iḍāfa
bi-afḍala minhu: the elative with min, singular and masculine

tasks.prompt: Give the four ways of the noun after ḥasan in Zaydun ḥasan- al-wajh-, with their names.
tasks.answer: Ḥasanun wajhuhu (rafʿ, as its doer); ḥasanun wajhan (naṣb, as a tamyīz, indefinite); ḥasanun al-wajha (naṣb, by likeness to an object, the only naṣb with a definite noun); ḥasanu al-wajhi (khafḍ, by iḍāfa).

tasks.prompt: Why are ṭāhir and ḍāmir counted as resembling adjectives, though they have the pattern fāʿil?
tasks.answer: They name a lasting quality (being pure, being lean), not an act happening at a time. The resembling adjective is defined by permanence, not by its pattern.

tasks.prompt: Why does aḥsana raise al-kuḥlu in mā raʾaytu rajulan aḥsana fī ʿaynihi al-kuḥlu minhu fī ʿayni Zaydin?
tasks.answer: This is the question of the kohl: the sentence is negated, and the elative compares one thing, the kohl, with itself in two places. Only in that shape does the elative put a visible noun in rafʿ.
