text.original: وَالصِّفَةُ الْمُشَبَّهَةُ بِاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ الْمُتَعَدِّي لِوَاحِدٍ، وَهِيَ الصِّفَةُ الْمَصُوغَةُ لِغَيْرِ تَفْضِيلٍ لِإِفَادَةِ الثُّبُوتِ، كَحَسَنٍ وَظَرِيفٍ وَطَاهِرٍ وَضَامِرٍ. وَلَا يَتَقَدَّمُهَا مَعْمُولُهَا، وَلَا يَكُونُ أَجْنَبِيًّا، وَيُرْفَعُ عَلَى الْفَاعِلِيَّةِ أَوِ الْإِبْدَالِ، وَيُنْصَبُ عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ أَوِ التَّشْبِيهِ بِالْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ، وَالثَّانِي مُتَعَيِّنٌ فِي الْمَعْرِفَةِ، وَيُخْفَضُ بِالْإِضَافَةِ.
text.en: The adjective likened to the active participle of a verb transitive to one [object] (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha), which is the adjective formed, not for preference, to convey permanence, as ḥasan “handsome”, ẓarīf “witty”, ṭāhir “pure” and ḍāmir “lean”. What it governs does not come before it and is not a stranger [to it]. It is put in rafʿ as a fāʿil or as a badal; in naṣb as a tamyīz or by likeness to the mafʿūl bihi, the second being the only way with a definite [noun]; and in khafḍ by iḍāfa.

text.original: وَاسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ، وَهُوَ الصِّفَةُ الدَّالَّةُ عَلَى الْمُشَارَكَةِ وَالزِّيَادَةِ كَأَكْرَمَ، وَيُسْتَعْمَلُ بِمِنْ وَمُضَافًا لِنَكِرَةٍ فَيُفْرَدُ وَيُذَكَّرُ، وَبِأَلْ فَيُطَابِقُ، وَمُضَافًا لِمَعْرِفَةٍ فَوَجْهَانِ. وَلَا يَنْصِبُ الْمَفْعُولَ مُطْلَقًا، وَلَا يَرْفَعُ فِي الْغَالِبِ ظَاهِرًا إِلَّا فِي مَسْأَلَةِ الْكُحْلِ.
text.en: The elative (ism al-tafḍīl), which is the adjective that indicates sharing [a quality] and exceeding [in it], as akram “more noble”. It is used with min, and muḍāf to an indefinite, and then it is singular and masculine; with al-, and then it agrees [with its noun]; and muḍāf to a definite, and then both ways [are allowed]. It never puts an object in naṣb, and mostly does not put an explicit noun in rafʿ, except in the question of the kohl (masʾalat al-kuḥl).

lessons.title: The followers; the adjective (naʿt)
body: “Five follow what is before them in its iʿrāb”: the adjective (naʿt), emphasis (tawkīd), the explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān), joining by a particle (ʿaṭf al-nasaq) and the substitute (badal). A follower has no governor of its own; it takes the ending of the word it follows. The adjective is “the follower that is derived, or taken as derived, and differs from the wording of what it follows”: derived, as ḍārib or ḥasan; taken as derived, as a demonstrative or dhū meaning “possessor”. “Differs from the wording” leaves out verbal emphasis, which repeats the word itself.

It serves to particularize an indefinite (rajulun ʿālimun, “a learned man”), to make clear a definite (Zaydun al-tājiru, “Zayd the merchant”), to praise (bi-smi llāhi al-raḥmāni al-raḥīmi), to blame (mina al-shayṭāni al-rajīmi), to show pity, or to emphasize (nafkhatun wāḥidatun, “a single blast”, Q 69:13).

It always agrees with the noun it describes in one of the states of iʿrāb and in definiteness. If it raises a hidden pronoun, referring to that noun, it agrees also in gender and number: rajulāni qāʾimāni, imraʾatun qāʾimatun. If instead it raises a visible noun after it (the adjective called causal, sababī), “it is like the verb”: it agrees with what follows it in gender and stays singular, as a verb would: marartu bi-rajulin qāʾimatin ummuhu, “a man whose mother was standing”, as one says qāmat ummuhu. The book ranks the choices: jāʾanī rajulun quʿūdun ghilmānuhu, with a broken plural, is best; then qāʿidun, singular like the verb; then qāʿidūna.

An adjective may be “cut off” from its noun's iʿrāb when the noun is known: in rafʿ, with huwa, “he is”, understood; in naṣb, with aʿnī, “I mean”, amdaḥu, “I praise”, adhummu, “I blame”, or arḥamu, “I pity”, understood. So wa-mraʾatuhu ḥammālata al-ḥaṭabi, “and his wife, the carrier of firewood” (Q 111:4), in the reading of ʿĀṣim, puts ḥammālata in naṣb: “I blame the carrier of firewood”.

terms.en: the followers: five kinds of word that take the iʿrāb of what they follow
the adjective: a derived follower
the causal adjective, raising a noun after it, like a verb
cutting an adjective off from its noun's iʿrāb

examples.en: a causal adjective: it agrees with ummuhu, like a verb
the best way, with a broken plural
cut off in naṣb, “I blame…” (Q 111:4)

tasks.prompt: Say what each adjective does: rajulun ʿālimun; Zaydun al-tājiru; nafkhatun wāḥidatun.
tasks.answer: ʿĀlimun particularizes an indefinite noun. Al-tājiru makes clear a definite one. Wāḥidatun emphasizes, since nafkha already means one blast.

tasks.prompt: Why is it qāʾimatin in marartu bi-rajulin qāʾimatin ummuhu, though rajul is masculine?
tasks.answer: It is a causal adjective: it raises ummuhu, a visible noun after it, so it behaves like a verb and agrees with ummuhu, as one says qāmat ummuhu. It still follows rajulin in jarr and in indefiniteness.

tasks.prompt: Why is ḥammālata in naṣb in wa-mraʾatuhu ḥammālata al-ḥaṭabi?
tasks.answer: The adjective is cut off from the iʿrāb of imraʾatuhu, which is known, and put in naṣb by an understood adhummu, “I blame”: “I blame the carrier of firewood”.

quiz.prompt: How many followers does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Naʿt, tawkīd, ʿaṭf al-bayān, ʿaṭf al-nasaq, badal.

quiz.prompt: The adjective is a follower that is…
quiz.explanation: Ḍārib, ḥasan; or a demonstrative, dhū.

quiz.prompt: An adjective of a definite noun serves to…
quiz.explanation: Zaydun al-tājiru.

quiz.prompt: The adjective always agrees with its noun in…
options: its state of iʿrāb and definiteness
quiz.explanation: Gender and number only if it raises a hidden pronoun.

quiz.prompt: A causal adjective, raising a noun after it, is…
quiz.explanation: Qāʾimatin ummuhu, as qāmat ummuhu.

quiz.prompt: Which way does the book call best?
quiz.explanation: Then qāʿidun, then qāʿidūna.

quiz.prompt: An adjective cut off in naṣb is governed by an understood…
quiz.explanation: In rafʿ, huwa is understood.

text.original: يَتْبَعُ مَا قَبْلَهُ فِي إِعْرَابِهِ خَمْسَةٌ: النَّعْتُ، وَهُوَ التَّابِعُ الْمُشْتَقُّ أَوِ الْمُؤَوَّلُ بِهِ، الْمُبَايِنُ لِلَفْظِ مَتْبُوعِهِ، وَفَائِدَتُهُ تَخْصِيصٌ أَوْ تَوْضِيحٌ أَوْ مَدْحٌ أَوْ ذَمٌّ أَوْ تَرَحُّمٌ أَوْ تَوْكِيدٌ.
text.en: Five [kinds of word] follow what is before them in its iʿrāb. The naʿt, which is the follower that is derived, or taken as derived, and differs from the wording of what it follows. It serves to particularize, to make clear, to praise, to blame, to show pity or to emphasize.

text.original: وَيَتْبَعُ مَنْعُوتَهُ فِي وَاحِدٍ مِنْ أَوْجُهِ الْإِعْرَابِ، وَمِنَ التَّعْرِيفِ وَالتَّنْكِيرِ، ثُمَّ إِنْ رَفَعَ ضَمِيرًا مُسْتَتِرًا تَبِعَ فِي وَاحِدٍ مِنَ التَّذْكِيرِ وَالتَّأْنِيثِ، وَوَاحِدٍ مِنَ الْإِفْرَادِ وَفَرْعَيْهِ، وَإِلَّا فَهُوَ كَالْفِعْلِ، وَالْأَحْسَنُ: جَاءَنِي رَجُلٌ قُعُودٌ غِلْمَانُهُ، ثُمَّ قَاعِدٌ، ثُمَّ قَاعِدُونَ.
text.en: It follows its manʿūt in one of the ways of iʿrāb, and in definiteness or indefiniteness. Then, if it puts a hidden pronoun in rafʿ, it follows [it] in one of the masculine and the feminine, and in one of the singular and its two branches; otherwise it is like the verb. The best is jāʾanī rajulun quʿūdun ghilmānuhu “a man came to me whose boys were sitting”, then qāʿidun, then qāʿidūna.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ قَطْعُ الصِّفَةِ الْمَعْلُومِ مَوْصُوفُهَا حَقِيقَةً أَوِ ادِّعَاءً رَفْعًا بِتَقْدِيرِ هُوَ، وَنَصْبًا بِتَقْدِيرِ أَعْنِي أَوْ أَمْدَحُ أَوْ أَذُمُّ أَوْ أَرْحَمُ.
text.en: An adjective whose described noun is known, truly or by claim, may be cut off [from its iʿrāb]: in rafʿ, with huwa “he is” understood, and in naṣb, with aʿnī “I mean”, amdaḥu “I praise”, adhummu “I blame” or arḥamu “I pity” understood.

lessons.title: Emphasis (tawkīd)
body: Emphasis is of two kinds. Verbal emphasis (lafẓī) repeats the word itself, a noun, a verb or a particle: akhāka akhāka inna man lā akhan lahu, “your brother, your brother! for he who has no brother…”; atāki atāki al-lāḥiqūna, “they have come upon you, they have come upon you, the pursuers”; lā lā abūḥu bi-ḥubbi Bathnata, “no, no, I will not reveal my love for Bathna”. Not of it are dakkan dakkan and ṣaffan ṣaffan (Q 89:21–22): there the second is not a repetition but a new one, “pounding after pounding”, “rank after rank”.

Emphasis of meaning (maʿnawī) uses set words. Al-nafs and al-ʿayn, “the self”, ʿayn after nafs if both come: jāʾa Zaydun nafsuhu; with a dual or plural they take the plural afʿul: anfusuhum, aʿyunuhum. Kull, “all”, for what is not a dual, if it can be divided by itself (al-qawmu kulluhum) or by its governor (ishtaraytu al-ʿabda kullahu, since the buying can be of a part).

Kilā and kiltā, “both”, for the dual, but only if a singular could stand in its place and the predicate is one for both: jāʾa al-Zaydāni kilāhumā, “the two Zayds came, both of them”. So one does not say it with “quarrelled”, since one cannot quarrel alone, nor with two different acts. All these words are joined to a pronoun of what they emphasize. Ajmaʿ and jamʿāʾ, with their plurals ajmaʿūna and jumaʿ, take no pronoun: fa-sajada al-malāʾikatu kulluhum ajmaʿūna, “so the angels bowed down, all of them together” (Q 15:30).

Two differences from the adjective. Words of emphasis are never joined to one another by wa-: one does not say kulluhum wa-ajmaʿūna. And they do not follow an indefinite noun, since an indefinite has no fixed whole to emphasize; the verse yā layta ʿiddata shahrin kullihi rajabu, “would that the count of a whole month were Rajab!”, is “rare”.

emphasis of meaning: nafs, ʿayn, kull, kilā, ajmaʿ
the set words of emphasis

examples.en: akhāka akhāka: verbal emphasis of a noun
jāʾa Zaydun nafsuhu: emphasis with al-nafs
kilā for a dual, the predicate one for both
kull, then ajmaʿūna without a pronoun (Q 15:30)

tasks.prompt: Why is dakkan dakkan not verbal emphasis?
tasks.answer: Verbal emphasis repeats the same thing to make it firm. In dakkan dakkan the second is a new pounding after the first, “pounding after pounding”; it is not a repetition of one word's meaning.

tasks.prompt: Why can one say ishtaraytu al-ʿabda kullahu, though a slave is one person?
tasks.answer: Kull needs something that can be divided, by itself or by its governor. One may buy a part of a slave, so the buying can be divided, and kullahu says that the whole was bought.

tasks.prompt: Why is kilāhumā not used with a verb of quarrelling?
tasks.answer: Kilā and kiltā are used only where a singular could stand in their place. One person cannot quarrel alone, so the meaning of “both” adds nothing there and the emphasis is not allowed.

quiz.prompt: Verbal emphasis (lafẓī) is…
quiz.explanation: Akhāka akhāka; atāki atāki.

quiz.prompt: Dakkan dakkan is…
quiz.explanation: The book says it is not of emphasis.

quiz.prompt: When nafs and ʿayn come together…
quiz.explanation: Jāʾa Zaydun nafsuhu ʿaynuhu.

quiz.explanation: Al-qawmu kulluhum.

quiz.explanation: Ajmaʿ, jamʿāʾ and their plurals are not muḍāf.

quiz.explanation: Not kulluhum wa-ajmaʿūna.

text.original: وَالتَّوْكِيدُ، وَهُوَ إِمَّا لَفْظِيٌّ نَحْوُ: أَخَاكَ أَخَاكَ إِنَّ مَنْ لَا أَخًا لَهُ، وَنَحْوُ: أَتَاكِ أَتَاكِ اللَّاحِقُونَ، وَنَحْوُ: لَا لَا أَبُوحُ بِحُبِّ بَثْنَةَ إِنَّهَا، وَلَيْسَ مِنْهُ: دَكًّا دَكًّا، وَصَفًّا صَفًّا.
text.en: The tawkīd is either verbal (lafẓī), as akhāka akhāka inna man lā akhan lahu “your brother, your brother! for he who has no brother …”, atāki atāki al-lāḥiqūna “they have come upon you, they have come upon you, the pursuers” and lā lā abūḥu bi-ḥubbi Bathnata innahā “no, no, I will not reveal my love for Bathna, for she …”; and not of it are dakkan dakkan “pounded to dust” [89:21] and ṣaffan ṣaffan “rank upon rank” [89:22].

text.original: وَإِمَّا مَعْنَوِيٌّ، وَهُوَ بِالنَّفْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ، مُؤَخَّرَةً عَنْهَا إِنِ اجْتَمَعَتَا، وَتُجْمَعَانِ عَلَى أَفْعُلٍ مَعَ غَيْرِ الْمُفْرَدِ، وَبِكُلٍّ لِغَيْرِ مُثَنًّى إِنْ تَجَزَّأَ بِنَفْسِهِ أَوْ بِعَامِلِهِ، وَبِكِلَا وَكِلْتَا لَهُ إِنْ صَحَّ وُقُوعُ الْمُفْرَدِ مَوْقِعَهُ وَاتَّحَدَ مَعْنَى الْمُسْنَدِ،
text.en: Or of meaning (maʿnawī), which is with al-nafs “the self” and al-ʿayn “the self”, [ʿayn] coming after [nafs] if the two come together; the two are put in the plural on afʿul with what is not singular; with kull “all”, for what is not dual, if it can be divided by itself or by its governor; and with kilā and kiltā “both” for the dual, if a singular could rightly stand in its place and the meaning of what is predicated is one;

text.original: وَيُضَفْنَ لِضَمِيرِ الْمُؤَكَّدِ، وَبِأَجْمَعَ وَجَمْعَاءَ وَجَمْعِهِمَا غَيْرَ مُضَافَةٍ، وَبِخِلَافِ النُّعُوتِ لَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ تَتَعَاطَفَ الْمُؤَكِّدَاتُ، وَلَا أَنْ تَتْبَعَ نَكِرَةً، وَنَدَرَ: يَا لَيْتَ عِدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كُلِّهِ رَجَبُ.
text.en: and these are made muḍāf to the pronoun of the emphasized [word]; and with ajmaʿ, jamʿāʾ and their plurals, not muḍāf. Unlike the nuʿūt, the words of emphasis may not be joined to one another by ʿaṭf, nor follow an indefinite; and yā layta ʿiddata shahrin kullihi rajabu “would that the count of a whole month were Rajab!” is rare.

lessons.title: The explicative apposition; joining by a particle
body: The explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) is a follower that is not derived and not taken as derived, which makes clear a definite noun or particularizes an indefinite one, and agrees with it: aqsama bi-llāhi Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru, “Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar swore by God”, where ʿUmar makes clear who Abū Ḥafṣ is; hādhā khātamun ḥadīdun, “this is a ring, iron”, where ḥadīdun, a noun, not an adjective, says what kind of ring.

It can usually be parsed also as a badal of the whole for the whole, but not where putting it in the place of the first is impossible. In anā ibnu al-tāriki al-Bakriyyi Bishrin, Bishr could not replace al-Bakriyy, since al-tāriki Bishrin would join a word with al- to a noun without it (lesson 37). In ayā akhawaynā ʿAbda Shamsin wa-Nawfalā, a badal would be like a name called by itself, yā Nawfalu, but the poet says Nawfalā in naṣb. In both, only ʿaṭf al-bayān is possible.

Joining by a particle (ʿaṭf al-nasaq) has its particles, each with its meaning. Wa- joins without order: jāʾa Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun, either may have come first. Fa- gives order at once; thumma order after a while. Ḥattā gives the end and the steps up to it, “not order”: what it joins is the last or highest part of what came before. Aw gives one of two or more: after a demand, choice or permission; after a statement, doubt, or making the hearer doubt: labithnā yawman aw baʿḍa yawmin, “we stayed a day or part of a day” (Q 18:19).

Am asks which of two, after a hamza: a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun?, “is Zayd with you, or ʿAmr?”. Three particles correct an error: lā after an affirmation, jāʾa Zaydun lā ʿAmrun; lākin and bal after a negation, mā jāʾa Zaydun bal ʿAmrun. And bal after an affirmation turns the judgment to what follows: jāʾa Zaydun bal ʿAmrun, “Zayd came, no, ʿAmr”.

joining by a particle
the particles of joining: wa-, fa-, thumma, ḥattā, aw, am, lā, lākin, bal

ḥadīdun particularizes khātam

tasks.prompt: Why is ḥadīdun in hādhā khātamun ḥadīdun an explicative apposition and not an adjective?
tasks.answer: An adjective is derived or taken as derived; ḥadīd, “iron”, is a plain noun. It particularizes khātam and agrees with it, so it is ʿaṭf al-bayān.

tasks.prompt: Why can Nawfalā in ayā akhawaynā ʿAbda Shamsin wa-Nawfalā not be a badal?
tasks.answer: A badal is treated like a name called by itself, which would be fixed on the ḍamma: yā Nawfalu. The poet says Nawfalā, in naṣb, following akhawaynā; so it can only be ʿaṭf al-bayān (with Nawfal joined to ʿAbd Shams).

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between jāʾa Zaydun fa-ʿAmrun and jāʾa Zaydun thumma ʿAmrun?
tasks.answer: Both say that Zayd came first. Fa- says that ʿAmr came right after him; thumma that he came after an interval.

quiz.explanation: Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru.

quiz.prompt: ʿAṭf al-bayān cannot be parsed as a badal when…

quiz.explanation: Anā ibnu al-tāriki al-Bakriyyi Bishrin.

quiz.explanation: Either may have come first.

quiz.prompt: Thumma gives…
quiz.explanation: Tartīb with tarākhī.

quiz.prompt: Ḥattā as a particle of joining gives…
options: the end, by steps, not order
quiz.explanation: What it joins is the last part of what came before.

quiz.explanation: A-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun?

quiz.prompt: Bal after an affirmation…

quiz.explanation: Jāʾa Zaydun bal ʿAmrun: it was ʿAmr.

text.original: وَعَطْفُ الْبَيَانِ، وَهُوَ تَابِعٌ مُوَضِّحٌ أَوْ مُخَصِّصٌ جَامِدٌ غَيْرُ مُؤَوَّلٍ، فَيُوَافِقُ مَتْبُوعَهُ كَأَقْسَمَ بِاللَّهِ أَبُو حَفْصٍ عُمَرُ، وَهَذَا خَاتَمٌ حَدِيدٌ. وَيُعْرَبُ بَدَلَ كُلٍّ مِنْ كُلٍّ إِنْ لَمْ يَمْتَنِعْ إِحْلَالُهُ مَحَلَّ الْأَوَّلِ كَقَوْلِهِ: أَنَا ابْنُ التَّارِكِ الْبَكْرِيِّ بِشْرٍ، وَقَوْلِهِ: أَيَا أَخَوَيْنَا عَبْدَ شَمْسٍ وَنَوْفَلَا.
text.en: And the explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān), which is a follower, non-derived and not taken as derived, that makes clear or particularizes. It agrees with what it follows, as aqsama bi-Allāhi Abū Ḥafṣin ʿUmaru “Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar swore by God” and hādhā khātamun ḥadīdun “this is a ring, iron”. It is parsed as a badal of the whole from the whole if putting it in the place of the first is not impossible, as [it is impossible] in the poet's saying anā ibnu al-tāriki al-Bakriyyi Bishrin “I am the son of the one who left the Bakrī, Bishr, …” and his saying ayā akhawaynā ʿAbda Shamsin wa-Nawfalā “O our two brothers, ʿAbd Shams and Nawfal!”.

text.original: وَعَطْفُ النَّسَقِ بِالْوَاوِ، وَهِيَ لِمُطْلَقِ الْجَمْعِ، وَالْفَاءِ لِلتَّرْتِيبِ وَالتَّعْقِيبِ، وَثُمَّ لِلتَّرْتِيبِ وَالتَّرَاخِي، وَحَتَّى لِلْغَايَةِ وَالتَّدْرِيجِ لَا لِلتَّرْتِيبِ، وَأَوْ لِأَحَدِ الشَّيْئَيْنِ أَوِ الْأَشْيَاءِ، مُفِيدَةً بَعْدَ الطَّلَبِ التَّخْيِيرَ أَوِ الْإِبَاحَةَ، وَبَعْدَ الْخَبَرِ الشَّكَّ أَوِ التَّشْكِيكَ،
text.en: And the ʿaṭf of order (ʿaṭf al-nasaq): by the wāw (wa-), which is for joining in general; the fāʾ (fa-), for order and succession; thumma, for order with an interval; ḥattā, for the end and gradation, not for order; and aw, for one of two things or more, conveying after a demand choice or permission, and after a statement doubt or making doubtful;

text.original: وَأَمْ لِطَلَبِ التَّعْيِينِ بَعْدَ هَمْزَةٍ دَاخِلَةٍ عَلَى أَحَدِ الْمُسْتَوِيَيْنِ، وَلِلرَّدِّ عَنِ الْخَطَإِ فِي الْحُكْمِ لَا بَعْدَ إِيجَابٍ، وَلَكِنْ وَبَلْ بَعْدَ نَفْيٍ، وَلِصَرْفِ الْحُكْمِ إِلَى مَا بَعْدَهَا بَلْ بَعْدَ إِيجَابٍ.
text.en: am, for asking to specify, after a hamza that comes on one of two equal [alternatives]; and for turning [the hearer] back from an error in the judgement: lā, after an affirmation, and lākin and bal, after a negation; and for turning the judgement to what comes after it: bal, after an affirmation.

lessons.title: The substitute (badal)
body: The substitute (badal) is “a follower that is intended by the judgment, without an intermediary”. Intended: what is said is said of it, the word before only leading to it, unlike the adjective or the emphasis, which serve the word before them. Without an intermediary: no particle comes between, unlike ʿaṭf al-nasaq, whose second word is also intended but comes after wa- or fa-.

It has six kinds. Of the whole for the whole: mafāzan ḥadāʾiqa, “a triumph: gardens” (Q 78:31–32), the gardens being the triumph itself. Of the part for the whole: mani staṭāʿa, “whoever is able” (Q 3:97), after al-nās, “people”, of whom those able are a part. Of inclusion (ishtimāl): qitālin fīhi, “fighting in it” (Q 2:217), after al-shahr al-ḥarām, the sacred month, which includes the fighting without being made of it. The part and the inclusion need a pronoun back to the first, spoken (fīhi) or understood (minhum).

The last three are shown by one sentence: taṣaddaqtu bi-dirhamin dīnārin, “I gave in alms a dirham — a dinar”. If the speaker meant both, saying the first and then turning to the better, it is the badal of turning away (iḍrāb). If he meant only the second and the first was a slip of the tongue, it is the badal of mistake (ghalaṭ). If he meant the first and then saw that he was wrong, it is the badal of forgetting (nisyān).

terms.en: the substitute: intended by the judgment, with no particle
the part for the whole, with a pronoun back to the whole
the badal of inclusion
of turning away, of mistake, of forgetting

examples.en: mafāzan ḥadāʾiqa (Q 78:31–32): the whole for the whole
mani staṭāʿa (Q 3:97): the part for the whole
qitālin fīhi (Q 2:217): inclusion
turning away, mistake or forgetting, by what was meant

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of badal in mafāzan ḥadāʾiqa, mani staṭāʿa and qitālin fīhi.
tasks.answer: Mafāzan ḥadāʾiqa: the whole for the whole (the gardens are the triumph). Mani staṭāʿa: the part for the whole (those able are some of the people). Qitālin fīhi: inclusion (the month includes the fighting).

tasks.prompt: Read taṣaddaqtu bi-dirhamin dīnārin three ways, and name the badal each time.
tasks.answer: Both meant, the speaker turning to the better: badal of turning away. Only the dinar meant, “dirham” a slip of the tongue: badal of mistake. The dirham meant, then the speaker saw his error: badal of forgetting.

tasks.prompt: How does the badal differ from ʿaṭf al-nasaq?
tasks.answer: In both the second word is intended by the judgment, but in ʿaṭf al-nasaq a particle stands between (wa-, fa-, bal…), while the badal follows with no intermediary.

quiz.prompt: The badal is a follower that is…
options: intended by the judgment, without an intermediary
quiz.explanation: What is said is said of it.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of badal does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Whole, part, inclusion, turning away, mistake, forgetting.

quiz.prompt: Mani staṭāʿa after al-nās is a badal of…
quiz.explanation: Those able are part of the people (Q 3:97).

quiz.prompt: Qitālin fīhi after al-shahr al-ḥarām is a badal of…
quiz.explanation: The month includes the fighting (Q 2:217).

quiz.prompt: Which kinds need a pronoun back to the first word?
quiz.explanation: Fīhi; minhum understood.

quiz.prompt: If the first word was a slip of the tongue, the badal is of…
quiz.explanation: Taṣaddaqtu bi-dirhamin dīnārin, the dirham a slip.

quiz.prompt: If both words were meant, the speaker turning to the second, the badal is of…
quiz.explanation: He says the first and then the better.

text.original: وَالْبَدَلُ، وَهُوَ تَابِعٌ مَقْصُودٌ بِالْحُكْمِ بِلَا وَاسِطَةٍ، وَهُوَ سِتَّةٌ: بَدَلُ كُلٍّ نَحْوُ: مَفَازًا حَدَائِقَ، وَبَعْضٍ نَحْوُ: مَنِ اسْتَطَاعَ، وَاشْتِمَالٍ نَحْوُ: قِتَالٍ فِيهِ، وَإِضْرَابٍ، وَغَلَطٍ، وَنِسْيَانٍ، نَحْوُ: تَصَدَّقْتُ بِدِرْهَمٍ دِينَارٍ، بِحَسَبِ قَصْدِ الْأَوَّلِ وَالثَّانِي، أَوِ الثَّانِي وَسَبْقِ اللِّسَانِ، أَوِ الْأَوَّلِ وَتَبَيُّنِ الْخَطَإِ.
text.en: And the badal, which is a follower that is intended by the judgement, without an intermediary. It is of six [kinds]: the badal of the whole, as mafāzan ḥadāʾiqa “a triumph: gardens” [78:31–32]; of the part, as mani istaṭāʿa “whoever is able” [3:97]; of inclusion, as qitālin fīhi “fighting in it” [2:217]; and of turning away (iḍrāb), of mistake (ghalaṭ) and of forgetting (nisyān), as taṣaddaqtu bi-dirhamin dīnārin “I gave in alms a dirham — a dinar”, according to whether the first and the second were intended, or the second, [the first being] a slip of the tongue, or the first, and then the error became clear.

lessons.title: Number
body: “The numbers from three to nine take the feminine form with the masculine and the masculine form with the feminine, always”: sabʿa layālin wa-thamāniyata ayyāmin, “seven nights and eight days” (Q 69:7). Layla, “night”, is feminine, so “seven” is sabʿ, without the tāʾ; yawm, “day”, is masculine, so “eight” is thamāniya, with it. “Always” means in every use, alone or compounded.

“And likewise ten, if it is not compounded”: ʿasharatu rijālin, “ten men”, ʿashru niswatin, “ten women”. In the compounds from eleven to nineteen, the ten agrees with the counted noun instead: aḥada ʿashara kawkaban, “eleven stars” (Q 12:4).

One and two, and the ordinal on the pattern fāʿil, thālith, “third”, rābiʿ, “fourth”, “follow the rule”, the ordinary agreement of an adjective: rajulun wāḥidun, imraʾatun wāḥidatun; al-rajulu al-thālithu, al-marʾatu al-thālithatu.

The pattern fāʿil has four uses. It stands alone: thālithun, “a third”. It is joined to the number it comes from, meaning “one of”: thāniya ithnayni, “the second of two” (Q 9:40); thālithu thalāthatin, “one of three” (Q 5:73). It is joined to the number below it, meaning “the one who makes it so many”: thālithu ithnayni, “the one who makes two into three”. Or, in that same sense, it puts the number below it in naṣb, as a participle governs: thālithun ithnayni.

the ordinal of the pattern fāʿil: thālith, rābiʿ

tasks.prompt: Why is it sabʿa layālin but thamāniyata ayyāmin?
tasks.answer: From three to nine the number takes the opposite gender to the counted noun. Layla is feminine, so sabʿ has no tāʾ; yawm is masculine, so thamāniya has it.

tasks.prompt: Does “one” follow the same reverse rule? Give an example.
tasks.answer: No: one and two, and the ordinals, follow the ordinary rule of agreement: rajulun wāḥidun, imraʾatun wāḥidatun.

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between thālithu thalāthatin and thālithu ithnayni?
tasks.answer: Thālithu thalāthatin, joined to the number it comes from, means “one of three”. Thālithu ithnayni, joined to the number below it, means “the one who makes two into three”.

quiz.explanation: Fāʿil may put the number below it in naṣb.

text.original: الْعَدَدُ مِنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ يُؤَنَّثُ مَعَ الْمُذَكَّرِ، وَيُذَكَّرُ مَعَ الْمُؤَنَّثِ دَائِمًا، نَحْوُ: سَبْعَ لَيَالٍ وَثَمَانِيَةَ أَيَّامٍ، وَكَذَلِكَ الْعَشَرَةُ إِنْ لَمْ تُرَكَّبْ. وَمَا دُونَ الثَّلَاثَةِ وَفَاعِلٌ كَثَالِثٍ وَرَابِعٍ عَلَى الْقِيَاسِ دَائِمًا، وَيُفْرَدُ فَاعِلٌ أَوْ يُضَافُ لِمَا اشْتُقَّ مِنْهُ، أَوْ لِمَا دُونَهُ، أَوْ يَنْصِبُ مَا دُونَهُ.
text.en: The numbers from three to nine take the feminine [form] with the masculine and the masculine with the feminine, always, as sabʿa layālin wa-thamāniyata ayyāmin “seven nights and eight days” [69:7]; and likewise ten, if it is not compounded. What is below three, and fāʿil, as thālith “third” and rābiʿ “fourth”, always follow the rule. Fāʿil is used alone, or muḍāf to what it is derived from, or to what is below it, or it puts what is below it in naṣb.

lessons.title: What keeps a noun from tanwīn
body: A diptote (lesson 6) takes no tanwīn and is put in jarr with the fatḥa. Nine causes make it so, and a verse gathers them: the verb's pattern (Aḥmad, a name, and aḥmar, “red”); the compound (Baʿlabakk); foreignness (Ibrāhīm); being a proper name; deflection (ʿadl), a word turned from another form (ʿUmar, ukhar, “others”, uḥād and mawḥad, “one by one”, up to four); the adjective; the plural (masājid, “mosques”, danānīr, “dinars”); the added alif and nūn (Salmān, sakrān, “drunk”); and femininity (Fāṭima, Ṭalḥa, Zaynab, Salmā, ṣaḥrāʾ, “desert”).

Two causes suffice by themselves: the alif of the feminine, short in Salmā or long in ṣaḥrāʾ, and the plural that has no like among the singulars, such as masājid. Every other cause works only together with one of two partners: the adjective or being a proper name. So Aḥmad is a name with the verb's pattern, aḥmar an adjective with it; Salmān a name, sakrān an adjective, with the alif and nūn; ʿUmar a name, ukhar an adjective, with deflection. The compound, femininity without the alif, and foreignness take only the proper name as their partner.

The conditions are exact. Foreignness counts only if the word was a proper name in the foreign tongue and has more than three letters: so Ibrāhīm is a diptote, but Nūḥ takes tanwīn, wa-Nūḥan hadaynā (Q 6:84). The adjective counts only if it was an adjective from the start and does not take the tāʾ: ʿuryān, “naked”, and armal, “needy”, take tanwīn, since one says ʿuryānatun and armalatun; ṣafwān and arnab used to mean “hard” and “abject” take tanwīn, since they were nouns first.

Some names allow both ways: Hind, a feminine name of three letters with a quiescent middle, may take tanwīn or not; Zaynab, Saqar and Balkh may not. Among the Banū Tamīm, names on the pattern of Ḥadhām are diptotes like ʿUmar, unless they end in rāʾ, as Safār; and so is ams, “yesterday”, for a particular day, when it is in rafʿ. And saḥar, “dawn”, is a diptote for all the Arabs when it is an adverb for a particular dawn.

being a proper name, being an adjective: the two partners
deflection: a word turned from another form, as ʿUmar
the plural with no like among singulars, as masājid

tasks.prompt: Give the two causes of each diptote: Aḥmad; aḥmar; Salmān; ʿUmar; Ibrāhīm.
tasks.answer: Aḥmad: proper name and the verb's pattern. Aḥmar: adjective and the verb's pattern. Salmān: proper name and the alif and nūn. ʿUmar: proper name and deflection. Ibrāhīm: proper name and foreignness.

tasks.prompt: Why does Nūḥ take tanwīn though it is a foreign name?
tasks.answer: Foreignness counts only in a name of more than three letters. Nūḥ has three, so it takes tanwīn.

tasks.prompt: Why does ʿuryān take tanwīn, while sakrān does not?
tasks.answer: The adjective with the alif and nūn keeps tanwīn away only if it does not take the tāʾ. One says ʿuryānatun, so ʿuryān takes tanwīn; the feminine of sakrān is sakrā, not sakrānatun, so sakrān is a diptote.

quiz.explanation: Gathered in a verse.

quiz.explanation: With the plural that has no like among singulars.

quiz.explanation: Ibrāhīm: a proper name and foreignness.

quiz.explanation: The pattern afʿal with the adjective.

quiz.prompt: Nūḥ takes tanwīn because…
quiz.explanation: Foreignness needs more than three letters.

quiz.prompt: Hind, a woman's name, …
quiz.explanation: Three letters, quiescent middle: both ways.

quiz.explanation: As in “I came on Friday at dawn”.

text.original: مَوَانِعُ صَرْفِ الِاسْمِ تِسْعَةٌ، يَجْمَعُهَا قَوْلُهُ: وَزْنُ الْمُرَكَّبِ عُجْمَةٌ تَعْرِيفُهَا * عَدْلٌ وَوَصْفُ الْجَمْعِ زِدْ تَأْنِيثَا، كَأَحْمَدَ وَأَحْمَرَ، وَبَعْلَبَكَّ، وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ، وَعُمَرَ، وَأُخَرَ، وَأُحَادَ، وَمَوْحَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْبَعَةِ، وَمَسَاجِدَ وَدَنَانِيرَ، وَسَلْمَانَ وَسَكْرَانَ، وَفَاطِمَةَ وَطَلْحَةَ وَزَيْنَبَ وَسَلْمَى وَصَحْرَاءَ.
text.en: What keeps a noun from tanwīn is nine [causes], gathered in the poet's saying waznu al-murakkabi ʿujmatun taʿrīfuhā / ʿadlun wa-waṣfu al-jamʿi zid taʾnīthā “the [verb's] pattern, the compound, foreignness, being a proper name, deflection (ʿadl), the adjective, the plural, add [the alif and nūn], and femininity”: as Aḥmad [a name] and aḥmar “red”; Baʿlabakk; Ibrāhīm; ʿUmar, ukhar “others”, and uḥād and mawḥad “one by one”, up to four; masājid “mosques” and danānīr “dinars”; Salmān and sakrān “drunk”; and Fāṭima, Ṭalḥa, Zaynab, Salmā and ṣaḥrāʾ “desert”.

text.original: فَأَلِفُ التَّأْنِيثِ وَالْجَمْعُ الَّذِي لَا نَظِيرَ لَهُ فِي الْآحَادِ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا يَسْتَقِلُّ بِالْمَنْعِ، وَالْبَوَاقِي لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مُجَامَعَةِ كُلِّ عِلَّةٍ مِنْهُنَّ لِلصِّفَةِ أَوِ الْعَلَمِيَّةِ، وَتَتَعَيَّنُ الْعَلَمِيَّةُ مَعَ التَّرْكِيبِ وَالتَّأْنِيثِ وَالْعُجْمَةِ.
text.en: The alif of the feminine, and the plural that has no like among the singulars, each suffice by themselves to keep [tanwīn] away; with the others, each cause must go together with the adjective or with being a proper name. Being a proper name is the only [partner] with the compound, femininity and foreignness.

text.original: وَشَرْطُ الْعُجْمَةِ عَلَمِيَّةٌ فِي الْعَجَمِيَّةِ، وَزِيَادَةٌ عَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ، وَالصِّفَةِ أَصَالَتُهَا وَعَدَمُ قَبُولِهَا التَّاءَ، فَعُرْيَانٌ وَأَرْمَلٌ وَصَفْوَانٌ وَأَرْنَبٌ بِمَعْنَى قَاسٍ وَذَلِيلٍ مُنْصَرِفَةٌ.
text.en: The condition of foreignness is being a proper name in the foreign language and having more than three letters; and [the condition] of the adjective is that it be an adjective in origin and not accept the tāʾ. So ʿuryānun “naked” and armalun “needy”, and ṣafwānun and arnabun in the sense of “hard” and “abject”, take tanwīn.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ فِي نَحْوِ: هِنْدٍ وَجْهَانِ، بِخِلَافِ زَيْنَبَ وَسَقَرَ وَبَلْخَ، وَكَعُمَرَ عِنْدَ تَمِيمٍ بَابُ حَذَامِ إِنْ لَمْ يُخْتَمْ بِرَاءٍ كَسَفَارِ، وَأَمْسِ لِمُعَيَّنٍ إِنْ كَانَ مَرْفُوعًا، وَبَعْضُهُمْ لَمْ يَشْتَرِطْ فِيهِمَا، وَسَحَرَ عِنْدَ الْجَمِيعِ إِنْ كَانَ ظَرْفًا مُعَيَّنًا.
text.en: In the like of Hind both ways are allowed, unlike Zaynab, Saqar [Hell] and Balkh. Like ʿUmar, among Tamīm, is the pattern of Ḥadhām, if it does not end in rāʾ, as Safār; and ams “yesterday”, for a particular day, if it is marfūʿ; some of them do not set these conditions in either. And saḥar “dawn” [is like ʿUmar] among all, if it is an adverb for a particular [dawn].

lessons.title: Wonder (taʿajjub)
body: Wonder has two forms. The first is mā afʿala Zaydan: mā aḥsana Zaydan, “how fine Zayd is!”. Its iʿrāb: mā means “something”; afʿala is a past verb whose doer is a pronoun hidden in it, referring to mā; Zaydan is its object; and the sentence is the predicate of mā. So the meaning is “something has made Zayd fine”. Most copies of the book add that mā is a subject meaning “a great thing”; our print has only “in the sense of something”.

The second is afʿil bihi: aḥsin bi-Zaydin, with the same meaning. It looks like a command but is not one. “Its origin is afʿala”, “he came to have such a quality”, as aghadda al-baʿīru, “the camel came to have a gland”; so aḥsana Zaydun, “Zayd came to have fineness”. Then the wording was changed into the form of the command, and a bāʾ was added to the doer “to set the wording right”, since a command form with a noun in rafʿ after it would be strange.
For that reason the bāʾ is necessary here, “unlike [the bāʾ] in the doer of kafā”: in kafā bi-llāhi shahīdan, “God suffices as a witness” (Q 4:79), the bāʾ is added but may be left out, kafā Allāhu.

The two verbs of wonder, and the elative of lesson 40, are made only from a verb that is triliteral; affirmed, not negated; admitting of degrees, so not from verbs like māta, “died”; complete, so not from kāna; active, not passive; and whose active participle is not on the pattern afʿal, the pattern of colours and bodily defects. Where a verb fails, the wonder is made with another verb before its maṣdar, as later books show.

the two forms of wonder
admitting of degrees: a condition of the verb of wonder

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of mā aḥsana Zaydan as the book gives it.
tasks.answer: Mā: in the sense of “something”, the subject. Aḥsana: a past verb, its doer a pronoun hidden in it referring to mā. Zaydan: its object, in naṣb. The sentence aḥsana Zaydan is the predicate of mā.

tasks.prompt: Why is the bāʾ necessary in aḥsin bi-Zaydin, but not in kafā bi-llāhi shahīdan?
tasks.answer: In aḥsin bi-Zaydin, Zayd is the doer of a past verb changed into the form of a command; the bāʾ was added to set the wording right, so it cannot be left out. In kafā bi-llāhi the bāʾ is only added to the doer, and kafā Allāhu is also said.

tasks.prompt: Why can no verb of wonder be made directly from māta or from kāna?
tasks.answer: Māta does not admit of degrees: one is not more dead than another. Kāna is incomplete, needing a predicate. The verb of wonder needs a complete verb that admits of degrees.

quiz.explanation: Mā afʿala and afʿil bihi.

text.original: التَّعَجُّبُ لَهُ صِيغَتَانِ: مَا أَفْعَلَ زَيْدًا، وَإِعْرَابُهُ: مَا بِمَعْنَى شَيْءٍ، وَأَفْعَلَ فِعْلٌ مَاضٍ فَاعِلُهُ ضَمِيرٌ عَائِدٌ عَلَى مَا، وَزَيْدًا مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ، وَالْجُمْلَةُ خَبَرُ مَا.
text.en: Wonder (taʿajjub) has two forms. mā afʿala Zaydan “how [very] … Zayd is!”. Its iʿrāb: mā in the sense of “something”; afʿala a past verb, whose fāʿil is a pronoun referring to mā; Zaydan a mafʿūl bihi; and the sentence the khabar of mā.

text.original: وَأَفْعِلْ بِهِ، وَهُوَ بِمَعْنَى مَا أَفْعَلَهُ، وَأَصْلُهُ أَفْعَلَ، أَيْ صَارَ ذَا كَذَا، كَأَغَدَّ الْبَعِيرُ، أَيْ صَارَ ذَا غُدَّةٍ، فَغُيِّرَ اللَّفْظُ، وَزِيدَتِ الْبَاءُ فِي الْفَاعِلِ لِإِصْلَاحِ اللَّفْظِ، فَمِنْ ثَمَّ لَزِمَتْ هَهُنَا، بِخِلَافِهَا فِي فَاعِلِ كَفَى.
text.en: And afʿil bi-hi, which has the sense of mā afʿalahu. Its origin is afʿala, that is, he came to have such [a quality], as aghadda al-baʿīru, that is, the camel came to have a [swollen] gland. Then the wording was changed, and the bāʾ was added to the fāʿil to set the wording right; and for that reason it is necessary here, unlike [the bāʾ] in the fāʿil of kafā.

text.original: وَإِنَّمَا يُبْنَى فِعْلَا التَّعَجُّبِ وَاسْمُ التَّفْضِيلِ مِنْ فِعْلٍ ثُلَاثِيٍّ مُثْبَتٍ مُتَفَاوِتٍ تَامٍّ مَبْنِيٍّ لِلْفَاعِلِ، لَيْسَ اسْمُ فَاعِلِهِ أَفْعَلَ.
text.en: The two verbs of wonder and the elative are formed only from a verb that is triliteral, affirmed, admitting of degrees, complete and built for the doer, whose active participle is not [on the pattern] afʿal.

lessons.title: The pause, writing the final alif, and the hamza of connection
body: The book ends with how words are said at a stop and how some are written. In a pause (waqf), in the most correct usage, raḥmatun becomes raḥmah, with a hāʾ; muslimātun becomes muslimāt, keeping the tāʾ; qāḍin, “a judge”, in rafʿ and jarr becomes qāḍ, without its yāʾ; al-qāḍī keeps the yāʾ. The reverse is also heard in each. In naṣb there is only the yāʾ: qāḍiyā, al-qāḍī.

Idhan, la-nasfaʿan, “We shall surely seize” (Q 96:15), and the tanwīn of naṣb in raʾaytu Zaydan are paused on with an alif, idhā, la-nasfaʿā, Zaydā, “as they are written”. An alif is written after the wāw of the group, qālū, “they said”, but not after a wāw that belongs to the root, Zaydun yadʿū, “Zayd calls”.

A final alif is written as yāʾ if it is beyond the third letter, istadʿā, “he summoned”, al-muṣṭafā, “the chosen”, or if it comes from a yāʾ, ramā, “he threw”, al-fatā; otherwise as alif, ʿafā, “he pardoned”, al-ʿaṣā, “the stick”. To find the origin, add the tāʾ to the verb, ramaytu, ʿafawtu, and make the noun dual, ʿaṣawayni, fatayayni.

The hamza of connection (hamzat al-waṣl) is said at the beginning and dropped in connected speech. It is found in the nouns ismun, istun, ibnun, ibnumun, ibnatun, imruʾun and imraʾatun and their duals, in ithnāni and ithnatāni, in aymun Allāhi, “by God”, and in the al- of al-ghulām. It takes a kasra, or a kasra or ḍamma in ismun, and a fatḥa in al- and aymun. In verbs it is in the past of more than four letters, istakhraja, its command and its maṣdar; and in the command of the triliteral, with a ḍamma where the third letter has one, uqtul, ughzu, ughzī, and with a kasra elsewhere, iḍrib, imshū, idhhab.

terms.en: the pause: how a word is said at a stop
the hamza of connection: said at the start, dropped in connected speech
the final alif written as yāʾ

examples.en: raʾaytu Zaydan: paused on as Zaydā, with an alif
qālū with an alif after the wāw; yadʿū without
ramā, from a yāʾ, written with yāʾ; ʿafā, from a wāw, with alif
the hamza of connection in verbs

grid.caption: The pause in the most correct usage (pp. 44–45)
head: Word
In a pause

tasks.prompt: How is each paused on: raḥmatun; muslimātun; qāḍin in rafʿ; raʾaytu Zaydan?
tasks.answer: Raḥmah, with a hāʾ; muslimāt, with the tāʾ; qāḍ, dropping the yāʾ; Zaydā, with an alif, as it is written.

tasks.prompt: Why is ramā written with a yāʾ and ʿafā with an alif? How can you tell?
tasks.answer: The final alif of a three-letter verb is written as yāʾ if it comes from a yāʾ, as alif if it comes from a wāw. Adding the tāʾ shows the origin: ramaytu (yāʾ), ʿafawtu (wāw).

tasks.prompt: Which vowel does the hamza of connection take in uqtul and in iḍrib, and why?
tasks.answer: In uqtul a ḍamma, because the third letter (the tāʾ) has a ḍamma; in iḍrib a kasra, because the third letter (the rāʾ) has a kasra.

quiz.prompt: In the most correct usage, raḥmatun is paused on as…
quiz.explanation: With a hāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Muslimātun is paused on…
quiz.explanation: Muslimāt: the tāʾ is kept.

quiz.prompt: In the naṣb of qāḍin, the pause has…
quiz.explanation: Qāḍiyā: the yāʾ is kept in naṣb.

quiz.prompt: Raʾaytu Zaydan is paused on as…
quiz.explanation: As it is written, with the alif.

quiz.prompt: An alif is written after the wāw in…
quiz.explanation: Only after the wāw of the group.

quiz.prompt: Al-muṣṭafā is written with a yāʾ because…
options: its alif is beyond the third letter
quiz.explanation: Istadʿā likewise.

quiz.prompt: The hamza of connection in uqtul has a ḍamma because…
options: the first letter has a ḍamma
the third letter has a ḍamma
quiz.explanation: Iḍrib has a kasra: its third letter has one.

text.original: الْوَقْفُ فِي الْأَفْصَحِ عَلَى نَحْوِ رَحْمَةٍ بِالْهَاءِ، وَعَلَى نَحْوِ مُسْلِمَاتٍ بِالتَّاءِ، وَعَلَى نَحْوِ قَاضٍ رَفْعًا وَجَرًّا بِالْحَذْفِ، وَنَحْوِ الْقَاضِي فِيهِمَا بِالْإِثْبَاتِ، وَقَدْ يُعْكَسُ فِيهِنَّ، وَلَيْسَ فِي نَصْبِ قَاضٍ وَالْقَاضِي إِلَّا الْيَاءُ.
text.en: In the most correct usage, the pause is made on the like of raḥmatin “mercy” with the hāʾ [raḥmah]; on the like of muslimātin “Muslim women” with the tāʾ [muslimāt]; on the like of qāḍin “a judge”, in rafʿ and jarr, by dropping [the yāʾ: qāḍ]; and on the like of al-qāḍī “the judge”, in both, by keeping it. It may be the reverse in all of these; and in the naṣb of qāḍin and al-qāḍī there is only the yāʾ.

text.original: وَيُوقَفُ عَلَى إِذًا وَنَحْوِ: لَنَسْفَعًا، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا بِالْأَلِفِ، كَمَا يُكْتَبْنَ. وَتُكْتَبُ الْأَلِفُ بَعْدَ وَاوِ الْجَمَاعَةِ كَقَالُوا، دُونَ الْأَصْلِيَّةِ كَزَيْدٌ يَدْعُو.
text.en: One pauses on idhan “then”, on the like of la-nasfaʿan “We shall surely seize” [96:15] and on raʾaytu Zaydan “I saw Zayd” with the alif [idhā, la-nasfaʿā, Zaydā], as they are written. The alif is written after the wāw of the group, as qālū “they said”, but not after an original [wāw], as Zaydun yadʿū “Zayd calls”.

text.original: وَتُرْسَمُ الْأَلِفُ يَاءً إِنْ تَجَاوَزَتِ الثَّلَاثَةَ كَاسْتَدْعَى وَالْمُصْطَفَى، أَوْ كَانَ أَصْلُهَا الْيَاءَ كَرَمَى وَالْفَتَى، وَأَلِفًا فِي غَيْرِهِ كَعَفَا وَالْعَصَا. وَيَنْكَشِفُ أَمْرُ أَلِفِ الْفِعْلِ بِالتَّاءِ كَرَمَيْتُ وَعَفَوْتُ، وَالِاسْمِ بِالتَّثْنِيَةِ كَعَصَوَيْنِ وَفَتَيَيْنِ.
text.en: The alif is written as yāʾ if it goes beyond the third [letter], as istadʿā “he summoned” and al-muṣṭafā “the chosen one”, or if its origin is the yāʾ, as ramā “he threw” and al-fatā “the young man”; and as alif in the others, as ʿafā “he pardoned” and al-ʿaṣā “the stick”. The case of the alif of the verb is shown by the tāʾ, as ramaytu “I threw” and ʿafawtu “I pardoned”, and [that] of the noun by the dual, as ʿaṣawayni “two sticks” and fatayayni “two young men”.

text.original: هَمْزُ اسْمٍ بِكَسْرٍ وَضَمٍّ، وَاسْتٍ، وَابْنٍ، وَابْنُمٍ، وَابْنَةٍ، وَامْرِئٍ، وَامْرَأَةٍ، وَتَثْنِيَتِهِنَّ، وَاثْنَيْنِ، وَاثْنَتَيْنِ، وَالْغُلَامِ، وَايْمُنِ اللَّهِ فِي الْقَسَمِ بِفَتْحِهِمَا، أَوْ يُكْسَرُ فِي ايْمُنِ اللَّهِ، هَمْزَةُ وَصْلٍ، أَيْ تَثْبُتُ ابْتِدَاءً وَتُحْذَفُ وَصْلًا.
text.en: The hamza of ismin “name” — with kasra or ḍamma —, of istin “buttocks”, ibnin “son”, ibnumin “son”, ibnatin “daughter”, imriʾin “man” and imraʾatin “woman”, and of their duals, of ithnayni and ithnatayni “two”, of al-ghulāmi “the boy”, and of aymun Allāhi “by God” in the oath — with fatḥa in these two, or it takes a kasra in aymun Allāhi —, is a hamza of connection, that is, it stands at the beginning and is dropped in connected speech.

text.original: وَكَذَا هَمْزَةُ الْمَاضِي الْمُتَجَاوِزِ لِأَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ كَاسْتَخْرَجَ، وَأَمْرِهِ وَمَصْدَرِهِ، وَأَمْرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ كَاقْتُلْ وَاغْزُ وَاغْزِي بِضَمِّهِنَّ، وَاضْرِبْ وَامْشُوا وَاذْهَبْ بِكَسْرِهِنَّ. تَمَّتْ.
text.en: And likewise the hamza of a past verb of more than four letters, as istakhraja “he brought out”, of its imperative and of its maṣdar; and of the imperative of the triliteral, as uqtul “kill!”, ughzu “raid!” and ughzī “raid! (f.)”, with ḍamma in these, and iḍrib “hit!”, imshū “walk! (pl.)” and idhhab “go!”, with kasra in these. The end.
